div.p: COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER.

BYE-LAWS for providing Rear Lights on Vehicles using the Streets, Highways or Roads in the ADMINISTRATIVE COUNTY OF CHESTER (excepting the Municipal Boroughs situate therein). IVOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the following -LI Bye-laws roltde by the Cheshire County Council, at a meeting held at Chester Castle on Saturday, the 15th day of March, 1913, under Section 5 (3) of the Lights on Vehicles Act, 1907, not having been objected to will come into operation on the date mentioned therein, i.e., Ist July, 1913, viz. : REAR LIGHTS ON VEHICLES.

L (1) Every person who shall cause or permit any vehicle to be in any street, high‘‘ay, or road, to which the public have access, during the period between one hour after smnset and one hour before sunrise, besides complying with requirements of the Lights on Vehicles Act, 1907, shall provide such vehicle either (a) with a lamp (or lamps) in proper working order, and so con- structed and capable of being so attached as when lighted to show to the rear a red light visible for a reasonable distance; or (b) with a reflector (or reflectors) at least LI inches wide, so constructed and capable of being so attached to such vehicle as to I reflect a red light from a light carried by a vehicle approaching from behind. If only one lamp or reflector is provided, it shall ha placed on the off or right side of the vehicle, or if such vehicle is used for the purpose of drawing behind it any other vehicle or load, on the off or right side of such other vehicle or load. _ _ _ _ _

(2) Every person driving or being in charge of such vehicle in any street, highway or road, to which the public have access during the period as aforesaid, 8811 seep such lamp or lamps properly attached and properly trimmed and lighted or such reflector or reflectors properly attached and in such condition as to reflect a red light. DEFINITION.
2. The expression " vehicle " in these Bye-laws shall mean every vehicle, machine or implement to which the Lights on Vehicles Act, 190 r, applies. EXTENT AND COMMENCEMENT OF BYE-LAWS.

_ 3. These Bye-laws shall have effect and be in force in the whole of the Administrative County of Chester, except in such parts as are comprised within any Municipal Borough, and shall come into force on the Ist day of July, 1913. PENALTY.

4. If any person offends against these Bye-laws he shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding Forty Shillings, and in the case of a second or subsequent conviction to a penalty not exceeding Five Pounds. Provided that if a person driving or being in charge of a vehicle is charged with an offence against these Bye- laws, he shall not be convicted thereof if be proves to the satisfaction of the Court that such offence arose through the neglect or default of some other person whose duty it was to provide the vehicle with a lamp or lamps or retlectnr or. reflectors. IiFIGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 3rd May, 1913.

THE INSURANCE ACT AND DOMESTIC SERVANTS.

-- Sir,—The ignorance (in some cases, I fear, wilful ignorance) which still prevails in regard to the bedefits of the Insurance Act so far as domestic servants are concerned, is a3tonishing. A few days ago a number of ladies were discussing the question, and no less than four of them asserted positively that no domestic servant could obtain the is. 6d. per week sickness benefit unless and until she had left or been turned out of her place in consequence of her illness. In other words, that a kindly oisposed and humane mistress who desired to give her sick servant the benefit of some measure of personal nursing and kindly attention and suitable food, in her own home, could only do it at the cost to the servant of the loss of her sick benefit allowance of is. Gd. per week. There is not the shadow of foundation for any such statement, and in proof of this fact I beg to refer your readers to the official explanatory leaflet note, issued by the National Health Insurance Commission and headed" Domestic Servants" as follows : "If contributions have been paid at the ordinary rate, the fact that the servant is being kept in her mistress's house when she is ill and is paid wages during sickness, will not take away her right to sick PIT" Further comment is needless.—Yours &c., THE CHAIRMAN of the Medical Benefits Sub- committee of the Warrington Insurance Committee.

CO-OPERATIVE STORES AND POVERTY. Sir,— Mr. Morton, as a politician and economist, is a study, for I think it is perfectly clear to anyone read- ing his letter that all we have to do io abolish poverty is to do all that Mr. Morton says we ought to do. One thing I think we all shall agree with him in is that, as far as possible we should display our in- dividual initiative. And, by waY of using a little of that excellent quality, I might say that lam not going to look to the Liberal party, as he suggests, to solve the poverty problem. Whether I might seem a stodgy thinker, as Mr. Morton infers or not, or lack a display of initiative I have abandoned hope from any political party as at present constituted much sooner in life than Mr. Morton. I have so far advanced in this direction as to believe that any person looking to the Liberal, Tory, Labour or Socialist parties to cure poverty does Dot understand either economics or politics. By way of preliminary cross-examination I would ask Mr. Morton if he believes that povetty will be cured without the mass of the people taking some hand in it.: I will give Mr. Morton credit for enough intelligence to know that no political or economic reform has ever been accomplished without there has been a large demand for it coming from the people. Whether there has been a Liberal or Tory Government in office has been immaterial. If that has been the ease it must of necessity follow that if poverty is going to be tackled we look to the mass of the people to tackle it. In the first place a good•number of people asserted that if only the workers had a voice in the government of the country things would be soon straightened out. They got the vote and a few, I must admit, beneficial social reforms. Matters then lulled a little while, and it dawned upon some of the people that riches were being piled up upon one side of the social scale, and got ,no bigger upon the other side. Alter some exhaustive study, a few of the people said that inequality in the distribution of wealth was due to the private ownership of the source of wealth ; therefore, as a constitutional people, we must get men in Parlia- ment who will steadfastly work for the emancipation of the worker. I just mention these facts to •draw Mr. Morton's attention to the fact that these efforts, not as successful as we would like, are the outcome of the energy of some of the workingmen. And I again say, to emphasise my point, that the person who attempts to ridicule these efforts does not understand either economic or political evolution. Perhaps some of us have taken up these ideas with enthusiasm, which subsequent events have not justified. But some of us are quite prepared to admit our mis- takes. For myself, I can now see that the Labour party is stifled by those who benefit by the poverty of the masses whether they call themselves Liberal or Tory. I can also see that if the Socialist theory is going to be any use to the mass of people they will have to understand Socialism. That means hard labourious years of education. Therefore I think it quite a feasible suggestion to ask the " Co-op " to take a hand in the education of the .people in the causes and remedy of poverty. I would ask Mr. Morton to believe me when I say , that I would not be a party to any scheme which would unduly, advertise one party over another. I think I know enough to believe that there are persons outside Socialist and Labour organisations who wish to see a better state of things than at present ex;sts. Therefore I would welcome at any conference any suggestion being brought to light that would assist in the enlightenment of us all. With the kind permission of the Editor of the "Examiner," I suggest that Mr. Morton and myself add a little contribution tlr way of discussion. And by way of opening out a discussion I assert :- 1. That the Liberal party cannot solve the poverty problem. 2. That Mr. Morton's unemployed scheme is

HOUSING OF THE WORKING CLASSES BILL. Sir,—Will you allow me a short space in your valuable newspaper in which to draw the attention of your readers to the heartbreaking manner in which the Housing of the Working Classes Bill has been treated in a Committee of the House of Commons. There is no question which is more pressing than t'la housing of our fellow-countrymen, and if this Bill had been introduced by a Radical or a Labour man all true social ref, rmers would have been quite as zealous to see it passed into law. There is no need to enlarge on the question, for most of us know how the present state of affairs leads to over-crowded dwellings and increasing slums, and consequently to a general rise of the death rate and poor rate. aud the spreading of discontent, disease, and immorality. Horses are, to-day in many cases, better stabled than are housed the helpless, unorganised poor of this wealthy country. Here, shortly, are the facts with regard to this Bill. Last year Sir Arthur Boscswen, Unionist M.P. for Dudley, and this year Sir Randolf Baker, Unionist M.P. for North Dorset, introduced a Housing Bill : (1) Proposing what would be practically an independent standing Housing Commission ; (2) giving the Local Government Board power to act in default of local authorities in cases where local authorities were held to be wilfully negligent of their duties ; (3) granting State aid to enable local authorities to deal more effectually with the difficult problem. Almost all housing reformers are agreed that with a few amendments the Bill would have been excellent, and in fact it was supported by almost the unanimous Unionist Press, several Liberal papers and the Labour Press as an honest attempt to try to deal with a national esil. Mr. John Burns, however, on May Ist, speaking for the Government refused to provide for the finance of the measure, and accordingly it has bad to be withdrawn. How far political capital or personal vanity or mere obstinacy were respcnsible for this direct hostility to the Bill only the Cabinet can tell, but certainly it has disputed many men, who care more for remedying social evils than for mere party scores. These are the opinions of three supporters of the Government on their action. Mr. Jowett, Labour M.P. for Bradford, voiced his disgust in these words: "The President of the Local Government Board, on behalf of the Government, had refused to do on a small scale for the workingmen of England and Wales that which they had done on a large scale in Ireland. He was hanging the door upon a scheme for improving the lot of the poor people who were housed in slums in this country." Mr. Chiozsa Money, Liberal M.P. for E. Northants, " claimed that the solution of the housing problem should be pro- ceeded with on the lines of the Bill." Mr. Atherley Jones, Liberal M.P. for N.W. Durham, "as a Liberal and a supporter of the Government expressed pro- found regret at the course pursued." All these strong protests were, of course, of no avail against the decision of the Cabinet, and the poor, about whom Cabinet Ministers construct glowing perorations, must continue to lack adequate sanitation, fresh air and sunlight. As the Government apparently will not move unless direct political capital can be obtained, it must be left to private individuals to make it clear that the Etousing Act of 1909 has not solved tbe problem. Surely men of different denominations and palitics will join in rousing public opinion by correspondence to local papers, by town-planning lectures, by asking Trades Unions to discuss the problem, by general pressure upon the public mind to appreciate the evils of bad and insufficient housing. I3y such means we shall compel legislative reform to be introduced.— Yours, etc., B. S. TOWNROE.
May 7th, 1913, Warrington. -- OXFORD DIVINITY DEGREES.

Sir,—lt would seem from a paragraph in your last issue that the attitude of the opposing majority in Convocation has been misinterpreted. They did indeed wish to maintain a "test," but the test was not Churchrnanship, it was Christianity. The object was not to score a triumph for the Church at the expense of Nonconformity, as seems to be the impression. It was to provide that every graduate in Divinity sl.iould be a Christian, and not merely a student of religions. So at least I gather from the antecedent newspaper correspondence. Their opposition may have been open to misinterpretation. But their action was made necetpary by the form in which the proposed Statute was drawn up. It was so worded as to admit Buddhists, for example; and this was felt to be anomalous. It is conceivable that in mathematics a man might take a firt class while yet regarding mathematics in his heart as a form of low cunning or as a study tending to the extinction of every noble thought (as Lunartine somewhere expresses it). But one can hardly blame those who resent the possibility of Divinity being treated after a similar fashion, its subject matter being what it is. To com- pare great things with small, the case is as though a convinced Tariff Reformer should win a prize for an essay upon the blessings of Free Trade, or vice versa, counting his own convictions for nothing, but just wishing to show that he knew both ' sides of tne question. It would not be wrong, but it would be anomalous. The man's own friends would jeer at him. It is indeed argued that the University's business is not to define Christianity in any way, or to say who is a Christian and who is not. This argument would have weight if the University were merely an examining body. But Oxford stands for a great deal more than that; as everybody knows. However, let but the statute be re-drafted with certain safeguards, and the opposition will cease, or at least be minimised, so long as " sacra " is retained before " theologia." The expression "country clergymen" is so used as to imply an element of rusticity. But there were probably as many from town as from country in the opposing majority ; and there were laymen in it its well, as clergymen. For instance, Lord Halifax, though he may be an "ecclesiastically-minded layman," is at all events not a country clergyman. And it should be further remembered that a certain proportion of the provincial clergy have themselves been Fellows and Tutors, so that they at least would know practically as much about the matter in hand as the residents. Meanwhile those who feel aggrieved (and whdcannot be satisfied with the D. Litt., which already meets their case) have their own remedy. They can leave Oxford severely alone and go to Cambridge instead. Yours,&c. L. J. T. DAR WALL, Walton Vicarage, Warrington.

The Joy of Life.

Preaching from St. Paul's words "Rejoice in the I Lord " (Philippians iii., 1), the Rev. H. Williamson, I 8.A., said that it. had been proclaimed for centuries that the aim of life ought to he happiness. The Puritanical mind found this idea distasteful, but the Puritans failed to find the goodness thst the gospel of happiness contained. It testified to the undying instinct in human nature that life could not he separated from happiness. This instinct had asserted itself in a variety of ways in human history. Both Christ and His disciples reverenced the demand for the existence of pleasure in life. Our Saviour lived no gloomy, ascetic life and His presence proved no bar to the festivities attendant upon a wedding celebration. The same note is sounded in the teaching of the Apostles, and joy ever held a Lirge place in their lives. But if Christ and the Apostles sympathised, their message was not simply Be happy." There were many ideas in their teaching which were contrary to this. Jesus demanded that man must he prepared to take up his cross, and vt hen writing his epistle Paul was a prisoner. The significance of this contradiction of ideas was siraplytthat Christ mightily enlarged the capacity for joy, and in the midst of unpleasantness, enabled the Christian to possess joy and gladness in the heart. Juy no longer depended upon health, success, or worldly prosperity but arose from the supernatural happiness which Christ gave to the heart. It is a complete misnomer to term Christianity "the religion of sorrow." There was not one word of despondency or gloom in the Gospel and true Christianity %4 BS only to be found in the joyful conception of life.

div.head: St. George's Mission.
div.p: St. George's Mission.

The sale of work in connection with St. George's Mission, Hopwood-street, vt as held in the Gymnasium, on Saturday afternoon and evening. The object was to liquidate the debt on the organ and form the nucleus of a chancel fund. There was a large attendance at the opening of the s.tle by Mrs. Arthur Bleckly, of Thelwall. The Rev. J. M. Buckmaster presided. Those present included Canon and Mrs. Willis, Canon Steven- son, the Rev. T. Vickers, the Rev. J. 11. G. 'lolling- worth, Mrs. Rylands (Massey Hall), Mrs. J. Charlton Parr, Miss Parr, Mrs. and Miss Buckmaster (Hindley Vicarage), Mrs. Seeker, the Misses White, Mr. Darby and the Mission sidssmen.

The following ladies and gentlemen were in charge of the stalls and other departments :—General stall (1) : The Misses White, Ales Baldwin. Mrs. Bolton, Mrs. Boyle, Mrs. Ball, anl Mrs. Neilson. General stall (2) : Mrs. Knight, Mrs. Harbourne and Mrs. Cook. Refreshment stall : Mrs. Hackett and Miss Wood.

Fancy work : The Misses Bradshaw, Harrop end M. and V. Sumner. Handkerchief stall: The Misses M. Knight and J. Lewis. Fruit and flower stall : The Misses M. Knight and J. Lewis. Fruit and flower stall : The Misses Pneir and P. Sumner. Sweets end ice cream : The Misses Griffith and Cooper. Bran tub : The Misses A. Knight and L. Bibby. Burlesque gipsy tent: Miss Millington. Shooting range competition and other amusements : Messrs. Peake, Gardiner, T. and F. Hackett, W.Buckley end H. Plinston and Miss H. Allen. Tea rooms : The Misses Bowles and Elosler, assisted by the Misses Bellis, D. Cook, F. Cook, Coughlan, A. Harrop, Houghton, Isherwood, Hughes, Tickle, Shaw, Massey and Witton. Songs and a sketch were given by Mrs..Tohnson, the Misses Ross and Hackett, toe Misses Lewis, Miller, Peake, Gardiner and Sumner, with Mr. J. Fratigleton as M.C. Two companies of children,who had been trained by Mrs. Cox and the Misses Ross, gave a pleasing entertainment. The proceeds of the sale amounted to 185.

div.p: Buckley-street P.S.A: Society.

The monthly meeting of the above society was held on Sunday, Mr. J. Adams presiding. rill speaker was Mr. Waddell, of Liverpool. The soloist, Iliss M. Jones, was beard to advantage in "The beautiful prayer" and "Beyond.' Miss Lee was the accompanist.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

Anniversary services in connection with Silver-street Wesleyan Sunday school were held on Sunday in the Bewsey—road ‘Vesleyan Church. The preacher. as is usual on these occasiccs, was the Rev. J. Grange Bennett, whose discourses were much appreciated. A musical service was held in the afternoon, and an address was given by Nlrs. Wheatley, of Latchford. Mr. James Povey presided. Special music was rendered at each service by the children and choir, under the con- ductorship of Mr. W. Hipkiss. Mr. W. Pearce presided at the organ.

div.head: Latuford Baptist Girls' Guild –
div.p: Latuford Baptist Girls' Guild -

A public demonstration and concert was given by members of the Guild 1.-ist week. Mrs. John Fair- hurst (President of the Guild) presided over a large sad enthusiastic audience. The programme included choruses, solos, action-songs and recitations. Two very amusing and well-rehearsed sketches were among the most popular items ; and the musical drill, for which the teams had been trained by Miss Amy Grounds, was most efficiently performed. The girls made a charming appearance in their white frocks and shoulder-sashes of broad scarlet ribbon. The whole function reflected the greatest credit on the ladies in charg3 of the Guild, who have been able to accomp iah so much in the short time since it originated seven

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

There was a good meeting on Sunday. presided over by Mr. B. Farrar who spoke briefly upon " Personal responsibility." Rev. I'. T. &Ines took for bis:subject "Vv hat we meet or stand for." They looked upon their meetings as religious, for they met to learn of Christ the great. Teacher, the great Light to lighten up their lives. Their meeting taught them to work and the importance of consecration. He had noticed in the best rooms in many homes beautiful brass tire orna- ments which were not for use, hot were kept bright, an old poker being used for the fire. Our lives were not to be simply polished up, but to be of practica use to ourselves and to others. Mr. Joynson read the lesson, the Chairman led the prayer. One new member wet; welcomed.

div.head: Brick- street Mission.
div.p: Brick- street Mission.

The May sermons were held on Sunday. Mr. Crumblehulrue, of Southport, being the preacher for the da3. At the children's service in the morning Florrie Barton sang very sweetly "Lord we children come to Thee." In the afternoon Alderman Burton presided over a mmical service. The choir gave " Witty's cantata, "From Manger to Cross„' with admirable effect. The attack in the heavy choruses was excellent and in the lighter part of the work they sang with much expression and finish. The solos, duets and quartette were rendered with taste and skill by the Misses Eva Saaw, E. Savory, E. Lightfoot, Alice Herding, E. Davies and E. Barton, Messrs. Jas. Tomkinson, W. Barton, jun., H. Lightfoot, and A. Morris. Mr. A. Trow, at the piano, accompanied with excellent taste. Mr. W. Tomkinsun presided at the organ with his usual ability. At the evening service Mr. Crumblehulme preached to a very large congregation. Mr. T. Goostry sang " Sun of my Soul" with fine effect. The choir also interpreted the anthem Abide with me," (Dunstor) in a very devotional manner.

div.head: St. Barnabas' Church Sale of Work. For Extension and Curacy Fund.
div.p: St. Barnabas' Church Sale of Work. For Extension and Curacy Fund.

A two days' sale of work in aid of the Church Exten- sion and Curacy Fund in connection with St. Barnabas Church, was opened in the Patten Hall on Wednesday afternoon by Mr. James Fairclough. The VICAR (ttev. J. G. Hollingworth), referring to prejudices against sales of work, said he would be extremely sorry if such functions were abolished by Act of Parliament or the Ecclesiastical Law, because in a c‘rtain way, they did a vast amount of good. They brought the workers together and each member of the congregation gained more knowledge of the needs of the parish. Then, again, money given in goods was as good as gold or silver, for the goods were turned into cash at the finish and often realised 50 per cent profit United effort for a given object made each worker fee that he or she was of some value to the church and which also tended to create a feeling of friendliness and neighbourliness. If worked in a right way it showed the world the spirit of Jesus Christ. (Applause.) Mrs. FAIRCLOUGII, in declaring the sale open, wished the members of the congregation every success in their efforts.

The Rev. G. A. COUPE (curate) proposed a vote of thanks to Mr,. Fairclough. He supposed it was gener- ally believed that sales of work were an evil, but they were a necessary evil. Especially were they necessary in a working parish like tueir own, where the people were better_able to give their labour and small gifts than large cheques to help in the upkeep of the church. He had never come across a body of workers who worked for a church so well, faithfully and loyally as those at St. Barnabas. (Applause.) Mr. W. BOYLE seconded and the vote was heartily carried.

The following were the stall-holders :—Work stall (1) Mesdames Shaw, Birchall, Parkinson and Lewis: work stall (2), Mesdames Handles, Tilling, Stringer and Oxley ; work stall (3), Mesdames Westwell, Sutton Howard and Miss F. Bennett; Bible class stall (men , and women's), Mesdamas J. H. E. Hollingworth, T. Oxley and the Misses E. Power. E. Kimberley, E. Sutton and S. Skelhorne, with Mr. B. Dimelow as, secretary ; men's stall, .Mesdames Morgan, T. Evans Hinde and the church officers; toy stall, Mrs. Coupe, and the Misses Bolton, A. Fry and R. Cole; refresh- ment stall, Mesdames Connell, Jones, W. Jones, Green- halgh, Ashley, Green, Mevbrick and the Misses White- house, S. Wnitehouse, Price and Singleton; flower stall, Mrs. Hands and the Misses D. Ingram and C. Ingram ; ice cream stall, Misses Daintith and Eva. Broadhurst; dips, Misses E. Hands and H. Hassell. The sale was re-opened on Thursday by Miss White. who was cordially thanked, on the proposition of the Rev. J. W. Glendenniog (vicar of St. Thomas', St. Helens, and formerly curate of St. Barnabas, seconded by Mr. Mayhew. The total proceeds amounted to £135 9s. 11d., and included donations of £25 from Lady Greenall, £5 each from Miss Parr and Colonel J. Reid Walker, £1 Is each from Councillor Penrhyn and Councillor Peacock, End £1 from Mr. T. S. Steel.

"EVERYONE AGAINST tilm.”—Johri Rigby, tanner, 29, Alexander Pope-street, Liverpool, was sent. to prison for three months with hard labour for running away on December 16th and leaving his wife aud firzi children chargeable to the Union.—Complainant said she had not received anything from her husband since January. She had received 10s. per week from the Union.—Prisoner said he did not seem to get on in Warrington, as everyone seemed to be against him.— The Clerk: You ran away and left your family charge- able.—Prisoner : That is so. I went away to try and better myself and did not intend to keep away. I have ' been tramping about for two months, trying to get work. lam willing to do all I can for her, if I can get work.—ln answer to the Clerk, prisoner said he had not worked since January so he could not send his wife money.—The Chief Constable: He does not want work, anyhow, for two or three weeks at a time. He has been up five times previously. He says everyone else is against him. Really he cannot expect anything else. SPECIAL RESERVIST'S ADVENTURE.—WiIIiam James Millar (19), cotton porter,B4, Whitefteld-road, Liverpool, was remanded until Thursday on a charge of stealing a bicycle value £2 from outside the hairdresser's shop,l9, Padgate-lane, on Saturday.—The Chief Constable said that at 1.30 on Saturday afternoon Mr. Harrison, the prosecutor,went into the hairdresser's shop for a shave, leaving his bicycle outside. Through one of the mirrors in the shop he saw prisoner mount the bicycle and ride away. He telephoned the police and, obtaining another machine, raced after the prisoner who had got to Croft. Here he had offored the machine for sale to Mr. Barton, Heath-lane, Croft, for is. Barton, however, knew that the bicycle belonged to Harrison, hut was unsuccessful in his endeavours to detain prisoner. Eventually Millar was caught and handed over to the Padgate police. Prisoner was on the Special Reserve and had his dinner at the barracks on Saturday. He climbed over the wall and absconded on the stolen bicycle.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN,
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN,
FARMERS' TRIALS.
BAD WEATHER AND UNREST AT HATTON.
Our Hatton correspondent wrote in the earlier part of the week :

The cuckoo has arrived, but his notes sound decidedly in a minor key. Possibly the cold, wet weather has damped his spirits. It certainly has had a very depressing influence on the farming comm unity, many of whom are despairing of getting their spring work done. Scores of acres of land lie drenched, and soaked, and it is impossible to cart manure on to them, or drill the land for potatoes, thousands of boxes of which are awaiting to be planted. It is also high time that turnips and mangels were sown, but, except on the lightest and driest lands those are yet unsown. The only consolation the farmer has is that grass is very plentiful and of good quality. Oats and wheat also look well. In the fruit world, apple and pear blossom seems to be well set, and that of stone fruit is moderate.

A few weeks ago the Irish farm labourers in this neighbourhood struck for an increase of wages, the terms to be .f.,1 a week and an allowance of two pints of beer per day, work to cease at four o'clock on Satur- day. Although not successful, they secured some advance. The farmers contend that, in addition to their wages, they found the men coal and shantys to live in, as well as beer or tea. If they gave the advance they would stop some of these allowances. Most of the farmers, however, raised the wages of the English teamsmen and cowmen a couple of shillings per week all-round, the average wage of th:s elms of men now being one guinea per week, with cottage. It is good sign of the times when masters begin to recognise their men and they will certainly lose nothing by it.

div.head: LANCASHIRE FARMERS ASSOCIATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE FARMERS ASSOCIATION.

At a meeting of the Lancashire Farmers' Associa- tion at Preston, a resolution was passed declaring that as the cost of administering the Tuberculosis Order had to be borne by the local rates the Association considered that the repayment of one-half the com- pensation paid for animals slaughtered under the Tuberculosis Order was quite inadequate, and that the whole of the compensation ehould be defrayed out of national funds. On the question of the indiscriminate slaughter of young calves, Mr. Shedley (Pilling) said calf-rearing would pay in some places and not in others. What was wanted was proper communication between those with calves for sale and those wishing to rear calves. Mr. Whittaker suggested that this could be done by the Board of Agriculture making inquiries from their district correspondents, and issuing leaflets giving the resulting information. A resolution urging the estab- lishment of communication suggested was adopted.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: THE TOWN COUNCIL.
An unusually harmonious meeting deals with many important matters.

div.head: RECORD TRAM PROFITS.
div.p: RECORD TRAM PROFITS.

The meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening was characterised by unusual harmony. There were few subjects of conteni ion, and not a single " scene " occurred. At the instance of Councillor Pemberton, there was another debate on the questi of architects' fees, but it failed to arouse any great degree of interest. Councillor Lashford, whose allega- tions concerning Corporation contracts created some turmoil at a recent meeting, was not present, and the reply which the Chairman of the Health Committee (Alderman James Evans) had prepared to his case as to that committee's method of accepting tenders, was accordingly deferred. The Council unanimously approved a proposition by Councillor Roberts that the slipper baths should, at certain convenient hours, be thrown open to all persons of either sex at a charge of one penny each, inclusive of the use of towels and

soap. The appointment of Dr. G. W. N. Joseph, medical officer of health, was unanimously approved. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided over the meeting and there were also present :—The Deputy- Mayor Alderman W. J. Forshaw), Aldermen J. Smethurst, W. Pierpoint, T. Burton, A. Bennett, W. Bolton, and James Evans, Councillors T. Birtles, H. Robert., W. H. .1. Jenkins, S. Taylor, P. Peacock, E. Cunnington, J. Dickenson, W. J. Wilson, E. Osborne, S. Gough, J. Pemberton, J. Chrimes, J. Wilkinson, J. Hawthorn, J. Shaw, J. Skelland, it. Henrhall, J. T. Locker, J. Halliwell, J. Broadhurst and T. Chantler.
ARCHITECTS' b EES.

COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AGAIN PROTESTS. Councillor PEMBERTON moved an amendment that the recommendation,of the Education Committee sanction- ing the payment of fees to the architects in respect of the quantities for Oakwood Avenue, Parr-street and Oliver-street schools be referred back. He argued that an alteration, which had not received the sanotion of the Council, had been made in the conditions whereby the cost of the proposed new schools had been increased by 12. 6d. per head, and maintained that that was unfair to the other architects who competed. Haying read the minutes relating to the question, he said it was absolutely begging the question—a subterfuge unworthy of a public body and of public life—to say that the matter had been sanctioned by the Council— as no mention of the amcunt appeared in any of the minutes. If the resolution was approved he calculated that it meant the expenditure of an extra £2,0000n the three schools. If the matter went through in its present form and the Council rode roughshod over the protest he contended that there would not be anything like the competition by architects for Council work that was desirable. "If you bind yourselves to this " he declared, "you are binding yourselves to a sohema which may involve £50,000. I implored you before and 1 implore you again not to sign this contract. I tell you that you are making a mistake. The matter has not been carried through according to the conditions publicly advertised, and in the interests of the Corporation and the ratepayers you ought to have further inquiry into this before you pass it." The councillor added that he had left a sick bed in order to make his protest. Alderman BOLTON said Councillor Pemberton's motion was like flogging a dead horse, and he really thought the councillor was in a fog. The resolution to pay the architects fl per cent. for the preparation of quantities on a figure of not more than Ell Vs. per head was put in as a maximum to protect themselves in the event of the plans not being carried out. The sooner Councillor Pemberton found another line of business the better. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS, chairman of the Education Committee, replied to the amendment. He declared that the Education Committee had no desire to conceal one jot or tittle of its business and he regretted that Councillor Pemberton always attributed improper motives to every committee with which he dieagreed. He explained that all the original conditions had been complied with, and that £lO 10s. per hind was not laid down as an amount which should not be exceeded, but was put in the conditions as a desideratum. They had already bad experience that their attempts to drive the economical horse or ass too fast and too far were going to result In considerable extra expense in years to come. They I wished to have schools that were going to be in permanent repair and not in continual disrepiir. The plans had passed-the Board of Education and everything had been sanctioned in due course. The reason why the figure of 11 per cent. was put in was to tie the architects down to the amount of commission that they should receive on the preparation of quantities in the event of the work not being proceeded with. There was, however, an over-riding commission of five per cent., into which the l 1 per cent. would merge if the scheme went forward. Only the mover and seconder voted for the resolution to send back the Education Committee minutes, which were then confirmed. Councillor PEMBERTON requested that the names should be recorded, remarking that the matter would not rest there. Alderman BOLTON: There's nothing to rest, because it has been confirmed by the Town Council and the Board of Education. WORKINGMEN AND THEIR HOUSES. - .

Councillor BROADHURST asked the Chairman of the Finance and Estate Committee: What number of applications had been made by tenants of small houses for loans from the Corporation to enable them to pur- chase their own houses under under the Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, 1899 ? (2) What were the necessary conditions, and what were the amounts which the Corporation would lend, and what interest would be required from workingmen applicants tor loans to purchase the house in which they reside? (3) Would the Finance Committee make it more publicly known that they were prepared to advance money loans to the workingclass tenants of small houses for the purpose of buying their own homes? Councillor WILKINSON replied that one application for a loan had been received, but no advance was made, as the conditions of the Act were not fulfilled. Before making an advance the local authority must be satisfied: (a). That the applicant for the advance was resident or intended to reside in the house, and was not already the proprietor within the meaning of the Act, of a house to which the statutory conditions applied. (b). That the value of the ownership of the house was sufficient. (c). That the title to the ownership was one which an ordinary mortgagee would be willing to accept. (d). That the house was in good sanitary con- dition and good repair. (e). That the repayment to the local authority of tbe advance was secured by an instrument vest- ing the ownership (including any interest already held by the purchaser) in the local authority, sub- ject to the right of redemption by the applicant, but such instrument should not contain anything inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. The Finance Committee were prepared favourably to consider all applications made to them. NEW MEDICAL OFFICER. DR. G. W. N. JOSEPH UNANIMOUSLY APPOINTED.

The Health Committee, having accepted with regret the resignation of Dr. J. Coote Hibbert, Medical Officer of Health, who is taking up a similar position at Black- burn, decided to recommend the appointment of Dr. O. W. N. Joseph, assistant Medical Officer of Health, as his successor. It was further resolved to invite applica- tions for the appointment of an assistant medical officer of health at a salary of £250 per annum, but tha question of fixing the new medical officer's salary was left over. Alderman JAMES EVANS, Chairman of the Health Committee, paid a high tribute to Dr. Hibbert, who, he said, had proved a very diligent, clever and hard- working official. The good influence and effect of Dr. Hibbert's work would be felt in years to come, and those most intimately acquainted with the inner work- ings of the Health Department would appreciate that fact. They would miss the zeal, energy and ability of Dr. Hibbert. The improvements which had been effected within the last six years testified to the doctor's excellent work and worth. The reduced death-rate, and particularly the infantile mortality rate was eloquent on that point. Credit was also due to the staff under Dr. Hibbert's direction for the diminution of the smoke nuisance, for he did not think there was such a density of smoke now as there used to be. The methods which Dr. Hibbert had employed in dealing with the people on persuasive lines had effeaed an improvement in the condition of what was styled a short time ago as slumdom. He wished Dr. Hibbert's work in Blackburn might bees succe..aful and that his relationship with the Council might be as happy as it had been with the Warrington Corporation. (Hear, hear.) He was confident that the , Blackburn Corporation had made a good choice.

DR. HIBBER'rS SUCCESSOR. When Dr. Hibbert's resignation was received the com- mittee at once looked to his deputy as a successor. It was quite true that as deputy medical officer Dr. G. W. N. Joseph had not long been associated with the Council, but long before his appointment to that position he was known to many of them, (Hear, hear.) Dr. Joseph came to them with excellent credentials, and nothing had transpired from the day of his appointment to the present time to shake their great confidence in him, either as regarded his abilities, qualifications for the higher post, or disposition. It had been remarked to him that Dr. Joseph had not been with them long, and

that he was a young man. Well, he was an exceptional young man. (Hear, hear.) From his own experience, observation and association with other public bodies he could affirm that it would be a very difficult thing to place a better man at the head of health affairs in Warrington than Dr. Joseph. SALARY NOT YET FIXED.

The question of fixing the salary had been left over. No medical officer appointed within his experience had had as many matters to deal with as faced the occupant of that position to-day. Medical officers to-day would have to deal with the Incurance Act, sanatorium treat- ment, the tuberculosis dispensary qiustion, and the medical inspection and treatment of school children. The committee asked for the indulgence of the Council that they might fairly consider some of the questions that would arise under those headings, and then they would bring a well-digested recommendation before the Council. When the tuberculous Insurance Act came into force the Local Government Board were insisting upon a special medical officer being appointed at .E5OO per annum. The Mayor satisfied the authorities that in Dr. Ilibbert they had a man of experience who would be able to to deal with the question, and who was in many respects above the average. They had another excellent man in Dr. Joseph. They would, perhaps, have the same difficulty to deal with again, as well as with the dispensary question. In all probability the dispensary would have to deal with the rural districts, including such places as Runcorn. The first figure mentioned was 20,000 people, but they had received an intimation that that figure might amount to 70,000. The medical cfficer would have to direct and manipulate all those things, and he hoped the Council would give a unanimous vote on Dr. Joseph's appointment. Alderman BURTON seconded the minutes and endorsed the remarks of Aldermen Evans in praise of Dr. Ilibbert and the new Medical Officer. Alderman BENNETT raid it must be a source of satis- faction to every humane man to know that as the result of the exertions of the Corporation, led by Dr. Hilahert and backed up by the Health Committee, the infantile death rate had been reduced and the health of the borough promoted to a very considerable extent. There was no nobler work than the continual fight against disease, involving, as it did, not only profes- sional skill but courage, fidelity and self-sacrifice. All those qualities had been exemplified in Dr. Hibbert, I who had brought a kind heart and tasteful dr meanonr to the aid of a very intelligent mind. He might fittingly be described as a statesman among medical officers of health. He (the alderman) willingly recog- nised that some effort had been made to deal with the smike nuisance under Dr. Hibbert's regime. Alderman BOLTON, in supporting the Health Com- mittee's recommendations, said that if they had appointed an outsider to succeed Dr. Ilibbert he would no doubt have brought some ex fads with him. (Laughter.) They had had instances on the Education Committee of the experiments which medical officers liked to make, and he would have been sorry if the committee had appointed a stranger who would no doubt have wished to give them a sample of another class of ideas. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS said Dr. Ilibbert had unquestion- ably ingratiated himself in the affections and respect of all those with whom he bad been associated. They had a high regard, not oniy for the character of his professional work, but. for the man himself, and they were certain he would find as cordial and happy inter- course in Blackburn as he had enjoyed in Warrington. Councillor Roberts went on heartily to endorse tbe appointment of Dr. Joseph, and said that as chairman of the Education Committee he was authorised to state that that body felt very strongly that the way in which Dr. Joseph had carried out the difficult work in connection with the medical examination of children had made him more than a persona grata with the parents. It was a pleasure to support the appointment on personal grounds, for be could not help thinking that Dr. Joseph's close association and relationship with the Mayor had had some measure of influence upon his professional career and personal reputation. Councillor BIRTLES predicted that they would hear more of Dr. Joseph before many ye:a were over. The MAYOR said he looked upon Dr. Hibbert as an ideal medical officer—ideal as a sanitarian and as a man.
The appointment of Dr. JoEeph was unanimously confirmed.
COUNCILLOR LASHFORD'S CHARGES.

Alderman JAMES EVANS expressed regret at the absence of Councillor Lashford, because he had pre- pared a statement in reply to the councillor's charges against the Health Committee in the matter of letting contracts. lie had undertaken to make a statement to the Council and the ratepayers, but he was hesitating to make it in the absence of Councillor Lashford.

Alderman BOLTON: Ob, let it drop. Alderman JAMES EVANS : If the Council thinks I should t ive the explanition-- Councillor BROADHURST : Give it. It is necessary. Alderman JAMES EVANS : My own feel.ng is that I wculd rather read it when Councillor Lashfori is here. Alderman BOLTON: Leave it alone then. Councillor WILKINSON: Read it and have done with

l'• Alderman BOLTON: Dirty linen is best washed in the dark. It can do damage and can do no good. Alderman BURTON also regretted that Councillor Lashford was not prevent. Ho thought the councillor onght to have attended and to have faced the matter out. The way the Health Committee had been treated was very unfair, and the Chairman ought to make hi 3 state- ment at the next Council meeting. The statement was reserved for a ful,ure meeting. A NURSE'S DEATH.

Alderman JAMES EVANS said it was with feelings of regret that he alluded to the record on the private agenda of the death of Nurse Mtilroy. She worked in the typhoid ward et the Aikin-street hospital and had unfortunately fallen victim to the disease. She was a bright and excellent nurse and the committee greatly regretted her death. It was decided to allow the relatives a grant of £lO towards the funeral expenses. He did not propose to say anything further about the resolution, but to leave it absolutely with the Council. Alderman BENNETT and Councillor ROBERTS spoke in feeling terms of the death of Nurse Mulroy, Councillor hoberts suggesting that the Council should place on record its sympathy with the relatives and its high appreciation of the character of the work dune by the deceased nurse. Councillor BROADHURST said the time had arrived when the Health Committee ought not to be in fear and trembling when it wished to make a substantial grant to the relatives of a nurse who died in their service. £lO was, in his opinion, a miserable pittance. If the nurse hid come under th,3 Compensation Act, what would nave been the liability of the Corporation ? He voted against the grant of £lO at the committee meet- ing and suggested £2O. He hoped that if any ot',er case of the kind should unfortunately occur, the committee would see that the grant did not fall short of that amount. Councillor WILSON said they ought not to wait until another nurse died before they granted £2O, but should allow it in this case. Alderman EVANS said that, in view of the expression of opinion, he was willing to withdraw the minute for the substitution of a larger sum. Undoubtedly the life of the nurse had been sacrificed In the service of others. The committee did not. however, wish to overstep what would be agreeable to the Council. It was not for want of charity or kindly feeling. TREES DYING IN THE CEMETERY.

Alderman BENNETT, referring to the Cemetery Com- mittee's inspection of the Cemetery grounds and build- ings; asked whether they noticed that the trees at one end of the Cemetery were in a state of slow decline. He predicted that in a short time they wauld have no trees left, unless something could be done to stop that pro- greksive miasma. Ile attributed it to the smoke flu' sauce. Alderman BOLTON said that unfortunately the Cemetery was composed of sand and, as there was nothing to feed the roots of the trees, they died off when they got too old. "I have been troubled with the complaint myself," added the alderman, amid loud laughter, hastening to add that he was referring to trees which he had planted. Alderman Bennett's talk about smoke and tree planting was all imagination. (Laughter.) RECORD TRAM PROFITS. Alderman SAIETHURST presented the annual report of the Tramways Department, which, he said, had had a record year. The passenger receipts showed an increase of £1,565, bringing up the figure to £22,903. That worked out at Is. Old. per car mile as compared with just under 11d, per car mile four years ago. Each route
Our forefathers neglected their eyes, the present generation
now suffers. Don't neglect yours, CONSULT
JOHNSTON WATSON,
SIGHT TESTING OPTICIAN, 84, BRIDGE STREET, WARRINGTON.
PLEASE NOTE—MB. WATSON attends on Monday and Tuesday from 11 to 4-30; Wednesday 11 to 5-30; Thursday 11 to 1; Friday and Saturday 11 to 5-30. Hours of Business; 9-30 to 7-30. Saturday; 9-30 to 9-30.
Steel Spectacles from 2/6. Rolled Gold from 8/6.

showed a gratifying increase in receipts, and even Sankey and Longford routes showed an increase per car mile of N. and Id. respectively. The other receipts were a little less, as no advertisements were now allowed inside the cars, but the total income had been £23,205, which was an increase or £1,532 over last year. The elpenditure had increased by £1,462 but the net profits had gone up from £2,456 to £2,981, £1,500 of this was to be transferred to the relief of the rates during thu current year and the balance had been carried forward. During the year the car miles had amounted to nearly 450,000, which was an increase of 5,615. The passengers carried were greater by 417,000 and were well over 6,000,000, which gave the average number of journeys per head of the population at 70. The ba!ance in hand after deducting £1,500 due to the rates was £1,820 and the reserve fund amounted to £lO,OOO, while the amount taken to the relief of the rates including that year's contribution was £6,000. Altogether the sum of £17,009 had been earned by the department since the system was opened. Councillor WILKINSON seconded the confirmation of the minutes.
A DANGEROUS CORNER. Councillor JENKTNS said he had been flaked to draw the attention of the committee to the condition of the
curve where the cars turned int() Scbtland-road from the Central Station terminus. A cyclist had an

unpleasant accident there the provions day, and another mishap bad occurred that day. Alderman BENNETT urged the great desirability of providing some hind of shelters at the car terminii. It would be a great publio convenience and would not cost much. As a matter of taste, he objected to any portion of the tramcars being used for advertising purposes, and he thought the municipality, from a !Anse of dignity, ought not to tol2rate it. SUNDAY WORK BY CARMEN. Councillor BROADHURST asked that, in view of the _ _
record scar's trading, favourable. consideration should

be given to the application of the tramway employes for time and a half for Sunc'ay labour, a question which was considered and deferred at the meeting of the committee. Every respectable firm in the town paid their employes such a ra" e for Sunday labour. Alder.nan flouroN said he would be sorry to see the advertisements disappear. Very often in a tramcar they had nothing to do and there was nothing to read. It was a pleasure to see someone advertising somebody's beer or something of that sort. (Laughter.) Councillur DICKENSCqs: called attention to the con- dition of the tramlines in ‘Vinwick-road, which, be said, made it unsafe to drive a horse and conveyance. Alderman SMETHURST said the committee were
making inquiries as to the amount paid for Sunday
work in other towns. As to the stdvertisements on the
csrs, they did nobody any harm and the committee did not feel justified in foregoing the revenue from that source.
WATERWORKS INCOME: INCREASED PROFITS. _Councillor ROBERTS, in proposing the confirmation

of the minutes of the Water Committee, called atten- tion to the Borough Treasurer's report on the revenue and capital accounts of the Water xorks undertaking for the year ending March 31st. He said that in spite of considerably increased exponditur3 on unexpected accounts the net pr, fit had gone up £571, which, con- sidering all the circumstances, was very satisfactory.
LADY BOWLERS. PROPOSAL TO RESERVE A GREEN FOR THEIR USE.

Councillor BROADHURST congratulated the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee on the excellent bowling green which bad been provided at Sankey Bridges. lie wculd like to know whether the con- - mittee would take into consideration the question of allowing the ladies the reserved use of the bowling greens on Tuesday afternoons. Thet/SIAYoR : They can go any time they like. Alderman BOLTON, chairman of the committee, did not suppose the committee would have any objection to the suggestion. They had so many bowling greens that there would be no difficulty in allocating one for that purpose. _ _

Alderman BENNETT did not see why, if it was con- sidered legitimate to spend money on healthy amuse- ments for the male sex, some similar provision should not be made for the ladies. He did not consider bowls the most ideal pursuit for them, but he had no parti- cular objection to it. Would it not be advisable to provide tennis courts for the ladies in smne parts of the town ? If the principle was admitted that it was part of the duty of a municipality V) provide for the recreation of those of its male citizens not able to provide for themselves, they should take a broad view and recognise that women were entitled to considera- tion as well as men. They were doing it gradually at the baths. He regarded the opening of the three bowling greens as a great triumph for the progressive members of the Council. He was surprised and disappointed that the new greens were not opened with befitting dignity and ceremony. He recalled the historic occasion when the foundation stone of the baths extension was laid behind hoardings and no one knew of it except by the merest accident. No arrangements were made for the formal opening of the greens, but he opened one informally. The MAYOR (humorously) : Shame. Aldermau BOLTON: It was a very dry opening. (Laughter.). Councillor LOCKER said the kbabitnnts of the Fair- field Ward appreciated the green provided for thera,but they were anxious to know how the remainder of the land was to be laid on.

Councillor HAWTHORN said he would like to impress upon Alderman 13olton that there was such a ward as Whitecross Ward. They ought to have a green in Lovely-lane. The MAYOR agreed with Alderman Bennett that the opening of the greens was worthy of a more formal an dignified mode of opening, lie knew nothing about them being opened. _

Councillor 'JENKINS said there was a cnnvenient place for a bowling green for the Town Hall Ward bAind the municipal offices. Alderman BOLTON: It is in use. Councillor JENKINS : Nt by the inhabitants. Alderman 13ot.ToN : It is not big enough. Councillor SKELIIORN put in a plea for a recreation ground for the children of Bewsey Ward, which was one of the poorest wards of the town. They should secure land before all the suitable plots were built upon. Alderman BOLTON said so far as the ladies were con- cerned he did not roe why they could allot a bowling green to them for a particular time. Ile was willing that lades should have an opportunity of playing bowls on municipal greens as well as at the Liberal Club. They might just as well play away from the Liberal Club as at it. (Laughter.) The matter re3ted with tke committee. With reference to the question of a green in the Whitecross Ward, the committee would know what to do as soon as they knew definitely how muc'a of the land was required for the new school. Replying to the criticisms regarding the opening of the bowling greens, he recalled what took place when he (the Alderman) tried to open the St. Elphin's Park to the children, and they had to rescind the opening. He did not know whether Alderman Bennett was there or not, but he believed he was, " and made a mess of it " by pulling the railings up. (Laughter.) At any rate, he (the speaker) did not think it was worth the candle to have another fiasco of that kind.

In the course of his speech, Alderman Belton with- drew a minute accepting a tender for the construction of a bowling green and Nalks of Winwick-rcad. He explained there had been some mistake over the matter.

div.head: Tim BRIDGE: BRIGHT PROSPECTS.
div.p: Tim BRIDGE: BRIGHT PROSPECTS.

Alderman SMETHURST said he was glad to hear the exprossions of public rejoicing at the progress that was now being made with the new bridge The most difficult part of the work had, he understood, been accomplished and he trusted that in eight or ten weeks the public would be able to cross the first half of the bridge. The MAYOR said that Alderman Smethurst and he had the pleasure of walking over the first section of the bridge a few days ago. He bad no doubt., however, that Alderman Bennett had crossed it long before them. (Laughter.) RATING ANOMILIES.

The minutes of the General Purposes Committee con tamed the report of a deputation appointed to attend a joint conference of County Boroughs and County Councils, at which a resolution was passed protesting against the continued delay on the part of Parliament to provide a just and adequate contribution by the Imperial Exchequer towards the cost of the various national services which are administered by kcal authorities. Alderman BENNETT said politicians seemed to be so absorbed in things that were merely a part of the tight- big game that they had not time to devote to a ques- tion like this, which would be of real utility to the people. He would not be satisfied until the whole system of imperial and municipal taxation was over- hauled to an equitable balance struck between the two. Councillor H ENS TIALL urged the necessity of municipalities availing themselves of the promise of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to devote half the proceeds of the increment duty to the municipalities. The MAYOR : I believe that promise has been with- drawn. Councillor HENSITALL : No, I don't think so. Alderman BOLTON : It is not worth anything, if it has not. Councillor HENSHALL said they had a definite promise from Mr. Lloyd George, but other gleaners would no doubt be at work when the harvest of the increment duty was to be gathered ; and it therefore behoved the municipalities to be watchful. Count illor HAWTHORN said Warrington was entitled to a grant from the Development Fund, as it was 'intersected by main roads which provided means of communication between the counties. He also contended that the local rate- payers should not have been called upon to bear the whole of the cost of the new War rington Bridge. The TOWN CLERK said the claims of Warrington had been placed before the Board, but until this year the authorities refused to mike any grants, except to County Councils. They had, however, recently made grants to acme county be.roughs. PENNY SLIPPER BATHS.

Councillor ROBERTS moved the rescinding of the resolution adopted at the previous meeting with refer- ence to slipper baths, and submitted the following notics of motion in substitution : "That the Town Hall, Parks and Biths Committee make provision whereby the slipper baths, at certain convenient hours

of the day, may be used at a charge of Id. eact), inclu- sive of the use of towels and soap." The difference between that resolution and the one rassed at the previous meeting was that the first revolution restricted the use of the baths to workingmen, whereas his proposition threw them open to all who wished to avail themselves of the privilege. The original resolution made a very invidious distinction between the various classes of ratepayers, which !ass very undrsirsble, and further, WbS not in the interests of the baths superintendent, who ought not to have it put upon him to differentiate between who was a workingman and who was not. Further, the original proposition restricted the use of the baths to the male sex, but this would open them to the ladies as well. The stipulation that bathers should bring their own towels and soap would also be abolished. Alderman BOLTON seconded the motion. What the Baths Committee proposed to do was to earmark all the new baths for that particular purpose at all hours. The MAYOR : Do I understand they will be restricted to residents in the borough. Alderman BOLTON : No. They are pu'slic baths open to anybody who will pay ths money—tramps or anyone else. The MAYOR : Tint is very objectionable. The motion was carried usanim )usly. The minutes of the Town, Parks and Baths Com- mittee, which were confirmed, contained a resolution instructing the Borough Surveyor to prepare a plan, estimate and specific tion for the provi:lon of additional slipper baths. Alderman BOLTON raid they were doing %bat they could to carry out the resolution passed by the Council at the lest meeting. Councillor Gouctt asked when they were going to start the completion of the new portion of the baths ? It had been standing for a long time. Alderman BOLTON said a lot of unforeseen circum- stances had arisen in connection with the carrying Out of the extension.

div.head: 'IRRESPONSIBLE LUN WIGS."
div.p: 'IRRESPONSIBLE LUN WIGS."
LORD WOLMER'S OPINION OF THE MILITANTS.

Viscount ‘Volmer (Newton) speaking in the House of Commons on Monday as a Conservative sUppotter of woman suffrage, said the House had as much of mandate to deal with this question as it had to deal with any other, such as Home Rule. That red herring, militancy, had been drawn across the path of the debatte already. It was the ditty of members to be turned neither to the right nor the left by the acts of those comparatively few irresponsible lunatics—(cheers)— who bad brought discredit upon the cause of women's suffrage. He wished to repudiate all sympathy of any sort in the methods of the suffragettes. They were a perfectly insignificant body in numbers, and to say that their outrages should prevent hundreds of thousands of law-abiding citizens from obtaining the vote was nothing short of a great injustice. When the Bill came to the committe stage be would willingly vote for a proposal to disfranchise any woman who had been con- victed of enact of militancy. Women of the typlle of Miss Pankhurst were not fitted for the exercise of the vote , —(cheers)—and should be excluded from its privileges. The attempt in the Coal Mines Bill to abolish the pit- brow girl, the opposition of Conservative lawyer mem- bers to his Bill for admitting women to the Bar, and the attempt in the Licensing Bill to abolish barmaids, were illustrations of the vsay in which the House of Commons always attempted to narrow down spheres of activity for women because women had not votes. (Laughter.) Unless the working women were enfranchised their interests would continue to be neglected by the House of Commons whatever Govern- ment was in power. For these reasons he asked his Conservative friends to vote for the Bill.

div.head: N.S.P.C.C. INSPECTOR'S REMOVAL.
div.p: N.S.P.C.C. INSPECTOR'S REMOVAL.

Mr. George Luff, who has been inspector for the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children in St. Ilellns, Prescot, and district for the past five and a half years, is being transferred to Bournemouth. It is proposed in future to have two officers in St. Helens on aocount of the heavy work.

div.head: Liberal Club, Bewsey St., as it will appear when the Memorial Hall is completed. FOUNDATION STONE LAYING.
div.p: The Liberal Club, Bewsey St., as it will appear when the Memorial Hall is completed. FOUNDATION STONE LAYING.

(Hear, hear.) The townspeople generally highly appreciated her splendid gift of the fine conservatory that adorned the Park. (Applause.) As far as her support of Liberalism was concerned, they particularly prized the encouragement which she had at all times given them. She had rejoiced with them when victory had crowned their labours—(applause)—and she had been a true, steadfast and encouraging friend when defeat had cast its shadow over them. She was now about to lay the foundation stone of a beautiful building in memory of a stalwArt aud unflinching Liberal, a friend of all progressive causes, a strenuous toiler for the realisation of the old Liberal ideals—peace, retrenchment raid reform. (Applause.) The name of the late Mr. John Crosfield was a household word in Warrington and they held his memory in the highest honour. (Applause.)

div.head: Mrs. John erosfield performs the Ceremony in happy circumstances.
div.p: Mrs. John erosfield performs the Ceremony in happy circumstances.
WHAT THE TOWN OWES TO lIER FAMILY. DESCRIPTION OF THE HALL.

Thursday was a day to belong and well remembered in the history of Warrington Liberalism, for it witnessed the laying of the foundatioa stone of the Memorial Hall, which is being erected at the Liberal Club, by Mrs. John Crosfield, of Colwyn Bay, to the memory of her late husband, who for many years was so closely and honourably identified with the political, commercial and social life of Warrington. There is no worthy to whose memory Warringtonians of all shades of opinion would more willingly unite in paying tribute than the late Mr. John Crosfield, who was our Mayor 1882-3, but it is peculiarly fitting that the memorial should take the form of a handsome
addition to the local headquarters of the political party of which he was a lifelong stalwart and con- sistent adherent.
The memorial hall is to cost upwards of £3,000, and architectually it will be a credit and an ornament to thA town. -

In accordance with the generally expressed desire, Mrs. John CroEfield laid the foundation stone, and the occasion was marked by one of the largest and most representative gatherings ever seen at the Liberal Club. Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield were present and had a most enthusiastic greeting, Mr. Crosfield delivering a most interesting and inspiring address on the ideals of Liberalism. The weather, which had been threatening, was bright and cheerful while the out- door proceedings were carried through. Additional interest was lent to a memorable occasion by the formal presentation of the silver spoons and photographs given by Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield to the parents of those children born in Warrington on the day when the maternity benefit of the National Inaarance Act came into force.

The erection of the Memorial Hall affords one of those opportunities for academic design which rarely fall to the lot of an architect in a manufacturing town. The external and internal design is of a well proportioned and dignified character, depending on mass and line for effect, rather than upon redundancy of ornamentation, and is based on the pre-Georgian pericd of classical Renaissance.

The present street front of the club is being rt faced and incorporated with the general facade, making a new total frontage length to Bewsey-street of 78 feet. The ground floor, to be allotted to the Women's Liberal Association, will contain a room for general purposes, fronting on, and with separate access from, Bewsey-street, 32 feet long by 23 feet wide. There will be a kitchen at the rear 19 feet long by Oft. Gin. wide, and a porch communicating with the main building, the general room and kitchen, and affording access to the bowling green. The Mc.morial Hall will cccupy the whole of the first floor of the extension and will overlap the present ground floor reading room, the outer side wall of the first floor over the latter being removed. The ball will be 511,. Gin, long by 331 t. wide by 241 t. high at its highest point and will accommodate upwards of 300 people. There will be a separate entrance and stair- case from Bewsey-street to the hall, making it possible t) use it for extraneous purposes without in any way interfering with the use of the club premises. The hall has been carefully planned in relation to the club premises, communication being established with the staircase and fist floor rooms of the latter. Ample, cloak room accommodation will be provided in con- nection with the hall for ladies and gentlemen. The new buildings will be lighted throughout by electricity and an efficient system of hot-water heating will be installed.

Externally the building will be encased with Ruabon rustic-faced bricks, resembling in tone and colour the handmade facing bricks of the Warrington Town hail. The doorways and window dressings, cornices, &c., will be of Yorkshire stone from the Sheffield district, and will be simply and effectively detailed.
A freize under the main c)rnice will bear the inecription in Roman capital :
"TIITS iIALL WAS ERECTED TO THE MEMORY OF JOHN CROSFIELD, FORMERLY OF
WALTON LEA, IN THE YEAR 1.013."

Internally the hall is to be celled with a central panelled dome, springing from arched ceilings at either end and will be executed in fibrous modelled plaster. The internal wall Bur faces will be broken with pilasters, also to be treated with panelled fibrous plaster with Dantzic oak dados, window frames and linings, window seats and doorways. The hall windows will be glazed with glass to a special design, to accord with the general treatment. The staircase and general room will also be finished in a manner to correspond with that of the Memorial Hall. The buildings are being erected by Messrs. John Broadhurst and Sons to the design of Mr. Albert Warburton, of Warrington.
MISS TRUDA H. CROSFIELD. no. Treasurer Women's Liberal Assotiation

Parker (president of the Liberal Association), Alderman David Tinnion (chairman of the Liberal Club), Alder- man Picrpoint, Councillor Henry Roberts, Mr.E.Wynne Jones (president of the Progressive Labour League), Mr. and Mrs. J. G. Withinsbaw, Mr. J. A. Ransoms, Mr. E Lloyd Jones (chairman of the Junior Liberal Associa- tion) end Mr. J. Jarman. Mrs. Osborne, who was attending the conference of the Women's Liberal Federation in London, wired : " All good wishes and success for Crosfleld Memorial Flail.— Osborne, hon. secretary, W.L. A."
Mr. Parker and the Liberalism of the Future.

Mr. Parker wrote :—I should like to express my appreciation of the very .handsome gift which Mrs. Crosfl Ad purposes putting in tru,t for the benefit of the Liberal party in Warrington. I recollect with pleasure the sturdy Liberalism of the late Mr. John Uroaield, and I am glad that this Hall is to he put up to per- petuate his memory. There is yet inure work for the Liberal party. In the past it was mostly concerned in removing fetters, in emancipating the individual and the community from legal and constitutional disabilities, in the abolition of religious tests, the regulation of legal status of Trade Unions and the like. But Liberalism is not only a policy interested in the exten• sion of liberty but it has its positive conceptions whereby that liberty may be made real. The Liberalism ot the future will concern itself, not so much in t emoving fetters, but with developments in connection with education, temperance, better housing, improved social and individual environment and a more equitable distribution of the benefits of civilisation. Liberalism is in a special sense the creed of the democracy, it is a creed of faith and confidence in the people. This creed acquires in each generation a newer and larger content. We are often taunted with advancing bey( nd old policies, deserting old names and old watchwords. This is inevitable with the party of progress. The party that rests content with the battlefield once won and ceases to advance is doomed to stagnation and decay. But this advance does not involve a breakage with the past, it is its natural outcome. 'I he rights and freedom for which such men as Mr. John Crosfield fought and worked has made possible the further progress we are now making. All honour to the Liberals of the past and all honour to the lady whose generous act will keep green the name of an honoured Warrington Liberal.

The late Mr. John Crokfleld was one of Warrington's noblest sons, of whom we are very proud, and whose fair name will live long in our memories for his noble life and many generous and kindly doe ds.

Councillor Henry Roberts wrote is a good thing to perpetuate the memory of one of Warrington's greatest benefactors, whose lifelong fidelity to Liberalism is at once a lesson and an inspiration to us all.

Liberal Association in his admirable letter.(Applause There were two questions which Liberals, taking a survey of the situation, might ask themselves. Firstly, were they to-day as earnest staunch, courageous and determined in maintaining the gloricus traditions of Liberalism as their forefathers were ? Secondly, was the Liberalism of to-day the natural development of the Liberalism of the past, or was there anything in the charges, which emanated chiefly from the Tory party, that they had broken altogether with the Liberalism of old time? Address- ing himself to the first question, he believed that, if they took the country as a whole, they would find a larger proportion than ever of our citizens who, by reflection and conviction, were as staunch and con- vinced Liberals as ever we had in the countiy. (Applause.) He might go even further and state that he was honestly and firmly convinced that there was a much larger proportion of thoughtful and responsible citizens who were to-day convinced of the great bless- ings to our nation which modern Liberalism conferred, than were to be found even in the great generations of the Liberalism of our forefathers. (Applause.) Moreover, there was every reason why the results of Liberal effJrt should justify themselves in an increasing degree, year by year, to a growing number of the citizens of our country. Why should all those who were connected with that magnificent party hold their heads high and feel proud of the outcome of their work ? It was because they had justified, in the positive results of the work they had accomplished, the great blessings of social reform, and because they had shown, at three general elections and with huge Liberal polls all through the country, the enthusiasm which the progressive cause was constantly inspiring. (Applause.)

div.head: TOLERATION OF TO-DAY.
div.p: THE TOLERATION OF TO-DAY.

If they felt inclined to blow their own trumpet and to pat each other on the back, it was well to recall that it was not quite so easy for their predecessors to carry out work of that kind. (Hear, hear.) If we to-day enjoyed a measure of toleration of Liberal and progressive thought and effort, and of comparative freedom from social and ecclesiastical tyranny, if altogether we breathed a larger and wider political atmosphere than our forefathers breathed, we must not forget how much we owed to their courage and faith which bad won for us those greater liberties and opportunities. (Applause.)

div.head: WHAT TORIES ARE SAYING.
div.p: WHAT TORIES ARE SAYING.

Dealing with the question as to whether the Liberals of to-day were developing the work that their lathers took in hand, Mr. Crosfleld said that if they put that question to some of their Tory friends—to some of the old fogies they found in the club-room windows of London—they would reply : "Oh, dear, no! Literalism is a thing of the past. You are only fighting for Socialism and Communism, and heaven knows what besides ! In the old days you could find men, but what a crew you are to-day ! " (Laughter.) Such expres- sions reminded one of the people who were so fond of saying: " You know Punch' is not what Punch ' used to be." (Laughter.) The answer was : " Punch ' is not the same as it used to he ;it never was." (Laughter.) When they heard people talking as if there were a conflict and contradiction between th• Liberalism of their fathers, an impassable gulf between the work they carried on and the task that lay to the hand of the Liberals of to-day, he thought the best way of showing the nonsensical nature of such talk, was to consider some of the work which the Liberal party was doing. He contended that it afforded unmistakable proof that the Liberal party was, literally and truly, continuing the efforts of their forbears.

div.head: BLESSINGS OF SELF-GOVERNMENT.
div.p: THE BLESSINGS OF SELF-GOVERNMENT.

Let them take the question of self-government. Who in the old days had the courage and the Aatesmanlike foresight to give self-government to the Colonies? Who brought peace, loyalty, and good government to Canada, but the Liberal party? In the old days the Liberal p Arty gave self-government to the Colonies and in our own time—while he had the honour of repre- senting Warrington in the House of Commons— (applause)—we saw the crowning and *shining example of the healing influence of that policy in the historic illustration of South Africa, which had set an example not only to ourselves but to every civilised government. (Applause.) The Liberals of former generations took in hand the extension of the principle of self-govern-

Liberal Association
THE DEMANDS OF EXCESSIVE MILITARISM.

During the seven years that the Liberal Government had been in power we had bad n war. The party had stood for peace, just as in the old days. Linked with that, they had another question about, which his father felt very strongly. In years gone by the Liberal party had to withstand the demand that came from time to time from thcss who were too inclined to favour exces- sive militarism. It wr,s no less their duty to-day to carry out the same principles and the recent declaration of the Chief Whip showed that there was a continuity of policy in thac respect and that the Government were not going to shrink from all that was necessary to keep the encroachments of excessive militarism in check. (Appian:se.) GOVERNNIENT BY THE PEOPLE.

No doubt many of them had read the last speech which the grand old Chief delivered in the House of Commons when he handed on as a legacy to the Liberal party the curtailing of the unbridled power of the Second Chamber which had so long " cribbed, cabinqd and confined " the efforts of the house of Commons. There again the party had risen to the occasion and this Government had proved to be a Government not merely of words and promises but of deeds and perform- ances. (Applause.) They had grappled with that extremely difficult and formidable problem, and had not only curbed the power of the Sec:did Chamber, but , had prepared the way for a necessary revision of its

the late Mr. John Crostleld. He was a man who could always be relied upon and he never looked over the heads of his fellow-men, hut had the greatest recpect for everybody, high and low. He was a true Liberal and in that respect his mantle had fallen upon Mrs. Crosfleld and Mr. Arthur Crosfield. (Applause.) He (the speaker) believed Mr.Crostleld was going to represent Warrington again. He was a real gentleman, an earnest Liberal, and or,e whose ereat object in life was the bett,—ment and uplifting of the poorer people. (Applause.) Finally the Alderman urged the workers never to vote tor the Protectionist policy which beggared and impoverished their class in years gone by. (Hear, hear.)
