constitution, which would be a blessing to Engl:ah government for all time. (Applause.) lie believed he had brought forward sufficient instances to prove that the Liberal party to-day were carrying on and developing the work of their predecessors. How natural it was that they should devote their energies to the work of emanciraloa ! The good old saying so often on the lips of 'Amends of former generations was " Government of the people, by the people, for the people, "and they concmtrated their efforts on getting government by the people which was the first step The Liberal party were now carry- ing out the very work which, by implication, was included in the watchword of their day and were help- ing to make government far more really than it ever was before " Government for the people." (Applause.) THE GREATEST MEASURE OF SOCIAL REFORM. However great and noble was the work of men like Cobden, Bright and Gladstone, the work of the Liberal party in our time was no less noble. (Applause.) They had just been asiisting at a ceremony to ce;ebrate the latest and he would venture to say—nit even excepting that blessed gift of Old Age Pensions—the gr ate3t measure of social reform which we had been able to carry in this country. (Applause.) When they th aicht that 14,000,000 people had been secured against a kind of adversity against which they were never safe- gearrt.d before, rind when they realized the extent to which ihe question of naenaJhyment had been dealt with, it was enough to fill every earnest-minded citizen with real hope for the future. (Applause.) Two I dead si ectres had haunted the homes of the

ing as being best for the country, best for the workman, and, in the long run, best for the employer too. (Applause.)
NATIONAL EDUCATION.

They all knew what Mr. Gladstone's Government did for the cause of education. His great ministry took over the reins of office in 186 S, when his rather was working actively for the Liberal cause mid when some ot their friends, like Alderman James Evaus—(applause) —were in the i hick of the fray. They knew the splendid work for education that was undertaken by tba•-, Ministry. (Applause.) What was going to happen next year ? A continuation and a development of that noble principle of national education which would raise our country, in that respect, to higher levels than we had ever reached before. (Applause.)

industrial world of Britain—sickness sufficiently pro- longed to bring about the unemployment of the bread- winner and, too often, the breaking up of the home in its train, and the unemployment which from time to time dogged the footsteps of cycles of bad trade. Do what they would, they coulo never make certain that those dread enemies wculd not invade a household. What the Goverhment had ensured was that the evil results of their tutees upon auy home were more than three parts done away with. (Applause.) The Act had been a shield and buckler to our indu-strial community, and, from the first moment, he had felt convinced that it was impussible to rate too highly the benefits it had confeirec. it was indeed the latest and greatest work ever nude taken by the Government in the direction of social tetorm. (Loud applause.)

div.head: PROTECTIONISTS ROUTED.
div.p: THE PROTECTIONISTS ROUTED.

Throughout his life, his father always had deeply at heart that great battle whicb was tougtit to a successful issue in the forzies of last century—the priceless work with which the names of Bright and Cobden would be for ever ass,)ciated. (Applause.) His father spe prized the friendship of those two great men, which he had the honour to claim for very many years. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Crisfield) used not tell them that Free Trade had beet' something ot a household world in their family for several generations. (Applause.) Was there no continuity between the Liberalism of old time and the Liberalism of to-day in the successful battle they had fought in the country in defence nf the sacred principles of Free Trade ? They had oefended them to some purpose, for they had nutted the Protectionists and repulsed them with great slaughter. (Applause.)

div.head: GOSPEL OF PEACE.
div.p: THE GOSPEL OF PEACE.

From his earliest youth, continued Mr. Crosfleld, he was brought up by his father to respect the great gospel of international peace, tor which Cobden and Bright strove all their lives. While h knew that some Liberals and people who did not belong to their party, might have had their misgivings about what had happened in recent years in Persia and Greece. he would ask them to consider all the difficult and conflicting claims that had to be balanced by any man responsible for the conduct of affairs in our Foreign Office. Let them take a broader v;ew and think of what was due to Liberal effort at the Foreign Office in the last twelve months, which had so helped to avert the threatened awful conflagration of a European war, that throughout the governments of Europe to-day Sir Eciw-iid Grey's praises were being sung, and they were only too anxious to recognise the patience, sagacity, tact and statsrnan- ship with which he had helped to recognise conflicting claims in a position of extreme delicacy, difficulty and, at times, ef extreme danger.

div.head: Long-felt Need.
div.p: A Long-felt Need.

Councillor J. T. LOCKER proposed a vat') of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. H. Crmfield. tie said Mr. Crosfield must be proud to Le present at the inauguration of a memorial to his beloved father. div.head: UNACKNOWLEDGED HEROES.
div.p: UNACKNOWLEDGED HEROES.

The Humane Society is, of course, largely cow- cerned with those who ,go down to the sea in sivps; nut its rascals -nave been worn -ny men who never saw the sea—deep down in the under- dark of flooded collieries. But the miner, battling for his comrades' lives with a more deadly element that, water —in the clutches of the terrible choke-damp— is beyond the pale of the Society's recognition. A Bristol child a few years since gave up his life in an act of heroic self-sacrifice almost with- out rival. Wandering in the fields with a younger boy, he was overtaken by darkness, and having lost his bearings, he laid the smaller boy under a hedge, and, taking off all his own clothes except his shirt, wrapped them warmly around him. When a labourer found them :n the Morning the younger boy was asleep and warm, but the protector died from the effects of exposure. The Trumane Society's medal has been awarded to a doctor for persevering for three tours in restoring animation to a child drowned in a wash-tub. But What form of recognition viil be found for that hero of modern science who has contracted the disease known as X ray- dermatitis, with the result of the loss of one arm and the danger of losing the second? Is there fire to be fought— deadly, and fierce, and unappeasable? Against the forces of a big fire, there are times ,when no skill can avail. The Society has no medal for the fireman who risks his life every time he enters a burning building. What medal is there for the plain labourer, quite unlovely to look upon in his befouled clothes, who spent a full day in the poisoned air of a great city sewer trying to find a com- rade who had lost his way. It is such men as he who carry out in pining times of peace the proud boast that for every brave deed that wants doing, there is a brave, Englishman ready and willing to do it.

Poverty a Drain on National Resources.
MR. J. R. CLYNES, M.P., ON MINIMUM
WAGE IDEA.

Mr. J. R. Clynes, M.P., was the principal speaker a a May Day oemonstration held by the Warringt Trades and Labour Council in the Co-operative Hall, on Saturday evening. In personal appearance, as well as in his style of speaking, Mr. Clynes presents a striking contrast to Mr. Tom Mann, who addressed a meeting in the same hall a few days previously. Of spare yet wiry build, he has little of the artifice of the typical "agitator," whereas Mr. Mann's e3mmsnd- ing physique and exceptional lung power, combined with an ability to run the gamut of emotions, make him a dorwinating figure at any meeting. But Mr. Clvnes can hold his audience all the same. There is determination in those keen eyes, and if his oratory lacks purple pitches or picturesque embroideries, he frames his speeches in clear cut, incisive phrases, which at once go home to the listener. Calmly, with- out gesture, yet with obvious earnestness, he builds up his case, his appeal being more to reason than to sentiment, although the latter element is by no means ignored.

div.head: NO BENEFITS WITHOUT SACRIFICES.
div.p: NO BENEFITS WITHOUT SACRIFICES.

Mr. CLYNES began hi 4 speech with an account of the May Day celebrations in the Welsh noßl fields, where the colliers not only suspended work for the day, but decided not to return to the pits with any man who had not a trade union card. The result was that many thousands of colliers were in a state of strike, refusing to work with a small minority of foolish and stubborn men who would not join the Miners' Feleration. They in the trade union movement did not desire to provoke strikes or induatrial troubles, but they welcomed the spirit which declared that the man who was willing to participate in the benefits procured by trade union work must also share in the sacrifices. (Anplause.) A BUSINESS PROPOSiTION.

Mr. Clynes declared that he was not pessimistic about the general indications that concerned their future progress. This was a very ancient kingdom, and it was only lately that the greatest section of the community, called the workingclass, had had any opportunity or admitted State right to have anything or to be any- thing. For centuries the position of the worker was that of an inferior or subject race, destined to do the drudgery, without property, without voice, or any opening for betterment. He (Mr. Clynes) saw in the slow progress that was being made, however much it might disappoint some of the more forward and enthusiastic spirits of their movement, the certainty of ultimate escape for the poorer classes from the con- ditions in which they were now chained. Putting the question as a business proposition, Mr. Clynes said it did not pay the country to make people poorer, as millions of money had to be poured out to relieve them. We spend huge sums in repressing the poor, in police- manising them, in keeping them in their place. We had great gaols and fortresses; we had the man behind the truncheon to give expression to the law ; we had a Workhouse system that was the guide of the world. (Laughter.) Most of the evidences of poverty of soul and of mind, most of the crime of our country could be traced back to the workshop where men were enslaved, brutalised, sweated and underpaid. NEW FANCY OF "SLUMMING." "You have ladies and gentlemen," continued Mr. Clynes' "taking up their time with the new fancy of slumming, going round to help the poor—particularly if an election is drawing nign—(laughter)— or it an act of charity can be linked up with something in the way of expectation for the hereafter. (Laughter.) Is this the best that can be done in a nation that prides itself on leading the world? We present to maakind the mother of Parliaments. We say that we stand for the world's freedom—that where the Union Jack waves there is no slave to be seen. (Laughter.) .IDLENESS AS A CLASS PRIVILEGE.

We have undoubtedly tlie material fOirn-a-icing a highly intellectual population. We have a class of men willine to work. for there are more design- ing idlers among the richer classes of our country than among the poorer classes. (Applause.) At lerst it can be said for 90 per cent. of the working poor that they are only asking for work on reasonable terms for as long as men and women can reasonably perform it. At the other end of the scale you have a class claiming idleness as a class privilege and the fullest wages for doing nothing. (L toghter.) The worker, who offers his services, ought to be put first in the claim for the best of what is going, instead of being pushed into the background and asked to take the leavings." (Applause.) " We do not," said Mr. Clynes, " taunt the middle and upper classes with being soaked in beer, but they are more frequently soaked in something worse—the sweat and blood of underpaid men, women and children.lt is in that way that many immense fortunes and ever-growing profits are made up." THE• BREWERY STRIKE. Mr. Clynes went on to deal with the dispute at the brewery of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Ltd. In the first place he pointed out that, an outstanding feature of recent labour troubles in Warrington was that they were not, in the initial stages, due to trade unionism, but to an arrogant repudiation of it. The carters' strike would have been settled long before it was, had it not been for the fact that a certain section of employers thought they were entitled to refuse to deal with accredited representatives of the trade unions. Mr. Clynes then recounted the circumstances of the brewery strike. He stated that the presentation of the men's claims by the union was followed by the dismissal—victimisation he termed it—of a number of employee, amongst whom were some of the oldest end best servants of the firm. There was nothing against them, so far as the union could find, except that they were associated with the claims which the union had pre-,ented for discussion. Toe firm denied that, as stated, no MAD had been dismissed without adequate cause.

A CHALLENGE TO THE FIRM. "If there is a sufficient and adequate cause," con- tinued Mr. Clynes, " let the firm state it. (Applause.) It is no u-e asking the public to accept a bare statement without any backing or evidence. We challenge the firm to prove that these men were stopped for sufficient-. reasons. I am prepared, together with any of my colleagues, to meet the repre-3entatives of the firm at any kiLd of conference or weeting, private or open, before any sort of tribunal, in order that we and f,ll Concerned shall see whether these men had been reason- ably stopped from working or whether, as we say, they have been made the victims of an unreasoning and arregant act of punishment." (Applause.) Unfortunately, continued Mr. Clynes, a number of men who voteo, freely and voluntarily, in favour of the union sending in claims on their behalf, had not had the pluck or the manners to marcb with their fellows and take their part in tho battle when it was forced on them. They might, for the moment, gain—but not in the respect of their employers. (Hear, hear.) Having asserted that it was an act of meanness on the part of any employer to want to deal directly with his own workpeople awl to sbut out the spokesmen whom they would prefer, Mr. Clynes said that even if the men were beaten in this particular fight, it would not settle the question, but would only begin it. (Applause.) CLERICS ECHO LABOUR CATCHWORDS. Mr. Clynes went on to refer to the increased emphasis which was being given to the human side, as distinct from the purely material aspect of trade unionism. Great ecclesiastics had begun to echo those old street- corner expressions that made up so much of Labour oratory in years gone by. Those great men, and even some statesmen, were saying that labour must be the first charge upon industry. By that they meant that a level of life at which it was reasonable to expect human being to live must be secured and guaranteed by the remuneration for a man's service. Hence they had the popularisation of the idea of a minimum wage. Standard rates of wages existed in many trades, not because they were settled by masters and men, but because for a certain sum—say 18s. a week—an employer could get as many men as he wanted for a. given job. Therefore, when the trade unions wanted to increase that rate and establish a minimum, they could not, at One jump, reach the level of a real living wage. Gradually, however, the principle was being translated into practice, and, although the Labour party's proposal for a minimum of 303. a week was resisted by the Government. many members on both sides of the House, as well as a Cabinet Minister, favoured the suggestion that a minimum wage should be legally guaranteed by the establishment of wage boards in all trades where the wages were below the subsistence level. The "subsistence level "was a very general and elusive term, but the workers by parading their poverty and wrongs would soon show what a subsistence wage was. They had to burn into the public mind the fact that a minimum of 30s. was as little as a family could be kept on, and then lay upon themselves the duty of supporting only those candi- dates who would vote far that wage. Trade unionism was the least of the great powers that the workman could put into use, but It had up to now been the toilers' first line of &fence. They must now link with it the great power of political organisation. (Applause.) "TYRANNICAL METHODS" OF THE POLICE. The meeting was presided over by Mr. S. H. Smith, president of the Trades and La Hour Council. _ _

Mr. ALBERT Lims,organiser for the Ga-s.w—orkers', and General Labourers' Union, said it was somewhat of a. disgrace that, while in Warrington, one saw evidences of trade unionism and industrial organisation in the wearing of the button, there was not a single working- class representative on the Town Council. In view of that fact, one could understand the tyrannical methods of the police. The force realised that the Watch Com- mittee was constituted in such a way that, if they were to give the workers the benefit of the doubt or show sympathy with them, the probability was that they would earn their masters' frown. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Chas. Dukes also addressed the meeting.

THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MAY 10, 1913.

div.head: LIBERALISM, OLD AND NEW.
div.p: LIBERALISM, OLD AND NEW.

It was natural that there should be a kind of political stock-taking at the laying of the foundation stone at the Liberal Club on Thursday and it was highly appropriate that that useful service should be rendered by MR. ARTHUR CROSFIELD, who has repre- sented the constituency in the House of Commons in the past and has a reasonable expectation of doing so again in the next Parliament. From a party standpoint it was a very hopeful review of the situation that MR. CROSFIELD was able to give; his method of dealing with the facts at his disposal was a personal triumph from a speaker's point of view. It must be con- fessed that the matter that came so readily to hand helped him well on the way to that triumph—to realise how substantial was that aid we need only imagine the plight in which a Conservative would find himself who essayed to imitate Mr. ICRosFIELD's bold plan of linking up the past with the present and then judging the proba- bilities of the future. The dreadful bungling and incapacity which culminated in the disasters in South Africa and the sordid uses to whicli our victories out in the sub-continent were put, might be recalled but they would produce no response in the breast of one who was honestly seeking for inspiration to go forward with a policy that could command respect or hold out any hope of success. The attempt, indeed, to obscure the causes that led to the greatest political debacle in our annals, in 1906,by the production of Tariff " reform" produced a policy which even its advocates do not under- stand. They only know it as a something that has completed their discomfiture at three general elections and a something they would like to bury till a convenient resurrec- tion day, somehow and at some time, comes round to add life to what are palpably and unmistakably ridiculous dry bones. Whether Tariff" Reform" means Protection or food taxes only Tariff Reformers can even pretend to say.

We are content to leave them to the solv- ing of these immaterial riddles and to turn to our own affairs and aspirations as Mr. CROSFIELD showed us, with such admirable tact and power, to do. As Mr. CHAS. PARKER stated in a letter to the meeting, the Liberal Party have prepared the ground and won the preliminary battles in the many spheres that go to the making up of the Pro-. gressive policy. We have now to consolidate and see that we advance to reap the full benefits of those initial victories. It was on these lines that Mr. CROSFIELD constructed his masterful review of the situation. In answer to the critics—the heroes of the Tariff " Reform " and other re-actionary movements—who say that Liberals are drift- ing away from the Liberalism of former clays, he replied with unanswerable arguments that prove that there is an absolute continuity of policy. Liberals of old demanded government by the people and this Government have made that possible for the first time by clipping the wings of the Lords; they asked for emanci- pation and we are about to abolish plural voting; they gave us Free Trade a-nd we are intent on protecting Free Trade to the utter- most of our power; they demanded justice for +lreland and we are in the midst of con- ceding that service in the name of all that is honest between two peoples so nearly one; they asked for soeial reform and we have given much, culminating to date in insurance against sickness and unemploy- ment; and. above all, Liberals called for peace and the present Government have had no war, though they have been strong enough to avert blood-shed on the grand scale. That does not complete the list but continuity of policy is complete. The Liberal Party have faith ,in themselves and con- fidence in the attainment of their well- defined aspirations; and the Progressive forces of Warrington will unite to secure ' such representation for the borough as will ; ensure their taking a proper share in I the garnering of the rich harvest that the future undoubtedly has in store for the , people of this country.

div.head: WOMAN SUFFRAGE.
div.p: WOMAN SUFFRAGE.
How the " Rights " Question Disturbed the Peace of the Roman Forum.
CATO'S LAMENT.
A correspondent writes :--

I have come across the enclosed speech by Cato in the Roman Forum. Perhaps you would like to make something of it in view of the present Suffragist agita- tion. There appears to be nothing new under the BUR. I sent it to some of my lady friends, but they think less of Cato than they do of St. Paul on this subject, and this is saying a good deal. As far as the vote question is concerned, Ido not think that this can in justice be denied, but I wish it was preceded by more education and evidence of more general interest among women themselves. No doubt those that are interested in the Suffrage are keenly interested, and are among our best women, but they have not yet created a general demand or a general interest. I hope this will come. But I rather shrink from the experiment of immediately introducing into the electorate an immense number of voters who will vote for all sorts of reasons other than the political cinerr. Of course the vote itself would be a great educational influence, and I suppose we always have to run some risk in the extension of the franchise. THE ROMAN HUSBAND'S MISTAKE. From Livy xxxiv. 2.

WOMAN'S RIGHT.—Cato the Elder in the Roman Forum: If, Romans, every individual among us had made it a rule to maintain the prerogative and authority of a husband with respect to his own wife, we should hsve less trouble with the whole sex. But now, our privileges, overpowered at home by female contumacy, are, even here in the forum, spurned and trodden underfoot; and because we are unable to withstand each separately, we now dread their collective body. I was accustomed to think it a fabulous and fictitious tale, that, in a certain island, the whole race of males was utterly extirpated by a conspiracy of the women. But ;he utmost danger may be apprehended equally .from either sex, if you suffer cabals and secret consultations to be held, scarcely, indeed, can I determine in my own mind, whether the act itself, or the precedent that it affords, is of more pernicious tendency. The latter of these more particularly con- cerns us consuls, and the other magistrates; the former, you, my fellow citizens ; for, whether the

/measure proposed to your consideration be profitable to the State or not, is to be determined by yon, who are to vote on the occasion. As to the outrageous behaviour of these women, whether it be merely an act of their own, or owing to your instigations, Marcus Fundanius and Laciins and Valerius, it unquestionably implies culpable conduct in magistrates. I know not whether it reflects greater disgrace on you, tribunes, or on the consuls; on you certtinly, if you have brought these women hither for the purpose of raising tribuaitian sedition on us, if we suffer laws to be imposed upon us by a secession of women, as was done formerly by that of the common people. It was not m ithout painful emotions of shame, that I, just now, made my way into the forum through the midst of a band of women. Had I not been restrained by respect for the modesty and dignity of some indi- viduals among them, rather than of the whole number' and been unwilling that they should be seen rebuked by a consul, I should not have refrained from saying to them : "What sort of practice is this, of running out into the public, besetting the streets, and addressing other women's husbands? Could not each have made the same request to her husband at home? Are your blandishments more seducing in public than in private, and with other women's husbands than your own? Altheugh if females would let their modesty confine them within the limits of their own rights, it did not become you, even at home, to concern yourselves about any laws that might be passed or repealed here. Our ancestors thought it not proper that women should perform any even private businefs, without a director; but that they should ever be under tie control of parents, brothers or husbands.

ROMAN WOMEN SEEK UNBOUNDED LIBERTY I We, it seems, suffer them now to interfere in the management of State affairs, and to thrust themselves into the forum, into general assemblies of election; for what are they doing at this moment in your streets and lanes? What, but arguing ; sorce in support of the motion of tribunes; others contending for the repeal of the law? . . . This is the smallest nf the injunctions laid on them by usage or the laws, all which women bear with impatience ; they long for entire riberty, nay to speak the truth, not for liberty but for unbounded freedom in every particular, for what will they not attempt, if they now come off victorious? Recollect all the institutions respecting the sex, by which our forefathers restrained them and subjected them to their husbands, and yet even with the help of all these restrictions, they can scarcely be kept within bounds. If, then, you suffer them to throw these of one by one, to tear them all asunder, and, at last, to be set on an equal footing with yourselves, can you imagine that they will be any longer tolerable? Suffer them once to arrive at an equility with you, and they will from that moment become your superiors."

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 10, 1913. THE PASSING WEEK. I
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 10, 1913. THE PASSING WEEK. I
NOTES and COMMENTS On Local and General Topics.
THE ROYAL VISIT AND WALKING DAY.

The Reception Committee appointed by the Town Council to make preparations for the Royal visit has got to work this week. One of its first duties has been to consider the date of Walking Day, although the decision on that point does not strictly come within its province. However, the committee, on being informed that Friday, July 4th, had already been set apart for the children's festival, decided not to suggest any altera- tion. One reason which strongly influenced them was that some of the local works have fixed their annual excursions for July sth and from every point of view, the arrange- ment cannot be regarded as other than satisfactory, as the Royal visit follows on Monday, July 7th, and a ten days' interval between the two great occasions would have been highly inconvenient, to say the Jeast of it. The committee recommend that there shall be a general holiday on July 7th. The list of ladies and gentlemen who are to have the honour of being presented to their Majesties has now been completed. It is as follows : The Mayor and Mayoress. The Town Clerk.

Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., C V.O. Lady Greenall. Mr. Harold Smith, M.P. Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield. Mr. and Mrs Robert Pierpoint. Mr. and Mrs. John Fairclongb. Councillor and Mrs. Henry Roberts. Alderman and Mrs. W .Bolton. Alderman and Mrs. J. Smethurst. Alderman W. J. Forshaw. Alderman and Mrs. W. Pietrroint. Alderman and Mrs. A. Bennett. Councillor and gre. J. Wilkinson.

We understand that Aldermen Pierpoint and Bennett have been included by reason of their claim to the senior aldermanship (after Alderman Bolton the " father " of the Council, who is to be presented as an ex-Mayor), while Councillor Wilkinson is the senior councillor
Mr. J. C. Parr, as an ex-Mayor and freeman of the borough, was to be presented, but he has intimated that, on account of ill-health, he will be unable to avail himself of the honour.

pictures, I left the Museum, and then had to wait for a train at Arpley Station. I found that my sight had been quickened to note the delicate variations of light-and-shade on the neighbouring buildings, mills and old cottsges ; that the perspective of the station itself, and of the rail way lines, and the signals, and telegraph 'wires looked more pictorial than usual; and then,as the train was moving away, I caught sight of the new bridge, in course of construction over the river, and saw that it, with the big crane being used by the buildsrs, and the surrounding buildings, would be admirable material for an,etcher. Indeed, a town like Warrington, with narrow streets, and old and new buildings side by side, is full of the kind of picturesqueness that the etcher loves, and that is seen in many of the pictures in this Exhibition. There is no need to go to other English towns or abroad to see such beauty, it is here at our own doors ; and this Exhibition Ought to lead to its fuller enjoyment. This is a phase of beautiful Warrington that most of us will have failed to see; Mr. Phythian has given us a very powerful reason why we should at once place our- selves under the spell of these line drawings, which certainly have a fascination peculiarly their own.

div.head: NEW LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: THE NEW LIBERAL CLUB.

The best spell of sunshine that this week provided, burst, let us hope as the best of omens, upon an important and interesting ceremony on Thursday, while Mrs. John Crosfield was laying the foundation stone of the Memorial Hall which she is generously adding to the Liberal Club premises, an addition which will make the headquarters of Warrington Liberalism one of the finest buildings in Warrington. The Hall will be at once a fitting monu- ment to the life and work of the late Mr. John Crosfield, in whose memory it is being erected by a devoted widow, and an effective centre for the advancement of political ideals, the propagation of which has devolved upon a worthy son, Mr. Arthur Crosfield. The size and character of the gathering that welcomed Mrs. Crosfield showed Warrington Liberalism to be ps robust as ever; the speeches and the pro- ceedings generally proved that the party is strong at heart and full of the right kind of inspiration for the future. Mr. Arthur Crosfield, speaking of the continuity of aim and the fixity of purpose in the party as a whole, made a statesmanlike utterance. It is dealt with more fully in our leading article, but we may say here that it sounded a clear clarion call, which, for local purposes, will assuredly have a decided and lasting effect.

Stress was laid upon the long continued generosity of the Crosfield family towards Warrington that has found, and still finds, many outlets other than along political lines. This generosity has been productive of much good and an appreciative town, as well as a loyal and confident party,is profoundly grate- ful for the studied consideration that has been displayed through so many years.

The club in its new form will have a front- age to Bewsey-street of 78 feet and the Hall will, among other things, provide suitable accommodation for the Warrington Liberal Women's Association that already has a bona-fide membership numbered by thousands, and will be a force to be reckoned with in the stirring political times that lie directly ahead.

div.head: MR. ARTHUR CROSFIELD'S WARRINGTON
div.p: MR. ARTHUR CROSFIELD'S WARRINGTON
HOME.

Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, their many Warrington friends will be delighted to hear, have taken a house in Warrington and intend to make it their home in the autumn and the spring of each year. The house is conveniently situated at 31, Bold-street. This development will be highly pleasing to Warringtonians, who will be happy in the increased facilities thus afforded them of seeing those whom they desire to have more frequently in their midst. Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Crosfield may rest assured that they have never done a more popular act than in providing themselves with this permanent Warrington home. We shall be in a positiOn in a short time to state the exact date upon which they will take up their residence amongst us.

div.head: MODERN ETCHINGS AT THE MUSEUM.
div.p: MODERN ETCHINGS AT THE MUSEUM.

We are glad to learn that the exhibition of modern etchings, which has been open for the past month at the Museum, has attracted a fair amount of attention—though the visitors have been fewer than the excellence of the exhibits would seem to demand. Perhaps if a charge were made for admission increased interest would be shown, but we can assure our readers that the Museum Committee are upon this occasion offering a rich treat for nothing, and all who are artistically inclined —and we are all artists in a way— should make sure of seeing these pictures during the remaining few days that they will be on view. There are 114 of them, the works of some of the chief living English etchers. The mysteries of line, mezzotint, aquatint and dry-point engraving are explained in an introduction, finely written. by Mr. Ernest Phythian for the official catal- logue, which will be found to be as attractive in its way as the exhibition itself.
ADMIRABLE ART MATERIAL IN WARRINGTON.

Mr. Phythian is a thoroughly practical- minded man. As soon as he had seen the collection of masterpieces and had left the Museum, he found he had to wait for a train at Arpley station. We must confess that we had never thought of a wait at Arpley station as an aid to poetic or artistic inspira- tion. div.head: FROM 'Bus TO MOTOR CAR.
div.p: FROM 'Bus TO MOTOR CAR.

There is plenty of room for moralizing and reflecting, if one is given to such exercising of the mental faculties, in the story told in to-day's "I remember" column by an old 'bus conductor. His recollections of his duties nearly forty years ago resolve them- selves into a list of names of those who used his 'bus ; but, in the light of present-day experience, it is a really startling piece of history. We have only to imagine our. heads of firms, our bank managers, our Mayors, and our landowners, to say nothing of our M.P.s, travelling to and from town in those old'buses and then remember how they cover the same ground to-day in the luxury and with the speed of their motor cars to realise how rapidly the world lute progressed in a remarkably short space of time. Between the tramcar of the working classes and the lumbering 'buses of forty years ago that largely served the better classes there is a gap that requires some bridging over, even in the imagination.

div.head: MISPLACED CONTEMPT.
div.p: MISPLACED CONTEMPT.

In his lecture during Health week, Dr. Hibbert drew special attention to the fact that measles claimed far more victims than any other disease, notifiable or unnotifiable, many more in fact, than several of them taken together. Yet parents are so unenlightened, not to say recklessly indifferent, that they are prepared to run all kinds of risk with a disease for which, for some unknown reason, they continue to have the utmost contempt. In the "Manchester Guardian" Miscellany, this week, it is recorded that in some districts in Lancashire the school grants are suffering because virulent epidemics of measles are reducing the average attendance. That ought to be sufficient warning; but, we are told : The other day an infant school teacher was alarmed to find only four children in her class at

' ' the opening hour of afternoon school. A hurried • search discovered the missing children waiting • in a queue outside the door of a school companion ,rlv4 had died of measles, and quio a number of the children had viewed the body before the , appearance of the teacher put au end to the proceedings.

div.head: OH DEAR!
div.p: OH DEAR!

On Monday night a serious-faced and evidently serious-minded individual was holding forth from 4 "Conservative van," stationed in Cornhill,upon the question of the Insurance Act, that greatest of Acts in the history of social reform, as it will rapidly prove itself to be. Calmly and deliberately he was showing, with the emphasis and gesture appropriate to the open-air speaker, that all wealth came from the workers and that it necessarily followed that the State, which was also made up of the workers, was simply extorting money from them in order to give it to them back again. The three- pence, the fourpence and the twopence—all was lumped together; and the "Hear hear," which came from several quarters of the very sparse audience, told plainly how the contention that everything had its source in labour was understood better than Conserva- tives are usually willing that it should be understood. So far as the writer learnt during his short stay,there was no reference to the fact that this insurance money is wealth made by the worker that would go into other very different channels had not Mr. Lloyd George diverted it. That the working classes shall have a fair share of the wealth they create, whether it be in the form of old age pensions, insurance against sick - ness and unemployment, the feeding of starving school children, medical inspection to discover and treat our youthful defectives and the like, is the work which Mr. Lloyd George and the Liberal Government have set themselves out to do. The Insurance Act has, in brief, put the working classes on an equality with the rich. That is, if they are feeling ill and in need of medical attention they may get it without fear of a doctor's bill that might cripple them for life, and: they may cease work without being deprived of all income at a time when money is more needed than ever. Poverty no longer forces a sick man to work on until he breaks down simply because he is poor. The working classes are indeed getting a little of their own back,using the phrase in its highest sense, but we were scarcely prepared to hear such candour proceed from a Conserva- tive van.

An unconscious, but capital, comment on the speech was provided by an opposition show run by a few waifs and strays, who had set up one of their number as a May Queen. Merrily they danced around their decorated pole and the refrain that reached the ears of the small audience in front of the van was :
Oh dear ! what can the matter be?

div.head: DAWN.
div.p: THE DAWN.

There's a silence in the gardea. where the scented violet grows ; There's stillness in the meadow where the gentle strearnlet flows, There's a waiting for the message that another day is born ; 'Tis the gentle hush that tells us of the coming of the dawn. There's a glimmer on the silent pool beneath the willow's shade; There's a ray that brightens on the trees in tender

_ green arrayed There's a faint pink flush that's growing in the east whence comes the morn : 'Tis tke pale clear light that heralds the approaching of the dawn. There's a bird's sweet note that lingers on the violet- scented air; There's a gentle breeze that whispers—all the flowers its secret share ; There's a roseate glow that glistens o'er the dewdrops on the lawn; There's a burst of light and gladness and of song—it is the dawn. ELSE J. RANSOME.

div.head: DEMAND FOR LIVING WAGE.
div.p: DEMAND FOR LIVING WAGE.
Our Propositions Discussed By Correspondents.
READERS' DIVERSE VIEWS.

The article we published in last Saturday's " Examiner" advocating the need for estab- lishing a minimum wage of 255. a week, being the lowest amount that could be regarded as a "living wage" for a working- man and his family in present-day conditions, has created wide-spread interest. We have received the following, among other letters, from our readers on the subject AN EMPLOYER'S POINT OF VIEW.

Sir,—Your last Saturday's article under the title "Demand for Living Wage" raises a vital problem, one that we will hear a good deal of in the imtnediate future. All must agree from a social‘ point of view that for a man with a family living in Warrington 2ls. is not a living wage, and, further, that the community, apart from those of us who are employers, have a real interest in the matter. When, however, we turn from the social to the economic aspeetq of the question the difficulties become very real. I take it that the writer would fix a minimum wage of 25s.,which the employer must pay, with no assistance from the State as in the case of the Insurance Act.

lam of opinion that all labour is underpaid. All wealth is created by labour, and, as under pres.nt conditions a good deal of wealth is appropriated by those who give no equivalent either in the form of individual labour or of stored labour in the form of capital, it must follow to the extent that such wealth is diverted to those who do not work that labour is robbed of its reward. It would be more logical if instead of altering the reward of labour by law at one point, we were to restrict all forms of monopoly so that all produce should belong to the producers. Were this possible then labour's re mard would rice as a whole, and then the bottom dog would get his increase with the rest. It may be contended that before this comes about radical alterations must be made in our system, alterations about which we are in no wise agreed. Hence, howeyei logical snch a plan may be it affords no present hope for the Warrington labourer who has to half starve his family on 21s. a week.

Putting aside, therefore, the true method. of advance as for the time being impractical, let us consider your proposition of a minimum wigs of 255. It must be conceded that the relative -value of tho 21s. man is, tak- ing labour values as a whole, approximately rightly assessed at 21s. That is, the value of the services toi the community of a mechanic earning 425. a week is worth double that of a man with a besom sweeping dirt. Probably they are both underpaid, but for value of contribution the mechanic is as much underpaid as the sweeper. The reason for the relatively low value of the work of such men is that we have in the elm- munity a considerable number of men who physically or mentally are not capable of rendering service of greater value. The ease with which the brewery , filled the places of the men on strike is proof of the number of those who cannot offer more valuable service. Into the reasons why there are ench . a number it is not necessary here to enter. No doubt you are right in. saying that a man's capacity of service is kept down by his low remunera- tion, and that if those employing such paid higher wages the men's efficiency would increase. There is truth in this, hut it is doubtful if the efficiency would increase proportionately. The result of a legal minimum wage of 2.15. would probably be that the least efficient, the aged, the feeble, and the drinkers, would be thrown out of employment and become a burden on the State. A. rise in wages wonld not make the aged young, the men of permanent feeble physique able-bodied, or the dull-witted alert. lam not writing to oppose a minimum wage. For social reasons, for the general well-being, it ought to he granted, but you no doubt desire the problem dis- cussed from every pint of view, and this is the contri bution of an
EMPLOYER.

div.head: COUNTERACTING SYSTEII OF INDUSTRY.
div.p: COUNTERACTING SYSTEII OF INDUSTRY.

[To TIIE EDITOR OF THE " ARRINGTON ENAMINEII."] Sir,—Your readers will, I arn sure, fully appreciate the opportunity you are giving them of an all-round discussion of the problem on the right solution of which depends the happiness or misery of millions of human beings, and I hope advantage will be taken of the opportunity by all, irrespective of party, who feel that they can, in any way, direct attention to some phase or other of this many-sided subject. At the outset I should like to point out that there is some danger of being misled by this suggestion you throw out that because the State has been able to deal with Old Age Pensions bud Sickness Insurance it can as easily deal with the establishment of the Minimum Wage, which is of an altogether different nature. It would be as well to remind ourselves that the mere giving of old age pensions or sickness benefits although, no doubt, a boon under present conditions to the recipients, does not tell the whole tale. It has often been remarked that a measure of reform creates as many evils as it cures. Without affirming the absolute truth of this we are witnesses to-day that in spite of all the legislation of the past half- century dealing with a great number and variety of evils, the general complexion of our individual con- dition remains pretty much the same. How this comes about is indicated (perhaps unconsciously) in your article when you state that the carters' dispute was "settled by compromist half-way because of the con- tracts which the masters bad for dealing with blocks of traffic at given prices. This illustrates that it is not a matter of prune importance to the contractors what they pay the men as it simply gets handed on to the employers of the contract ,rs and becomes a charge on industry generally." Employers must make profits or eventually cease to be employers and as a class are probably human enough to desire at least a standard of comfort for their men so long as their business will stand it. The increase in the carters' case, there- fore, apparently does not affect the employers because the extra charge becomes one on "industry generally." This means that some other portion of the community bears the burden in some form or other. It may tend along with a multitude of similar adjustments to increase that cost of living about which we have heard so much of lane and which in the end will deprive indirectly the worker of the gain that he gets directly by a strike ; or it may operate as an aggravating influence on the already sufficiently wretched condi- tion of the "submerged." Under our system of industry in which competi- tion is unrestricted, all such palliatives eventually lose their brce and in the consideration of the possibility of fixing a minimum wage we have the same economic forces to take into account. There is a tending in some quarters to flout " economic laws," but I think we shall find that economic forces will not be defied kit may be controlled. The fatal objection to any form of legal minimum is that it is an attempt to limit the operation of economic forces without controlling them and must fail If the mere passing of an Act of Parliament making it illegal for an employer to pay less than 255. per week would compass the end, it would be a simple matter, but I have sot as yet seen it suggested that such an Act should contain a provision making it obligatory on employers to employ anybody, and so long as some millions of people are not employed at the 255., but left to starve as an alterna- tive, no such law could be enforced against the pay- ment of a wage lower than the minimum. lam quite aware that there is also a proposal that those not taken up at the minimum should be found some sort of work or maintenance by the State, but this is only a varia- tion of the principles of State relief works and charity which have always and must always fail. Even if the minimum of 255. could be fixed and worked to, there is still the fact that competition reduces wages to the subsistence level and though we measure the wage by 2.5, the real wage or purchasing power would return to its normal level. This is the point I have referred to above and the objection is well recognised. To meet this difficulty a suggestion was made at the Progressive Labour League meeting on Monday night by Mr. J. B. Martindale, that the minimum should be based on the value of wheat and would in that case vary with the price of that article. This is another way of trying to dodge the economic forces without controlling them. The attempt to regulate wages by Act of Parliament has been made repeatedly in this country ages ago, but without success simply because Parliament has not control of industry, and one would think past experi- ence on these lines would be sufficient to deter further attempts in this direction. Tulips in the Park. The particularly hue display of tulips in Bank Park has attracted much admiration. Its arrangement does great credit to the head gardener (Mr. R. Whitfield) beds of red, yellow, pink and maculated tulips presenting a beautiful picture. In addition, the trees are now ahnost in full leaf, and in a few weeks the rhododendron bushes, which are very numerous, will be in bloom.

Death of Mr. E. F. Jennings. We regret to annoui ce the death of Mr. E. F. Jennings, 77, Manchester-road, painter and decorator, which took place at his residence yesterliy morning, at the age of 56. :qr. Jennings, who came from Brcsley, Shropshire. bad lived in Warrington for fifty years, and was well-kbown in his ti-ade circles, %Oleic+ he was held in h;gh esteem. He leaves a widow and three children.

St. Mary's C Y.M.A Last Saturday a largely attended social was held in the rooms of the above society in connection with the rambling club. A flying billiard handicap, whist drive, and tea were among the proceeding of the day, which were thoroughly enjoyed. Mr. W. McHugh, the orgauit•er, is to be congratulated upon the com- plete success of the functirm and thanks are also due to the Misses Cross, for preparing the tea.
Local Members and the Woman Suffrage Bill.

_ In the division on Tuesday night which resulted in the rejection of the Woman Suffrage Bill, which was designed to give the vote to about 6,000,000 women, by a majority of 47, the voting of local and district members on the Bill was as follows :—For the second reading : .T. S. Harinool Banner, S. Walsh, Ince (Labour), Viscount Wollner, Newton (C)., who was one of the tellers for the " Ayes." Against: R. Barnston, Eddisbury (C), J. F. L. Brunner, Northwich (L.), Harold Smith, Warrington (C.) Colonel W. Hall Walker, Widnes (C.) The " Examiner" Staff.

_ By the kindness of Mr. Charles E. Parker, chairman of directors, the whole staff of the " Examiner" were entertained to tea at Atkinson's Cafe last Saturday evening. Between forty and fifty employes and several directors enjoyed an excellenfrand well-served tea, after which Mr. Parker (who presided),Mr. Upson, Mr. "Mounfield and the Editor (Mr. T. Weston), made short speeches, bearing mostly upon the future of the paper, which was regarded as exceedingly bright. A musical programme, in which the services of members of the staff were augmented by the humorous sorgs and sketches for which Mr. W. Whittle is so justly famed, followel Dancing at intervals added much to the pleasutes of the evening. Funeral of a Mission Worker.

- - The funeral of the late Mrs. Cross, of Stockport, .who died at the home of her son, Mr. W. H. Mayers, of Warrington, in her 7l i ith year, took place n Warring ton Cemetery on Sunday. Mrs. Cross had .been member of the Bank Quay Mia,ion for a considerable time, and did a great deal, in a quiet way, to promote its welfare. The funeral service was conducted by Mr. Thomas Dale, of the Mission. The chief mourners were : Mr. and Mrs. Mayers (son and daughter-in-law), Miss Ada Mayet s, Mr. and Mrs. Frank Danelow, Mrs. L. Mayers, Mrs. Sharpies, Mies Goodison, Mr. and Mrs. Gibbs, Mr. and Mrs. Billinge, Mr. and Mrs. Chadwick, In addition other rt lstives and friends from Sto,;kpo,t. Eleaviley and litaton Norris were present. The Women's Bible 4.)lass, the Society Class and the church and school members of the Mission were represented. TI e coffin was borne to the grave by Messrs. S. Thomson, D. Brown, J. Davies, J. Rigby, T. Woolley, J. H. Edwards, A. Roberts and A. Walker. Wreaths were sent by Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Mayers, Miss Ada Mayers, Lavinna Mayers, Mr. and Mrs. Dimelow, " Master Georgie, " Mrs Sharpies, Miss M. E. Goodison, Mrs Parry, Mr. and Mrs. Gibbs, Mr. and Mrs. Billinge, Mr. and Mrs. Chadwick, the Worn-n's Bible Class, Society Class and church members of the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay. Warrington Canine Society. The annual general meeting of the Warrington and District Canine Society was held at the headquarters, the Lion Rite), on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Sanderson. It was unanimously decided to ask Sir Gilbert GreenalL Bart., C.V.0., to act as president in place of Mr. W. L Steel, resigned, and Messrs. Harold Smith, M.P., Roger C. Parr, A. Lister-K:iye and Vere B. Davies as vice-presidents. Mr. J. Sanderson- was unanimously elected a vice-president. Mr. Leslie being unable to continue in office, Mr. Sydney Brimelow was, on the proposition of Mr. Leslie, seconded hy Mr. Townley, elected honorary treasurer Mr. F. W. White was re-elected honorary secretary. and, owing to the retirement of Mr. J. Sanderson, Mr. F. Hatton was elected chairman. Mr. Milling was thanked for his services as honorary auditor. and Messrs. H. H. Ferguson and S Hewitt were re-elected bon veterinary surgeons. Mr. Leslie mentioned that the Kennel Club proposed to introduce compulsory registration. It would, he considered, mean the down- fall of such societies as theirs, and he suggested that they ought to write to their representative on the Kennel Club—Colonel Edelsten—requesting him to voice the views of the meeting on the question. After same discussion it was decided that the Secretary inform Colonel Edelsten that the members disapproved of the proposed compulsory regstration of dogs. It was agreed to hold the next show not later than the end of July and also to hold a second show in the late autumn.

div.head: Gigantic Show.
div.p: A Gigantic Show.

Broncho Bill's great Wild West Exhibition, together with a large two-ring circus, will visit Warrington, on Monday, the 19th inst. Pictures of Wild West episodes have been produced with success, and have always appealed to audiences, but, to see the zeal thing, one must visit this Exhibition. Life on the prairies is represented with striking realism, cowboys, cowgirls, Indians and fiery prairie mustangs taking part. Some of the finest lasso throwers in the world will show their adroitness and dexterity, and able and clever whipstock crackers will ai pear, together with expert and experienced broncho busters. Thrilling episodes are given with grand effect. One of them—the Indian and cowboy's ride for life, portrays an exciting race infinitely more vividly than cinematograph pictures can hope to. Another breath taking performance is the log chariot racing by backwoodsmen. But the greatest spectacle of all is•the attack on the Deadwood Coach. It is so 'strikingly illustrative of the old days when fights between the "Pale Face "and the Red man were of frequent cccurrenee, that to watch it is more like reading one of those stirring narratives. The circus acts, which are produced in two separate rings, are novel and varied. Among the special features are extra,rdinat y exhibitions of hurricane cycling inside the smallest track in the world by The Quetas. The audience will witness the marvellous doings of Herbert Oregon, popularly known as the "Wondrous Handcuff Marvel." The Papilicns appear in a new and sensational piece. They are two daring young ladies, who, when suspended by their teeth and revolv- ing at rapid speed at the top of a large marquee, per- form a series of thrilling evoluticns. " Comical Nalker," who will provided the humour, is regarded as the "King of Fools." Besides all these, there is ' a beautiful ten-horse act, and Prairie Bob's Great Cowboy Band will be in attendance. There will be two exhibitions daily.

div.head: LUNATICS IN HOSPITAL.
div.p: LUNATICS IN HOSPITAL.
Much-Needed Improvement Proposed at the Workhouse.
PROTEST AGAINST COUNTY EXPENDITURE.

A proposal to transfer the female lunatics from the crier al hospital to a separate ward gave rise to con- siderable discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday. Mr. E. L. Bent prEsided, and there were also present: Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. Hall, Miss Broadbent, Rev. A. M. Mitchell, viessrs. A. J. Jolley (vice-chairman), J. Billinge, W. Houghton, G. Mather, IV. C. Brooks, W. Furness, R. Lee, T. F. McKinley, J. A. Hughes, W. Flanagan, G. Allen, T. Dale, M. W. Seton, A. BAtomley '(clerk), R. I. Partridge (assistant clerk), W. J. Brown (master of the Workhouse) and C. A. Lowrance (superintendent of Cottage Homes). Mr. A. B. Lowry, Local Government Board Inspector, was also in attendance. PArIENTS DISTURBED BY LUNATICS.

The MAsTER presented a report suggesting the advisabili,y of transferring the female lunatics (eleven in number) from the hospital to the old infirm warda. At the present time they hsd accommodation for 35 patients in these wards, but billy twenty beds were occupied. If the sugeestion were carried into effect, the Guardians would be able to dispense with ihe services of one of the four female lunatic attend- ants ; as thres attend AZIGa (hy doiog a duty of eight hours each) would sii!fice for this work. The urralge- nu-nt would also relieve the present cosgested ncoorn- mooation of the hospital and contralis, tile lowile lunatics until such times as the new mental bioc was ready for occupation. 1 Mr. MATHER pointed out that the ward in the hospita which would be liberated by the transfer' hag of the limatics would he availale for plithiscal patients, wbo were at present overcrowding another part of the build- ing. He proposed that the Board should give the House Committee power to act in the matter and that the Master should have the rooms cleaned and prepared for the reception of the lunatics. Considerable discussion ensued as to the arrangement, which, Mr. Jolley pointed out, wouid only be a temporary expedient. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell and Mr. Billing° took exception to the House Committee being authorised to carry out the proposal without further consideration, Mr. Billinge pointing out that it was pro- posed to remove the lunatics from a first-class hospital to an inferior building which the Board knew nodal, g about. He moved an amendment that the question be referred to the House Committee and the medical officer for report. Mr. LOWRY said he had not the remotest doubt that the suggestion was mace in the nest interests of the Union. As a general principle, however, it wAs a mis- take for Boards of Uuardians to delegate their power of action to a committee until they nad formed their conclusion on principles. Oa the evidence presented he did not see that on this occasion there was any particular urgency for departiug from the usual pre- ceeding of having a report from the committee and then deciding the matter in full Board. He deprecated the idea (which one or two members had advanced) that be himself should report to the Guardians as to the suitability or otherwise of the building. The responsi- eility must rest with the Board, but, if necessary, he would report to the Local Government Board on the question.

• Mr. JOLLEY contended that a great deal of fuss was being made about a small matter, as toe Board was merely acting upon a report by the Workhouse Master. The arrangemeet under which the female lunatics were Put in the general hospital and allowed to disturb the other patients was in itself utterly wrong. The building was never designed for lunatics, and the arrangement, which meant a small saving of money, had been tolerated by the Board for a dozeu years. If they tolerated it another fortnight it would not matter much after twelve years, but he objected to people posing as bane- fitters of the poor white trying to delay a desirable improvement. Toe CHAIRMAN said he had gone into the hospital and heard the lluatics screaming and upsetting the whole institution. Some alteration was necessary. The BoLird authorised the House Committee to carry the matter forward. REGISTRAR'S RESIGNATION.

Mr. W. H. Harrison wrote :—" With great regret I write to ask if you would be eood enough to bring before the members of the Guardians at yonr next meeting this letter. You will well know I have been requested II the Registrar General to retire from my position as Registrar of Births and Deaths after thirty- tour years' service to my native town. 111-health bas been the sole cause of this, and unfortunately L have not been a member of the superannuation Fund. Con- tinual illness and other matters have consideranly taken from my income, so that you will quite under- stand I cannot live and providl for myself and wife without doing some kind of work. If my position could be in any way considered after so long a service, which was also rendered by my late father and grand- fat h,r before me, lab-mid feel very grateful."
The letter was referred to the Finance Committee. COUNTY CALL RISING. REV. A. M. MITCHELL AND " ENORMOUS SALARIES."

The CLERK repor‘ed a large increase in the County call. The amount was E 12,211 ss. Bd. as compared with £10,700 ss. 91. tor the corresponding half of last year. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL : Could you tell us what proportion of that goes to pay the Clerk .C 5,500 a year? The CHAIRMAN: I suppose £5,500 will go out oh that to his salary. Mr. MATHER : I don't know whether we ought to say anything about this. Probably they won't tame any notice if we do. (Laughter.) Still it is a bit rough on us that we have to keep finding this money time after time. Professional men may be able to II d it, but the poor agriculturists are on their beam ends us to where to get a few coppers from, let alone paying heavier rates. I think INe ought to make some protest. The Rev. A. M. AItTcHF,LL said the increasing expenditure was not to be wondered at if the County Council paid enormous salaries and paid one man several times over.
Mr. MATHER : He is a lucky man. I wish I were he. RELIEVING OFFICERS. MORE STRINGENT REQUIRENIENTS.

Mr. Lowitv then addressed the Board. Referring to the tact that the Guardians were about to appoint a new relieving officer, be called their attention to the ques- tion of qualiflcationß. It was perfectly true that the Warrington Guardians had in the vist appointed some admirable relieving ollicerF, who had been men with no previous experience of the work. They had, however, to face the fact,,,, and he thought it was right that he should tell them that since the last appointment was made the Local Government 15 .ard had issued a circular to every Union in the country, in which they had particularly stated that they wero not going to assent to the appointment of inexperienced persons to the post of relieving officer in important districts.

div.head: FIELD FOR WOMEN.
div.p: A FIELD FOR WOMEN.

The Local Government Board had not (as some Guardians had stated) issued any order requiring that every relieving officer should visit every case with which he had to deal every week. Personally he was inclined to think it was a pity that such an order could not he issued, hut it could not. The question of visitation of • cases led him to mention another matter which be hoped they would bear in mind and consider when there was a cari.. venient opportunity. The visiting of cases by a relieving officer was an extraordinarily. valualla thing, i,ut one of the most difficult and perhaps largest class Boards of Guardians had to relieve was that of wid,,ws and children. The visit of a male relieving officer would be very valuable in such cases, but there was a much more valuable thing, and that was a visit by a woman. He wished that Board would consider, when occAsion arose, whether they would not be wise in annointing a female assistant reliev- ing officer, whose duties would be to visit those cases. There was other work for which women were especially suited, and that was in the hands of Boards of Guardians —the work of visitation in connection with Infant Life Protection. He was astonished constantly to find that there were still so many cases in which people pleaded ignorance of the requirements of that Act; and he thought it was only through the appointment of a female officer that a full knowledge of the Act was likely to be spread through the Union.

div.head: PENKETH FOOTPATH.
div.p: A PENKETH FOOTPATH.
Right of Way Questioned.
Inquiry Committee Appointed,

At the meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council on Wednesday, the Cleik read correscondence which had passed between Mr. B. Bates, the agent for Captain Michael Hughes, and himself with reference to the closing of a footpath at Fiddler's Ferry, of which it was stated that the public had had the uninterrupted use for at least seventy years. Captain Hughes con- tended that the footpath was a private way to and from the Ferry Inn, which was his property. The public had no right to use it, and the privilege was only intended for person's coming, from the golf course to the inn. As it had been abused, Captain Hughes gave instruc- tions for the path to be _closed.

- The Surveyor said old residents bad informed him that the footpath was the only way to the ferry across the river, and the only means by which the boatmen who used the river could return to their homes at Sankey or Penketh. The Council appointed a committee of inquiry, con- sisting of the Cuairman (Mr. G. Mather), Messrs. %V. Furness, J. Backhouse and P. C. Garnett.

div.head: MAY QUEEN CROWNED.
div.p: MAY QUEEN CROWNED.
BAND OF HOPE FESTIVAL AT THE PAR HALL.
PICTURESQUE PAGEANTRY.

The streets of Warrington, swept by the pitiless rain, looked dreary and cheerless on Wednesday even- ing. The conditions were the very antithesis of those traditionally associated vrith the incoming of the " merrie month," and a May festival was about the last thing that the dripping pedestrian would have thought of. But in the Parr Hall, where the Rind of Hope Union was holding its annual C.)ronation of the May Queen, there were all the old-time rejiiieings and, with limelight doing duty for the absent sunshine, we did our hest to imagine that we were gazing upon rustic revels in their proper setting. The scene had all the elements of colour and picturesqueness but, apart from the mere spectacular side, it was cheering to see such a large muster of children who had come under the influence of the Band of Hope movement. They were perfectly happy in the parts allotted t.) them end gave the events of the evening that air of reality and spontaneity which constituted their chief :success..

div.p: THE REAL NATIONAL SERVICE.

The duty of patriotism had heen ranch spoken of and enforcea—ana rightly so—but what could he so patri.)l.l3 as to try ti tenin tip a generation that would esche v that which was working such evil in our country ? The choice and crowning of the May Qieen 'via enacted with st,tely ceremonial and it was eruient that all the details bad neen mist clrefully 8.7 mug, d. First there wasa procession for variety of ch4racters and kaleicluscopio hel-uty, v,uuld nave he-,it hard to excel. Nursery rhyd,e nutabilties. representatives of flowers and nstiuoalities, taint-a, troupes of fancy dancers, comical personalities—all help,cl to make up a dehghuul pergtan,_. the retiring queen (Amy Little wood), being escorted to the throne which was illuminated with varie-coloured electric lights. When the 400 children had taken their places on the platform, all joined in singing the hymn " The boys and girls of England," which was followed by the sparkling chorus "The merry month of May." An old-fashioned country dance ushered in the characters concerned in the selection of the Queen. There were the usual games on the village green and a sleepy late-comer was clapped into the stocks to encounter the jeers of the onlookers. However, he was released through the good offices of the fairy queen—a part charmingly taken by Eva Tanner whose exceptionally sweet voice was heard to advantage in a solo. True claims to the throne of the representatives of various flowers were then put forward, the Fairy Queen deciding in favour of" toe fair maiden with the hawthorn gay "—Maud Kirkland, who was joyfully acclaimed as Queen by her youthfui subjects. S. Pemberton then gave, as to the manner born, a humorous song on the adventures of a country yokel in London. Leaving the throne, the retiring Queen greeted her successor, who was crowned with flowers, invested with the garland and sceptre, and promised that " temperance, faith and hope shall be jewels in my crown." There was_ next an imposing procession to the throne, after which Miss Bessie Dutton presented a lovely bouquet to the retiring Queen, who also received a locket at the hands of Miae The multitude then lustily hailed "Her Msjosty " in the chorus "We hail th,e our Queen." At this juncture reference should be made to the excellent singing of the chorus who, under the tactful conductor- ship of Mr. A. Spruue, contributed a number of choice items in a way wnich showed painstaking and efficient training.

div.head: TIIE REVELS.
div.p: TIIE REVELS.

A group of lads and lases then tripped on to the stage end began the revels with that qw.int measure, indispensable at ail May FestivAls—the Morris Ounce— the treedom of their movements and the jingling ot bells combining to please both the eye and toe ear. 'They had been admirably taught by Miss Mo.:ks. The presentation of nationalities gave opportuuiLy for effective tableaux in which sorke of out Coionies and dependencies were happily allied. Sodie little tuaids, in long flowing dresses, danced a vocal gavotte with charming grace and dignity. Tnis was one of a series of fancy dances for wilier.' the perfumers had been trained by Nisi Spinks aud they were undoubtedly the most novel and enjoyable features of 5 lung and inter- esting progiaatme. Tire girls who took part in the Javinese dance looked dainty in their oriental garb and their actions were characterised by remark- able celerity and neatness. The tamb,,urine dance, per- formed by girls in pretty gipsy costumes witu an abundance ot gay ribbons, WAS equslly plesiing, while contrasting strongly in st)le. Finally we had some- thing genuinely English in the suape of a hunt, danceny red-cdatect followers ot hounds who seemed to delignt in the free and infections lilt of this itew.

div.head: VARIED PROGRANINIE.
div.p: A VARIED PROGRANINIE.

A capital action song" Good night little curly head" gave much pleasure and arnusemeni. " Curly head " was a small boy who, weary of his toys and obviously finding it hard to keep awake, was being urged in song to retire t.) dreamland. The children, who had been in:hied by Mrs. Fellows and Mrs. Nurs..., entered into the spirit of this simple yet attractive piece ;.n a natural end entirely su3cessful manner. A contingent of tios (tang-it by Mr. Plinston) had an opportunity of distingukning themselves in a sword drill and they certainly shone. In naval uniform, they went through some difficult evolutions in smart and finis'aect style, fully deserving the round of applauie vvith which they were rewarded. A select choir which Mr. Spruce has got together s +rig " Jack and Jill " and " The distant chimes." Their voices blended beautifully, while the expressiveness of their singing was most marked. A detachment of boys, trained by Mr. G. Shaw, gave an action song "The Postman" with much gusto. They were equipped with formidable-looking postal bags, and sang ot the great variety of missives which they were called upon to handle. Ada Harter, sang "Poor child of a drunkard" in touching style, the feeling which she infused into her rendering being quite exceptional for one so young. A delightful action song" Beautiful Rainbow ' was interpreted by girls for whose tuition Miss M. Isherwood had been responsible. As the title suggests, the item gave scope for the display of tasteful colours in dresses, and the girls also coorried fans. Vocally and spectacularly, this feature was worthy of special note.
