div.head: CANDID CRITIC.
div.p: A CANDID CRITIC.
Rev. W. Cooper's impressions of Warrington.
HOUSING AND WAGES.

The Rev. W. Cooper, who will leave•Warrington at the end of June to take charge of the Primitive Methodist circuit at Leigh, is one of those personalities that count in the life of a community. Of a distinctly progressive turn of mind, he has never hesitated to voice his convictions, even at the risk of incurring resentment in some quarters, but no one who knows him intimately won d think of accusing him of narrowness or bigotry. He appreciates good work, quite irrespective • of the sectarian agency through which it is accomplished and, during his three years' stay io Warrington, he has actively allied himself with the heads and workers of all denominations in what may be described as social welfare movements.

First Impressions. To a representative of the " Exarriner," Mr. Cooper gave some candid impresions of Warrington, its people aud its problems. He first recalled the fact that years ago, when travelling from Chester to Man- chester, he saw Warrington, enshrouded in smoke, and was led to express the fervent hope that he would never be called upon to live in such a town.

div.head: Not a Typical Lancashire Town.
div.p: Not a Typical Lancashire Town.

" Later," he said, "when I was invited to come to Warrington and accepted the call, many of my personal friends sympathised with Me in what lay before me. Now, after three years' work in the town, lam able to speak with first-hand knowledge. Having had a fairly extensive experience of Lancashire towns and of Lancashire life, I may say, first of all, that Warrington is not a typical Lancashire town. It is too much under the influence of its neighbours, Manches.ter and Liverpool, to retain the impress of the Lancashire stamp. Concerning the town generally, it has the sdvantage of Liverpool in ttiat its piincipal park is in the very centre of the town, and personally I have found War- rington a healthy place of residence. My relationships with the people have been all that one could desire. On many occasions his Worship toe Mayor has wine out of his way to show personal kindness, and from individual members of the Council one has received

nothing but the most courteous consideiation. One's fellow townsmen generally may, perhaps, have special leanings towards alcoholism, but, bearing in mind some of the industries of the townioneis not surprised at that. One misses the usual rowdy Lancashire element, and the people have proved themselves a fine set of companions during one's brief sojourn among I hem."

Our Position Musically. In musical circles Warrington took a high place and one could not but rejoice at the proposal to instal a a new organ in the Parr Hall. "Do you regard Warrington as a really musical town? " asked the interviewer.

"Comparatively sptaking," replied Mr. Cooper, "it occupies a very good position. The rank and file aenerally have musical taste and ability in advance of what one usually finds in Lancashire. One might find more experts elsewhere, but the public interest in music is more widespread here. "

"Bow do you account for the apathy so frequently shown towards high-place musical enterprises ? " "I should say it is generally due to the high prices of admission which are prohibitive to working people. The popular concerts and recitals at the Manchester Town Ball and St. George's Bail, Liverpool, do not lack appreciation on the part of the public, and the high class concerts in the Free Trade Hall, Man- chester, and the Philarmonic Ball Liverpool, are able to survive because of their rich partons."

div.head: Craving for Amusements.
div.p: The Craving for Amusements.

"What is your view of the craving for picture palaces and other forms of 4musements which is said to have made such rapid strides in Warrington ? " "I don't think it is above the average here. if statistics were available, I think they would show that Warrington has not as many picture palaces as several other towns one might name. Moreover the present craze for pleasure and light pursuits, while it may be the outcome of commercial and industrial pressure, it. only a passing phase,which, when tested by humanity, will be abandoned and followed by a return to more sJlid interests."
"I suppose you do not regard picture palaces as undesirable in themselves."

I do not —in fact, lam often a patron of them. My only fear is that they may absorb too much of the time and attention of our young people, to the detriment of education and other more necessary tastes." The Housing Problem.

Mr. Cooper was next invited to turn his attention to the needs of the town and to suggest directions in which he regarded improvement as urgent. "The authorities," he said, "would do well to take their courage in both hands and face the housing problem. It would be a great pity if, after the admirable propaganda of Health Week, the matter were allowed to drop. Warrington might earn for itself everlaating fame by boldly taking the initiative in this sadly needed reform. Common decency, morals and any deg? ee cf sound health seem utterly impoasible in some of the houses which still remain to disgrace our town."

"Would you advocate a municipal housing scheme, in the fo,m of tenement dwellings ? " " Considerir g the size of the town, the question of tenement dwell ngs is yet premature. Our population could be comfortably housed within easy reach of business and employment. We need to space out the homes near the centte of the town and extend the building area of the borough. This ought to be faced immediately, before the town assumes impossible dimensions, as in the case of Liverpool, where terements have been regarded as the only possible solution."
" But is not one of the chief difficulties of housing reform to be found in the low wages received byt the dweller in slum districts? "

"One cannot pretend exhaustively to discuss the problem of labour, wages and housing, but one's impression of Liverpool was that the slum had pro- duced a type of workman who was scarely worth the standard wage. From observations, one is quite con- vinced that a properly housed and nourished workman can earn sufficient wage to pay for a respectable home."' Praise for the Library. Mr. Cooper said one of his most pleasant recollec- tions of Warrington would be his association with the Free Library. Be had received the most cheerful courtesy from the staff and the book shelves had afforded continual surprises by their up-to-date and catholic contents. It was to be regretted that some of the best books had so few readers, and that a wonderful mine of information received comparatively scanty patronage. Touching upon religions matters, Mr. Cooper remarked : " One has never been so happy in one's tnil as during the past three years. In one's own church life, members, officials and adherents seem to have conspired together to co-operate with their minister in older that the work as a whole might be a success. ' In preaching I have always found a demand for one's best 'and the chief desire was for the essentially spiritual. Sometimes subjects have been suggested by people in difficulties, but one has always had an appreciative congregation in the borough." The Churches' Temerity.

"Are you a believer in the topical sermon ? " "A topical sermon can be spiritual, and I have tried to meet the strong desire for the spiritual- ising of every day life and affairs. One has been wonderfully struck by the way in which mist of the Churches in the town would come into line upon any special demaud. I am inclined to think that if that occurred oftener and the spirit were fostered, it would not only appear better in the eyes or the public, but would materially strengthen the bulwarks of Church life. There seems to be a deep-rooted temerity at over-stepping the line of demarcation in individual Church life, and the Churches generally have yet to learn what their united strength could accomplish. I have had a most genial comradeship with the members and heads of well-nigh every Church in the borough and closer acquqintanceshin has considerably enhanced one's esteem and regard for other creeds than one's own." "D) you regard the religious life of the town gener- ally as healthy ? " "It is not as demonstrative as one finds it in some centres of religious activity, but one is firmly con- vinced that its roots run to unusual depths and, on occasion, it can give a creditable account of itself." Finally, Mr. Cooper avowed that he was more than pleased that be came to Warrington. The town had a fine history and teemed with romance, and he con- fessed to much regret at leaving it. He should ever remember his ministry here with grateful affection.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

SALVATION ARMY WEDDING AT RUNCORN. The first Salvation Army wedding to take place in Runcorn was solemnised at the Primitive Methodist Church, Greenway-road on Monday afternoon. The bridegroom was Captain Parker, of Runcorn, and the bride Captain Violet Cape, of Colwyn Bay, who was given away by her father, Adjutant Cape. There was a good muster of officers present in full uniform, and they wore sprigs of white heather. The ceremony was performed beneath the Salvation Army flig by Col. G. W. Mitchell, conductor of the international staff band of the army, in London. In the evening a public banquet was held at the Citadel, in High-street, and was largely attended.

div.head: CHILDREN'S HOME.
div.p: THE CHILDREN'S HOME.

The Clerk reported that the Children's Home Com- mittee met on Thursday last. Mr. Joseph Spruce was elected chairman for the ensuing year and Mr. Thomas Wood vice-chairman. It was resolved that the Super- intendent with the assistance of the older boys carry •out the haircutting of the establishment. That, for the present, the boot repairing contract be continued ; that the Clerk make inquiries into the possibility of obtaining a suitable piece of ground adjoining the House for the use of the boys in games of cricket, football, Scc. That the existing lawn in front of the house be utilised for the present for both boys and girls and after other land has been obtained for the boys it be retained for the use of the girls. That suitable swings be erected, and if found possible the services of a joiner from the Worktdouse be obtained to assist the Superintendent in the erection. That for the present the Superintendent be charged at the rate of £3 15s. per annum for the maintenance of his child aged five years in the Home. That the sum of £1 over and above the amount of return railway fare be allowed for him- self and wife for additional expenses in connection with their application for the position of Superin- tendent and Matron of the Home. The Clerk reported that as instructed at the last meeting he had conferred with the Superintendent with respect to the officers' duties in the Home and in view of the decision of the Board to retain both boys and girls in the Home for a period of one year after leaving school, the superin- tendent had withdrawn his application for additional assistance.
The minutes were confirmed. SHAVE, SIR!

Morris, Broom, Linaker and Spruce be appointed to report on the following matters : Hospital staff alterations, alterations to quarters recently cccupied by the boys and girls. It was also decided that votes of thanks be accorded :qr. J. G. Kidd and Mr. A. Fryer Runcorn, for gifts of periodicals. MAKING HIS WAY IN THE WORLD.

By dint of bard work Arthur Aston, a smart yonng man, 21 years of age. has improved his position so much that he can now claim that he has risen from Workhouse boy to butler-valet in a well-known Liverpool family. Mr. Spruce introduced the young man, who had -expressed a desire to show how a former inmate at the house had made his way in the world. Mr. Spruce said his duty was a very pleasing one. The young man went from the house six years ago and, step by step, he had made his way until now he had obtained a highly respectable appointment. He was an ambitious young man and was determined to improve his position still further. So many of the inmates had gone out and had been returned because they had not done so well that he thought the Guardians would be glad to see an instance where one of their inmates had done really well. It was something to be proud of. The young man was not above owning his ralationship with the Institution, for in his own words he said "because I was

GRAPPENHALL AND MOORE SEWERAGE SCHEMES.

At a meeting of the Weston Parochial Committee on Wednesday last,Mr. J. B Chadwick was appointed chair- man and Mr. J. Tudor vice-chairman of the committee Messrs. div.p: HOUSING AND TOWN PLANNING.

Mr. A. Lister-Kaye gave notice that he would bring before the Council matters concerning the Grappenhall Sewerage scheme. MOORE SEWERAGE.

At a meeting of the Moore Sewerage Committee it was resolved that the engineer examine the four lowest tenders for dividing the No. 1 and No. 2 mitten works and report as to the exact cost of each. div.head: NO INFECTIOUS DISEASESS.
div.p: NO INFECTIOUS DISEASESS.

Dr. Adams, medical officer, said they had again been very free from infectious diseases during the past fort- night. There was one case of diptheria at Halton, one case of pulmonary tuberculosis at Frodsham and one at Stockton Heath, which had terminated favourably. The report was adopted.

Mr. Jeeves, for the promoters, addressed the Com- mittee on this report, and urged that, while the pr f sent population of Lymm was lin.ited, there would be an early and large development, and that it was desirable that they should have powers to deal with such matters as the culverting of streams, the closing of wells, and the sale of icecream, &c., remarking that Lymm was a great day resort of Manchester day-trippers. Mr. Rhodes, for the Local Government Board, and Mr. Whickard, for the Home Office, urged that it was most unusual for Parliament to give these powers in such cases, and that the Lvmm Council should first avail themselves of Public Act powers and bring their by-laws up to date. The Chairman, after the Committee had consulted in private, announced that the Cimmittee had given very careful consideration as to the course they should take on these two parts. They had given full weight to the probable development of Lymrn. They felt that there were a few clauses ' that might be an advantage to the Council, but they had to bear in mind their duty, from a public point of view, not to grant exceptional legislation to one district that should be granted to the country as a whole, and also that before granting statutory powers under a local Act they must be satisfied that the locality had by-laws or the public powers that could be obtained by by-laws. Therefore, while they made no reflection upon the pro- moters for including these parts in the Bill, they could not entertain them.
Parts 5 and 6 accordingly were struck out.

„ The Uommittee passed the clause fixing the periods for repayment of money borrowed, giving, after some hesitation, the period of 50 years for the repayment of the purchase money of the waterworks. %Nith regard to the charge for gas, the promoters agreed to make the maximum price ss. per 1,000 cubic feet. At present the maximum is Gs. 83., but the actual price is 3s. The remaining clauses of the Bill presented no features of public interest. The Bill as amended was ordered to be reported to the House.

TIM MAY QUEEN.—We would draw our readers' attention to the advertisement on the front page relating to the Lymm May Queen festival, which is to take place next Thursday. The procession will leave the Cross at 2.30 p.m. and follow the same route as last year, namely, Church Green, Brookfield, Eaglebrow, the village, Pepper-street, and on to the vow well-known football field. As will be seen by the advertisement a large and efficient variety of attractions have been secured for both the afternoon and evening perform- ances, and a peep at the practices convinces one that the audiences will not be disappointed with the festival if the committee are granted a fine day.

MOTOR CoLusion—The cross roads between Booth's-hill and Eagle-brow are r.-cagnised as the most dangerous spot in the whole of the Lymm district and on Wednesday about 12.15 p.m. another bad mark had. to be placed to the already lengthy record. As a motor car belonging to Messrs. Holt Bros., of Broom Edge, conveying a party of girls from High Legh, who had been having a cooking lesson at the Council Chambers, approached the corner, another car, /driven by the owner, Mr. J. H. Holt, builder, of Lyra, came out of the road from the village. Both drivers at once turned their cars to one side, with the result that instead of one car being run into broadside-on, in which case it would have been overturned, the front of the cars collided, as it were at the apex of a V. The glass screens, front wheels, mudguards, Aso., were broken, but beyond one of the girls getting slightly cut, and some of the others suffering from the shock, no further damage was done. It was very fortunate that neither car was travelling fast at the time or the collisionr would have been much more serious.

PRIMROSE LEAGUE.—The annual general meeting of the Lymm (No. 1,141) Habitation of the Primrose League took place on Wednesday night in the Con- servative Club, when the Ruling Councillor, Mrs. Legh, of High Legh Hall, supported ny Alm Callender, Mrs. Rylands, Miss Moorehnuse, Mr. A. W. Callender and Mr. W. P. Wands, presided over a good attendance. The report upon the past twelve months was presented by Mrs. A. W. Callender, the hon. secretary. The hon. treasurer, Mrs. W. P. Rylands. gave her report, which showed that the finances of the Habitation were in a very satisfactory condition. Addresses were given by Mrs. Legh and Mr. W. P. Rylands. A musical programme, consisting of part songs by the Thelwall Choral Class ; duet, Mr. and Mrs. Williamson; and solos by Mr. H. E. Odber and Mr. H. E. Gibbon made the proceedings more enjoyable. A vote of thanks to Mrs. Legh was proposed by Mr. W. P. Rylands, seconded by Mr. F. W. Druce, and carried with acclamation. All the retiring officers and members of the Executive Com- mittee were re-elected. Mr. Ernest Morris proposed, and Mr. Latham seconded, a vote of thanks to the artistes which was carried.

FARM FlRE.—Last Sunday at 11.40 the peacefulness of the night was rudely disturbed by the penetrating clang of the Lymm fire bell. Footsteps were soon about and enquiry elicited the fact that a fire had broken out at Mr. W. Shakeshaft's farm, Broom Edge. Within twelve minutes the firemen were on the way to the spot. It appears that a motorist passing through Broom Edge noticed flames issuing from a Dutch barn and came down at once to the Lyrum Fire Station, wbere at the same moment the sierra was being received on the Council Office telephone. When the brigade arrived they found the fire had got a very firm hold, in fact the roof had just fallen in. Pipes were laid to a pond close by, but, owing to its small capacity, this was soon run dry. The attention of the firemen were then directed to prevent the Eire from damaging the surrounding crops, in which they were successful, though two men had to remain on the scene until Tuesday. The fire' which is believed to have been started by a tramp, destroyed the barn, a lurry, cart, horse rake, other farm implements, and two bays of oats which were to have been threshed the very next day, the damage amounting to between £250 and £3OO, of which only part is insured. The farming implements destroyed were the property of Mr.Shilton, of Heatley, who had unfortunately left them on the site of the fire preparatory to completing his removal to the small holdings he has rented from the Cheshire County Council, on which land the destroyed barn was stand- ing, his own farm having been recently sold. PRIMITIVE METHODIST ANNIVERSARY.—Last Sun- day and Monday the Primitive Methodist Sunday School anniversary was celebrated. Though the promoters received no assistance from the atmospheric conditions, which were of the now too familiar order, the services were in every way a pronounced success. In the morn- ing the Rev. T. D. Phillipson' of Manchester, gave au instructive story to the children about the oestructive wind and the discontented flowers after which he preached an appropriate sermon from the latter portion of verse 3, in the fourth chapter of Phillipians, speaking briefly about anonymous workers and what a great deal the world owes to the obscure labourers of the past, and the reward that one day falls to each one who has been faithful. At the afternoon meeting a closely packed congregation were kept interested by the excellent programme provided by the scholars, which consisted of songs including "Little helps for Jesus," "Gently falls the rain" in which solos were sung by Eliza Shaw,Cissie Tonge,May Vost, Esther Warhamand Florrie Wibberley : Bible lessons, admirably read by the Misses Lois Priestner and Eva Tonge •, well given recitations and a dialogue by Frances Mottershead, James Henry Appleton, Jack Atherton, Edward Griffiths and Alfred Priestner ; a small solo by an equally small singer, Ernest Wibberley ; and an earnest address on "The Friendship of Christ" by Mr. Phillipson.—Mr. Phillipson's sub- ject at the evening service was " The instinctive worship of God by mankind" (Acts 'Evil., 23). The music at this meeting was especially good, the scholars giving delightful renderings of " Elysian" ; "0 Light Everlasting" and "The Bells of the Gloam- ing," the original beauty of the latter piece gaining piquancy from the bell device manipulated by Mr. J. Atherton.—On Monday evening a public tea was pro- vided in the schoolroom. At the meeting which followed the choral element predominated, and the choristers further enhanced their reputation. Specially noticeable was the case with which they surmountea the difficulties of Lehman's "Choral march," in which the abrupt changes of key form a trying ordeal for untrained singers, and their performance should be very gratifying to the conductor, Mr. J. Edwards. A _ .

ialojuell Words with wings" was creditably given by the Misses M. Ackerley, M. Broadey, M. Evans and M. Tonge ; as were the recitations contributed by Miss Edith hckerley and Messrs. A. Appleton and A. Miller. Mr. H. Champ, who presided, delivered a most typical Sunday School address on the word " Forward ' as taken from one of the pieces sung that evening. The exacting duties of accompanist were tastefully per- formed by Miss Shore. This year the proceeds of the anniversary were supplemented by a substantial amount collected by Mrs. Edwards, the Misses Esther and Emily Warham, E. Tone, E. Shaw, B. Cross, J. Thornicroft, N. Mairs, and Messrs. Alfred Priestner, P. and S. Wellord, W. Moss, W. Downward, F. Cheetham, E. Moss, C. Moss, J. Clare and J. Guest.

div.head: LYMM. FUTURE OF LYMM.
div.p: LYMM. FUTURE OF LYMM.
Waterworks Bill in Committee,
GREAT DEVELOPMENTS CONTEMPLATED.

The future development of Lymm will be profoundly affected by the Lymm Urban District Council Bill which was on Tuesday before the Local Legislation Committee of the House of Commons, presided over by Mr. W. Middlebrook. The Bill is to secure powers for the purchase of the water undertaking, and also for the purpose of extending the present gas and water under- takings. In addition, general district powers are being sought. Mr. W. J. Jeevee, who appeared for the District Council, stated that it was practically an unopposed Bill, the petitions of the Cheshire County Council and of the London and North-Western Railway having both been withdrawn. THE CLERK'S EVIDENCE.

Mr. William Mulford, the clerk to the Urban District Council, said the Council were unanimous in their resolution to promote the Bill. A poll of the electors gave 566 votes in favour of the Bill and 204 against. The opposition was not to the Bill as awhole, but to the question as to whether the district known as Warourton should be included in the water or the gas limits. The present estimated population of Lynam was 5,025.

div.head: DISCOVERY OF SALT.
div.p: THE DISCOVERY OF SALT.

In his general statement on the Bill, Mr. Jeeves said that the five sections of the Bill included the transfer of the undertaking of the Lymm Water Company and the acquisition of lands of the Lymm Estate Develop- mens Company. With regard to general powers, the Council considered that, as they had to come to Parliament to acquire the water under- taking, it was desirable that they should provide in other ways for what they believed would shortly be a very much enlarged district. Lymm ten years ago was almost wholly a residential place in which people carrying on business in Manchester and Warrington came to live. When a discovery of salt was made in one part of the district there was then added to the residential population a working population. Even after that development,however, Lymm did not advance to any great extent, one reason being that the main landowner, Mr. Dewhurst, offered no inducements to people to come and build. This position changed about two years ago,wben the land belonging to the Dewhurst family was bought by Sir William Lever,who purchased some 1,500 acres. Of that he offered 956 acres in 150 lots, and these were mostly sold. As to the balance of his purchase, Sir William Lever retained a part for a building estate, which now belonged to the Lymm Estate Development Company and was in process of being laid out. NEGOTIATIONS WITH SIR WILLIAM LEVER. Sir William Lever also retained a part of his purchase for a salt area. Of the countryside in which Lymm was situated one part was semi flat and lay low down, while another part stood very high. It was in the low part of Lymm that the salt was found, and the salt lands were divided from the adjoining lands by a fault and by rising ground. It was therefore perfectly consistent with the growth of Lymm as a residential place that the low-lying lands should be developed for salt purposes without damage to the other parts of the district. The third part of the estate retained by Sir William Lever was the Lymm water under- taking. On several occasions the Council had made unsuccessful attempts to purchase the undertaking from the previous owners. They opened negotiations with Sir William Lever, and the only condition he made as to selling was that there were about 32 acres of land which the Council must also take, including Lymm Lake and the adjoining lands. The price ultimately agreed upon was £20,250 for the water undertaking and the lands. The value of the lands might be put at from £4,000 to £5.000. The income which the Water Company had been receiving was about £BOO a year net, and this the Council would receive as against the interest and sinking fund they would have to pay on the purchase money. The water supply was very arnple,and was quite capable of supply- ing a much larger population. FUTURE DEVELOPMENTS.

As to future developments of Lymm, Counsel said that, in addition to Sir William Lever coming into the district, Mr. Verdin Cooke, salt manufacturer, had bought 100 acres in the salt area, and great develop- ments were expected on that estate. Lymm was also a pleasure resort for the people of Nlancheiter and the adjoining towns. The Council could therefore look to some revenue from the lake if they chose to develop it on the recreative side. But the main reason why they felt that they must have the aoutrol of these 32 acres of lands, including the lake, was that they were abso- lutely essential to the preservation of the amenities of the district. The Council further desired to extend the water limits so as to include the parish of Warburton, which adjoined that part of Lymm in which the salt was situated. Whatever industrial salt developments took place they would be located in Warburton and Heatley jointly. The Manchester Ship Canal ran close by and the London and North-Western Railway went through the Heatley district, so that there would be the fullest possible opportunities for getting the salt away cheaply. Messrs. Verdin Cooke had been inquiring whether the Council could supply them in the Warburton area with' both gas and water, and all the evidence went to show that they were on the eve of development both from tae industrial and the residential points of view. The promoters calculated that the cost of the proposals would place a penny or twopence on the rates for about five years. MR. WELFORD AND INDUSTRIAL PROSPECTS.

Evidence in support was given by Mr. George Welford, solicitor, of Manchester, who lives at Lymm, and is chairman of the Parliamentary and Finance Com- mittee of the District Council. In answer to the Chair- man, Mr. Wilson said that Mr. Verdin Cooke had told him that he had had an application for a site on the Ship Canal for the erection of chemicil works. He had no idea of the probable number of men to be employed at the Verdin Cooke salt works. All he knew was that Mr. Verdin Cooke would put up works. They anticipated that the cost of pro- moting the bill would be about £l,OOO. He understood that the Manchester Ship Canal Company were preparing to build n wharf on the fringe of the estate capable of berthing large ships. After hearing further evidence, the Committee, through the Cnairman, announced that without express- ing any opinion upon the figures which had been placed before them of purchase and of future outlay, they were of opinion that the public interest of Lymm and Warburton would be met by the proposed scheme, and they therefore found the preamble proved.

div.head: GAS SUPPLY.
div.p: THE GAS SUPPLY.

Mr. Jeeves next proceeded with the rart of the Bill dealing with the extension of the gas supply limit to Warburton, and with the reconstruction of the existing gasworks. He mentioned that all the capital liabilities on the existing works and land had been paid off with the exception of £.190 on the land. The Council wanted fresh borrowing powers to the amount of £20,000 to reconstruct on a larger scale. The land was ample for that purpose. Evidence was given that the existing plant was anti- quated and out of date, and that it would pay to recon- struct. Mr. W. W. Carr, consulting engineer, put the saving at 7d. par 1,000 cubic feet. The £20,000 would pay for new works and mains capable of dealing with double the present annual ssipply of 25,000,000 cubic feet per annum. In reply to the Chairman, Ms. Carr said that electric lighting did not diminish the demand for gas. In Ormsk irk, where he was manager and where there had been such competition, the gas supply had increased 30 per cent. in the past two years. The committee passed the preamble and then adjourned.

div.head: COMMONS REJECT PART OF THE BILL.
div.p: COMMONS REJECT PART OF THE BILL.

When the Committee resumed its proceedings on Thursday, clauses carrying out the purchase of the waterworks and the reconstruction of tha gasworks were considered and passed. On parts 5 and 6 of the Bill, in which there were 58 clauses, the Local Government Board reported that, although there were precedents for the clauses in recent local Acts, they doubted whether many of them were necessary or appropriate to the circumstances of the Gymno district. Before applying to Parliament for these special provisions the Council should, urged the Local Government Board, have availed themselves to the lull of the powers which were open to them under

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

WESLEY GUILD.—The monthly devotional meeting was held on Monday evening when a thoughtful address on Psalms xxiii. was given by Mr. R. J. Peake. The sacred solo "The King of love my Bbepherd is" was sympathetically rendered by Mrs. L. Bennett. Mr. F. Wright presided in the unavoidable absence of the Rev. E. Morgan.

div.head: RISLEY.
div.p: RISLEY.

INDEPENDENT METFIODIST CHURCH, FEARNHEA D. An open Sunday was observed in the above school on Sunday when a large congregation gathered to bear the songs, recitations, Ike., given by various scholars. Mr. K. Bold gave an interesting address on foreign missions and their work. Mr. John Houghton presided. Miss Gertie Hughes was at the piano.

Mr. Charles Franmore, as the old fisherman, Daddy Dean, is unsurpassable in his character studies, and patrons may anticipate an artistic treat. Nor must we omit that capable young actress, Miss Amy Dalby, who is making such a great name in the provinces. The play will be beautifully mounted and staged, the properties in one act alone costing over £3OO.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Wee Georgia Wood is undoubtedly the " star " at this popular place of amusement this week and he is amusing and entertaining large " houses " twice niuhtly. On the occasion of our visit this diminutive artiste played with marked success in his original scena " The Nursery." He takes the part of the impish boy who protests most strongly against the cajolery of the nurse who wants to get him to bed, in a very natural manner, indulging in the eccentricities of babyhood in a very realistic fashion, causing roars of laughter. Georgie is alal a clever impersonator and, as Neil Kenyon in the "Postman of Dunrobbin," he is decidedly popular, imitating the Scottish comedian very skilfully. His other impersonations in which he was highly successful were 111arie Lloyd and Vesta Tilley. To-night (Saturday) he will give his late success "Baby in India." Cosgrove and Burns, comedy duettists, entertain in a pleasing manner, and, whilst low comedy is the prevailing element, the male artiste scores as a tenor singer of some ability in "Bonnie Mary of Argyle." Mark Stuart sends the house into convulsions, for he introduces only the smartest of gags in his comedy " turn." lie is quite rightly described as the unconventional comedian and is extremely popular. Dorothy Miller is a vivacious comedienne and thoroughly captivates in her songs" Follow me home" and " On honeymoon Island." The four Joburg girls sing ragtime in the usual manner, but dance exceedingly well, a feature being the national dances introduced being given with marked effect. Goodall and Knox, cross-talking comedians with modern ideas and an abundance of clever gags, help to keep th house in good humour. The Three Jennetts, two gentlemen and a lady, are clever and smart acrobats, who present a comic train- ing act, in which there are seven well-trained doge and fifteen pigeons" schooled " to perfection in the various antics they perform. Miss Della is a vocalist who pleases the audience, her style being neat and her voice good. On the cinema we have "The line at Hogan& " a laughable comedy,

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

The special holiday attractions for next week will be Sammy Shields, the sporting enthusiast; Gillin, ventriloquial humorist; Edna Lyall, celebrated soprano; Doreen O'Connor and Co., in refined one act comedy "The future Lady Watteau " ; Grotto Troupe, hand jumpers; All Chesters, versatile comedian; and Will Geste and Winnie Hol, entertainers.

div.head: THEATRE ROYAL.
div.p: THEATRE ROYAL.

The popular domestic play " Why did she run away ?" has been presented before exceptionally large audiences at the Theatre Royal, bcotland-road, during the week. The play is a powerful one, full of sensa- tional incidents, and deals with the romantic love affair of Norman Helmsley and Sybil Vanborough. As usual their path is strewn with thorns, and it is only after many exciting adventures that a happy con- clusion is arrived at. Miss Phyllis Morton successfully solicits the sympathies of the audience in her realistic portrayal of the guileless country maiden, and Mr. Clavering Craig plays the part of the minister-lover in an impressive manner. Mrs. C. V. Charles as Cecil Whitley is also successful, and is ably assisted in his villianies by Vera Maxwell, a part undertaken by Miss Hazel Head. The other characters are well sustained. Mr. Jack Carroll and Mr. Roy C. Hilton as Willie Lightning and the Hon. Percy Cholduely respectively are responsible for the comedy which is rich and laughable.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

The Royal Repertory Company will appear next week in the new American version of the most daring play of the period, adopted from Ouida's great novel, "Moths." This should prove a capital attraction and the cast will be: Prince Sergius ZourofT, Mr. Clavering Craig; Lord Jars, Mr. Charles Vivian Charles ; Duke of Mull and Cantire, Mr. Jack Carroll; Raphael de Correze, Mr. Roy Hylton; Boris, Mr. Edwin Mackenzie; Valdimir and Ivan (Cossacks).

"I REMEMBER ---- REMINISCENCES AND STORIES OF

OLD WARRINGTON. GLEANED FROM MANY QUARTERS. To-day we continue our series of "I remember" stories, a column conducted by Mr. Arthur Mounfield, who will be pleased to receive hints or matter for articles. Readers must remember on their part that the stories are independent of each other, and are the recollec- tions of distinct personages. Mr. Mounfield here does but chronicle the recollections of other people, a fact which will account for the changing character of each succeeding paragraph. When Manchester-road was "in the Country." It was my fortune to be born in Man- chester-road nearly eighty years ago, and I thought you might like to know what Manchester-road was like about sixty-five years ago when I first knew it. Not that there is anything very interesting to describe. It is more a matter of saying what wasn't there than what was. For we looked upon Manchester-road from the point past School Brow as being "in the country," and when I describe it your readers will see how sparsely populated it was. We will begin at School Brow and take the buildings on the left hand. The block of cottages which stand at the corner of School Brow were there in those days, and the next building was the stately Fairfield Hall. The big plain wall shut it from the view of the pedestrian, but those who did get a view of the gardens had a treat, for the grounds were beautifully laid out, the front being done in landscape style. A sun-dial stood in front. There used to be a large open-air swimming bath surrounded by high walls, but I am not sure whether this was built at a later period. It stood upon ground which is now covered by Fairfield-street. After two fields lined with hedges and ditches we reached Fairfield Cottage. This is still standing, but it was a much more attractive place then with a spacious garden. Another fitld and then the old cottage known as Sand Hole Cottage. This also is still to be seen wedged in among more modern houses. This is all there was on the left-hand side. On the right-hand side there were no buildings whatever until the traveller reached a point nearly opposite Sand Hole Cottage. Here were the few old houses which still stand at the point where the Cemetery begins. The next dwelling was called " Nearer Finger Post Farm." It was a farmhouse with stables and shippons and a pump adorned the yard. The occupier farmed the fields now covered by the cemetery, and the house itself vanished when the cemetery was made. Right opposite to the farm a foot-road ran across the fields to Marsh House, another old farm that gave its name to Marsh House-lane. The only other building in the Man- chester-road which I remember was opposite to Padgate-lane. This was Finger Post Farm. A finger post stood at the juncture of the roads and the farm took its name from it. The farm had a big set of buildings, and a large yard with the usual pump. It was taken down when the cemetery was made and the Cemetery house stands on part of the site. Beyond Padgate-lane there was only Bruche House until the wayfarer had crossed the Twiggery Brook and reached Bruche Hall. It was a very lonely and depressing bit of road and tales of a highwayman hanged in chains by the brook did not help matters for those who traversed it after dark. I understand that this story of a robber being hanged at T wiggery Brook is based upon fact. The tradition was very fresh in my youthful days and did not lose anything when told for the benefit of naughty straying boys. Marsh House-lane. In Marsh House-lane there was nothing at all that I remember except the farm called Marsh House, which stood like a lonely farm - house. Your readers will not need to be told what it was like as it still stands, but I think the farm buildings have gone. It I looks very dingy now compared with what it was in the days when it was a clean and cheery farm, looking over smiling fields towards Orford Hall and Winwick Church. When I say there was nothing else in Marsh House-lane I am forgetting that at the corner of Gorsey-lane two or three cottages had been built. What I Remember as a 'Bus Conductor of nearly 40 Years ago. The 'bus started from the Central Station arches in Crown-street and was owned by Mr. Stanley Higham, the well-known gun- smith, whose shop stood where the Jubilee Buildings stand now in Horsemarket-street. It ran between Warrington, Latchford and Grappenhall four times a day, viz., 8.30 a.m., 1 p.m., 5.30 p.m., and 9 p.m. It carried as passengers some of the most prominent men of the town. On starting in the evening the first one to take his seat, as a rule, was Mr. Gray, director of the Tanners-lane tannery. The next was Mr. Banks, of the firm of Dakin and Banks, corn and flour merchants. At Parr's Bank we would pick up Mr. John Dunne, manager of Parr's Bank, and occasionally Mr. Edward Greenall, director. At Bewsey-street we picked up Mr. Joseph Davies, Mayor of the town. At Scot- land road we picked up Mr. Stubbs, tool manufacturer. At Lyme-street, Mr. Rowson, wine and spirit merchant, got in. Waiting for it at Market Gate would be Mr. Smith, of the firm of Smith and Milling's; Attorney Moore, town clerk ; Mr. Murray, director of the White- cross Co. ; Mr. Owens, grocer, Sankey-street; Mr. Blackhurst, jeweller ; and Mr. Lomax from Crosfields. At the corner of Dolmans- lane we would pick up Mr. Joseph Harrison, one time Mayor of the town. Lower down we would take up Major Pickmere and his son, who is now Town Clerk of Liverpool; also Messrs. Tom, John and Edward Greenall, from the distillery, and occasionally the present Mr. Henry Greenall. At Rylands- street we would take up Mr. John White, land agent. At Bridge Foot there would be waiting for it Mr. Tinsley and sons, tanners, of Mersey-street; Mr. Hutchins, tanner, and . of golf fame ; Mr. Thewlis, tool manufacturer; Captain Reynolds, Mr. Charles Broadbent, Mr. Tom and Mr. Walter Cartwright, bottle manufacturers, Bank Quay ; and at the Pin Mill Mr. Eddleston. We had for passengers, many times, the present Lord Cross, the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, the late Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, the present Sir Peter Walker and his brothers, the late Mr. Peter Rylands,M.P., Mr. John Rylands and Mr. Glazebrook Rylands, the Macquordale Bros. of Newton, and the Bolton Bros., glass manufacturers, Orford-lane, the late Mr. James Nicholson from Thelwall Hall, Major Nicholson and Mr. Stanton, Greenfield, Thelwall. J. P. HESSIAN.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 10, 1913
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 10, 1913
A RELIC OF SIR RICHARD ARKWRIGHT.
A Building whose Associations should Save it from Destruction.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S PART IN
div.p: WARRINGTON'S PART IN

In the heart of Manchester lying between Market-street and Cannon-street is a mass of old top-heavy architecture which, despite a hundred forbidding features, is well worth a few moments of study. It is only necessary to turn into one of the narrow passages which run from street to street to discover that behind Market-street there is a tiny world that has not changed for a century. Let the hurried passenger beware of entering one of these cross streets in the hope of dis- covering short cuts. Short cuts they may be, but a single lurry is large enough effectually to block his path and make necessary an undignified retreat. Yet, with a little leisure, a quiet meandering movement through these courts and alleys may prove quite interesting. It is a hundred years since these old warehouses arose, and they arose at the call of the new cotton trade. Here is the mill which Richard Arkwright built the in garden of his Cromford Court

div.head: INVENTOR'S WORK.
div.p: THE INVENTOR'S WORK.

pride. But the interior with the new machines in motion would please him more for, like John Gilpin, he knew the disadvan- tage of "want of pence," and it is nice to think that he lived to reap the reward of his mental toil.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE SPINNING
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE SPINNING
FRAME.

house, and where the machinery was driven by two men who turned a fly wheel at the end of a shaft. The house has gone, and of the garden no modern visitor could suspect the possibility ; but the mill remains. We visited it the other day to see how it looks in its honoured age. The sentence of destruction hangs over it, but it holds up its head serene and untroubled. Its strong brickwork bonded every three courses, looks as good as ever, and would outlast most of our modern stuff. A strong oak beam pro- jects at the third storey, holding a teagle windlass.
With a gabled clock tower, well designed, it holds up its head quite gracefully, and Richard Arkwright must have surveyed it from the windows of his house with no small

This ole building hemmed in among ugly warehouses and suffocating alleys marks an era in our history. The distaff and the spindle, so deftly handled in Lancashire homes spun their last reels in 1763. They are now in museums or kept in drawing-rooms (the pretty ones) to remind maidens why the prayer book calls them " spinsters " on their wedding day. This first cotton mill with its spinning frames turned these household tools into curiosities and ornaments. With a vision of Lancashire cotton mills and the cotton trade before us we look upon

- Reproduced by kind permission of the ".Manchester City News." THE FIRST COTTON MILL, Richard Arkwright's first mill and warehouse built in his garden at Cremford Court, Manchester. Soon to be demolished,

the old building with something more than Curiosity. We should like to put it in a museum with the old spinning wheels, or else, better still, make a cotton museum of it; but these things cannot be. The best we can do is to present our readers with a picture of the building and promise to tell in this column, upon another day, the story of Richard Arkwright and the War- rington colleague who worked out for him the mechanical part of his spinning frame. For the evidence does not leave us in any doubt that the machine which was to revolutionise Lancashire was designed, not in Bolton, or Manchester,but in Winwick-street, Warrington. A.M.

think I might say very important when we take note of developments and results. It was in Cloth Hall Yard and Bank-street that both Rylands and Greenings began their business career. I have been told that John Rylands, the father of Peter Rylands, at one time our M.P., along with Mr. Greening, carried on business in partnership as Rylands and Greening, the business, however, not being wire or metal, but the making of cart sheets. I may be wrong in this as it was a little before my time, but perhaps some other reader may put me right. I understand that they started business as wire makers separately, and not in partner- ship; Mr. Rylands having a place in Cloth Hall-yard and Mr. Greening on the other side. When we take notice of the develop- , ments which two generations have brought, it is rather interesting to think of these two businesses huddled together in Cloth Hall- yard, and finding it big enough.

Whitby's Stumps. In telling the story of "Whitby's Stumps" your informant has slipped into an error. I remember Whitby's shop very well. He was a druggist and his shop was not where the Maypole now is, but on the opposite corner on the site of the shoe shop. He had his place of business at one time where Mr. Leigh's shop stands in Horsemarket, and his son continued as a druggist in a shop in Bridge-street.

div.head: STORY WITH THE MORAL.
div.p: THE STORY WITH THE MORAL.

In quite modern times—the middle of las' century, ty be precise—a book appeared which was destined to make history in an unprece- dented fashion by arousing the better instincts ,Df a whole race. It was not for some years after Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe's "Uncle Pones Cabin" was first published in the "Wash. ington National Era" in 1850 that its full effect came to be felt and realised. But even as early as 1853, when the authoress visital England, she was presented with an address from the ladies of England which was handed to her at Stafford House by the Earl of Shaftesbury. She was well received also in France and Switzer- land. Undoubtedly during these years "Uncle Tom's Cabin," with its intensely pathetic pic- tures of slave life, was making a fervid appeal to the sympathies, and leavening the opinions of the whole eivilised world. It was inevitable in a country like the United States of Amer lea, where for generations up to that time negro slaves had come to be looked upou as mere chattels, that when a large body of publip opinion was aroused by the terrible state of thinos depicted in " Uncle Tom's Cabin" civil strife would ensue. The American Civil War is unfortunately a matter of history. " Uncle Tom's Cabin" was written with the best of motives, but few will doubt, or attempt to mini- mise the part played by that book in deter- mining the inhabitants of the Northern States to secure the abolition of slavery at all costs. _ _ _

There have been other books which have helped to make history by securing urgent social reforms for the people. Cases in point are Dickens' vivid picture of the workhouses in other days; Charles Read° in his " Hard Cash" completed the unveiling of lunatio asylums, which Cockton began in "Valentina VPX,"

div.head: DEATH. OF MRS. D'OYLY CARTE.
div.p: DEATH. OF MRS. D'OYLY CARTE.

Mrs. Stanley I3oulter, better known to the public under the name of Mrs. D'Oyley Carte, died at Savoy Court on Monday after a long illness. She joined Carte's staff just before the production in 1877 of " The Sorcerer" at the Opera Comique. She frequently visited the United States to arrange the production of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas, lecturing tours of Sir Henry Stanley, Bret Hart° and others, which D'oyly Carte directed while in England. She was his right hand iu the building of the Savoy Theatre and the management and production of its repsrtory, the building of the Savoy Hotel, and the building and starting of the English Opera House, Westminster, a few years later to become the Palace Theatre. In 1888 I-he was married to D'oyly, and after his death in 1901 she managed all the affairs of the Gilbsrt and Sullivan operas, including the great revival at the Savoy Theatre in 1006-1908,

WHERE THE FRENCH MOTHERS DO
BETTER.

In writing an article addressed to parents Miss Ellen Terry calls attention to a detail in which the French mothers improve upon the English ones. "I am told that French mothers reprove their children by appealing to their taste, rather than to their conscience. fais pas ca. Ce n'est pas joli ' (not pretty). The English mother always says Don't do that; it isn't right.' As the word 'right ' opens up controversy I think the French mothers have the best of it with their joli. ' A child may want to do what is wrong out of bravado, out of a spirit of contradiction. But very few children would not be ashamed to do something 'ugly.' Perhaps later on they will find that wicked and ugly things are near relations."

BAD FOR EVERYBODY'S DIGNITY. A few weeks ago there appeared in the " Daily News" an interesting article on Lord Strathcona and his work in Canada. After reading the account of how Lord Strathcona drove the last spike which completed the Canadian Pacific Railway, an officer on that railway who was present on that auspicious occasion has sent over a story. "When Lord Strathcona was called upon to drive the golden spike into the last sleeper of the Canadian Pacific Railway,the foreman in charge of the section was told to make a hole in the sleeper, so that the prEcious spike could easily be extracted and preserved under a glass case. As it was early spring, with a thaw setting in, the foreman bored out quite a substantial hole, and, to make the ceremony of 'driving the spike' appear real, he carefully made the deep hole and filled it with slush. When Lord Strathcona, bending low before a distinguished gathering, raised the mallet and drove the huge nail far into the sleeper, a great squirt of melted snow instantly darted back at him, covering his long beard and immaculate clothes in the most unexpected and embarrassing manner. But his Lordship did not forget to join in the chorus of half-smothered merriment that burst forth at his expense." PICTURESQUENESS OF THE INDIANS. Indians are always more picturesque, and in some respects distinctly better, than the nations which have hitherto accepted Christianity. It is perhaps a mark of British modesty that a large number of Christians in India prefer the Indian to their fellow Christians, and an unconverted to a converted Indian. Superficially, at least, the Hindu and Mohammedan are much more interesting, more polite, more charming than the British Christian with his exact clothing, his clean linen, his stiff manners, and aston- ishing want of something to say. And it may be freely asserted that no Indian looks the better for adopting European dress and manners. Boots preserve the feet from snake bites, and trousers are an admitted sign of advancing culture. The topee is a better protection from the sun, and gloves have their value in cold weather. But an Indian in boots, trousers, a topee and gloves is a lamentable spectacle; and an Indian woman who has changed the sari and chuddah for a hat and coat has assuredly fallen from grace.

The Indian population,in- tawn and country, might seem to e,--ist in order to please the aTtistie eye. The bright colours which everyone loves never seem gaudy in the Indian sun. They never seem to clash with one another. A chance group of men, seated on their heels in a conclave by the wayside, or the women that happen to be at the well for water, will inevitably form a beautiful study in red, terra-cotta, yellow, blue,salmon colour, or flower sprigs, on suit or sari. The brazen vessels, on the heads of the women, or the huge hookahs in the hands of the men, will complete the picture. The tiny children are allowed to run about the streets even of a large city, with no other dress than a necklace ; and the little chocolate bodies, with the shy looks, and the brilliant eyes, are more beautiful than the birds or the animals,which swarm in every field and tree. —Dr. R. F. Horton in the "Contemporary Review." THE VALUE OF LOCAL HISTORY. Those who follow the articles which appear upon this page and who appreciate the efforts of the " Examiner " to quicken interest in local history will be interested to read an extract--from an article in "Chambers Journal" written by G. M. Fraser, the Librarian of Aberdeen.

"People may wonder sometimes if there is any sphere of human interest untouched by present educational methods. I hope to show that there is at least one—the teaching of local history in our schools—which has received not so much attention as it deserves, but which as a grounding in historical and geographical study is full of promise for the community. In what I say I have Scotland specially in view ; but it applies with even greater force to many parts of England and Ireland, where the ancient historical interests are in some ways still more definite and abundant.

"It has been suggested that the teaching of local history to our children might tend to make them more parochial or provincial in their outlook. One can hardly think so seriously. Education in any subject cannot have a narrowing effect. And notice this, that local history is to be taught not as the sole history instruction given, but merely as a grounding; and also that you cannot teach local history without going far beyond your own locality and coming into touch with:the larger things of the outer world. The ancient local charters, priceless docu- ments, ought to be seen by our children. They, and the structures or lands they refer to, or the ancient church or well or ruin at our doors, enable one easily to touch the young imagination of the child, and so to move from these concrete, familiar things into the very heart of our national history." Mr. Fraser goes on to show how much of interest there is to learn in local history—in the coats of arms, the patron saints, place names, names of streets, the town boundaries. "The main purpose of introducing the teaching of local history, however, is not merely to give information and to brighten educational work; it is to give children a larger and fuller interest in life. The ordinary things about us in town and country, seem- ingly so commonplace, will become trans- formed for those who have the seeing eye and the understanding heart. At present, in respect of an intelligent historical interest of this kind, the condition of things in both rural and town communities is far from what it should be,"

div.head: TRAIN THAT WAS SEVEN YEARS LATE.
div.p: A TRAIN THAT WAS SEVEN YEARS LATE.

Sometimes I see "The Railway Magazine," and am rather fond of looking at the pictures and the stories. Like most other boys I decided very early in life to be an engine driver when I grew up, and though that has not come to pass I dearly love a railway engine yet and always feel a bit happier after I have seen a good one. I thought I would this week copy you a delightfully true story about arailway train. It is from " The Railway Magazine" and is beaded "Only seven years late." This is the tale in brief. It is American, of course, but quite true. "The train started from Beaumont, Texas, bound for Port Bolivar, at 11.30 a.m. on Sep- tember Bth, 1900. The distance is 71 miles, and the train was due in Port Bolivar at 1.55 p.m. It maintained its schedule for the first 33 miles to High Island. There it was surrounded by waters from the Gulf of Mexico, which had crept more than 38 miles inland and flooded the railway. When the waters subsided the train was high and dry on the prairie, the only rails left being those on which it stood. For miles up and down the line not a vestige of track remained. After hours of terror the passengers made their escape through the mud. The engine and four cars were abandoned, and remained a landmark.

Eventually the affairs of the railway revived. The road was rt-built, and at last the rails from either end were connected with those under the long overdue train. At first it was proposed to tow the weather-beaten engine to its original destination. The machinists looked over the rusty locomotive and found it in good condition, considering its exposure to the elements. They worked on her for a while, and pronounced her fit to complete her journey. Removing the sea- weed in her rusty firebox and raking away the debris round the wheels, they fired her up, and amid the cheers of everyone she moved off, creaking and 'rheumatic' in her joints, but still serviceable.

The news was telegraphed to Port Bolivar, and when the train, more than seven years late, arrived, the time of her re-appear- ance and length of delay were gravely chaiked on the bulletin board. Half-a-dozen of the original passengers assembled to greet the train, and the fact that it had actually reached its destination was telegraphed all over the country."
MY DADDY.
My daddy says that when be was A boy, he never cried Ner run away from 86031 to go A-swimmin' ; never tried To cut a lickin', never failed
To do as he was bid. (Well, maybe daddy didn't, then— But gran'ma says he did!)

My daddy brags a lot about The way he acted when Ile was a boy. (My ! but they must 'A' been most angels then!) He says he never dared to peep Beneath the cake-box lid. (Well, maybe not ; but, anyway, My gran'ma says he did!)

"I never tied a tin can to A dog's tail in my life ! " Says daddy. "An' I never carved My initials with a knife In great big glarin' capitals On the piano lid." (That's what he told me sollumly— But granima says he did!)

"I never cared for circuses An' brass bands an' such things." (Say—honest! that's just what he said I) " An' tops and devil slings. I never waited after school To lick some other kid." (Ile says he never done those things— But gran'ma says he did !) Say! but my gran'ma's mighty wise; She knew my daddy when He was a little runt, and says He was a terror then! Ile says he never cut up none The times he was a kid. (I know I ought to blieve him, but My gran'ula says he did!
THE WEEKLY SMILE. SQUARING THE BILL.
The bright little surgery at the rear of the, doctor's house was occupied by two—the medical man and a patient,who had got over his illness and was being attended to for the last time.

" es, yes," said the doctor; "you're all right now. You needn't come here again." "But, sir," remarked the patient, " vot aboot der bill? I ain't got mooch money. Viii you dake der bill out in trade?"

Th.e doctor looked the man up and down. " Well, I might," he rer lied. "What is your business?" "I am der leader of der liddle Cherman band, sair. Ve viii blay in front of your house every evening for von month."

div.head: WINTER DIET.
div.p: WINTER DIET.

In cold weather it is absolutely necessary to give careful attention to our daily diet. To combat success- fully the troubles that winter brings we must be well nourished. Foods that merely fill the stomach and appease the appetite are not sufficient. What we require and must have is pure, sound and efficacious nourishment. Some of the most valuable foods are the cheapest so far as money is concerned. The most striking example of highly-nutritious concentrated food that can always be bought at a low price is the Greek Currant. This little dried grape is a veritable store-house of nutriment and just the ideal food required at all times, especially in winter. It is merely Ei case of Nature craving for Nature; because to feel hungry is natural, and to satisfy it with Nature's own pure product is strictly in keeping with the fitness of things. Currants contain more than 80 per cent. pure nutriment—all put there by Nature. Quite immaterial is the form in which Currants are taken. So long as they appear in liberal quantities the body will be soundly nourished. An entirely new and interesting little book telling you all about Currants, and giving recipes for a great variety of sweet dishes which can be made with Currants, has just been published, and your Grocer .will give you a free copy on request. The book is called" Home Recipes for Cooking Currants."

div.head: LOCAL BUFFALOISM. "TOM SANGSTER "LODGE INSTALLATIONS.
div.p: LOCAL BUFFALOISM. "TOM SANGSTER "LODGE INSTALLATIONS.

A very interesting ceremony in connection with the above Lodge took place the other evening, when Primos John Wolfenden and Edwin Lawton were raked to Knighthood in the Order. The installation ceremony was impressive!, performed by the Grand Installing Officer. "Sir ' Thomas Davies, assisted by the D.P.G.P. " Sir " William Bradbury, John Holden (Past Grand Chamberlain). " Sir " W. H. Smalley, " Sir " Walter Sutton," " Sir " James Walsh, " Sir " William Bruce and others. Regalia visits were paid by tf e :members of the following Lodges :—‘ Duke of Connaught " (Manchester), 6" T. Wakefield," "Golden Fleece," "Fred Bonnell," " Victoria," "Coronation," and "Queen Alexandra" (all of Warrington), the 'Widnes Lodge" and the "Torn Siddeley," Earles- town, the visiting brethren being received by the W.P. " Sir " Walter Miller, who accorded them a very hearty welcome. Congratulation, were received from all present by the newly-elected knights (Wolfenden end Lawton), who both richly deserve the honour conferred upon tkem.—The Installing Officer (" Sir" Thomas Davies) was the recipient of many well-merited com- pliments, in the way in which he had performed the ceremony. The W.P. " Sir " Walter Miller, K.0.M., K.G.H. presented (on behalf of the "Tom Sangster" Lodge) a sp:endid propaganda jewel to " Sir " John Taylor, in recognition of his sterling qualities and the great services rendered by him to this Lodge in particular an i the Order in general. _ _ .

A beautiful ooliarette with suitable ornaments was also presented by the P.G.C. (on behalf of the Install- ing Officers), to "Sir "John Taylor, hs a token of the high esteem in which " Sir " John is held by the brethren. The P. Grand Chamberlain (John Holden) in making the presentation, said the recipient had endeared himself to the brethren not only by his assiduous attention to duty,—whicla included a great amount of spade-work, but by his geniality, which was no unimportant factor in mlintaining the prestige of the Ancient Honourable Order.
Primo George W. Taylor, was also presented with a Jewel of the Order and was heartily congratulated by the P.G.C.

div.head: LICENSING TRANSFERS.
div.p: LICENSING TRANSFERS.
RE-BUILDING OF THE LION HOTEL.

Extensive modernising alterations are about to be made at that old-established hostelry, the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street. At the Transfer Sessions at the Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor (in the chair) and other magistrates, Mr. T. S. Steel made application on behalf of Messrs. Peter Walker and bon, Ltd., for the altera- tions to be made. Ile submitted plars to the Bench, and said that their Wort hips would see that the object of the alterations was to provide better accommodation for dining and extra facilities for serving ; to give a distinct and separate entrance to the hotel in Bridge- street and to the meeting room on the first floor, and to provide modern sanitary conveniences. The magis- trates would see that the only entrance to the hotel at present was by the side door underneath the covered archway, which was very inconvenient, as persons had to pass the bar before they could get into any part of the hotel. On the first floor there was a lodge room, which was also used for dancing. The kitchen and servants' apartments would be upstairs, and the billiard room and drinking parts of the house would be down- stairs under one supervision. The kitchen would be on the same floor as the dining-room, which would be far more convenient than the present arrangements. Over the new entrance in Bridge-street there would be per- manent co-vered archway with a glass roof. They would remove the calisading in front of the hotel which would increase the width of the footpath, widening the street very considerably, Land was very valuable in Bridge- street, but his clients were making that concession. Any projecting portion of the building would he higher than eight feet. The Chief Constable said the police had no objection as the alterations would constitute a necessary improve- ment. The arrangements at the Lion at present were far from satisfactory. It would be a highly desirable improvement. The application was granted and the Bench suggested that the window to the vaults should be in keeping with the other windows overlooking Bridge-street. Mr. Steel said the suggestions would be carried out. Mr. Steel was also successful in his application for permission to carry out sanitary improvements at the Higher Seven Stars.

LICENSING TRANSFERS. The following licensing transfers were granted at the same Court :—Off-licence 18, Priestley-street, from C. W. Nsnnerley to William Henry Jones • Norton Arms, from John West to James Lodge ; flop Pole, from James Lodge to John Henry Savory ; Corporation Inn, from Elizabeth Bancroft re Frederick Roper ; otT- license in Hoyle-street from Richard Narroway to Thomas Lowe.

The police had no objection to any of the transfers, the whole of the new applicants having submitted satisfactory testimonials and the old licensees having conducted their houses in a satisfactory way.

Mayers, off-licence, Powys-street to Mr. Fair's licence, and Mr. Mayer's son-in-law (Mr. Dimrnelow), to the off-licence in Powys-street until it was closed. He was instructed to apply for an adjournment of the sessions for four weeks in order that Mr. Allison, of the Cemetery Hotel, could attend. Mr. Longland, who appeared for Afr. Allison convened with Mr. Browne in his application to adjourn those transfers ft r four weeks. The magistrates agreed on this course,

div.head: Examiner Saturday, May 10, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, May 10, 1913.
WOMEN'S QUESTIONS. Labour-Saving Devices to Meet the Dearth in Servants. MAY AS A MARRIAGE MONTH. THE GERMAN ROYAL WEDDING.

The approaching wedding of Princess Louise of Prussia ignores the popular superstition which is supposed to be of Roman origin, that May is an unlucky month to marry in. The King and Queen are to be i present at the wedding, which s to take placCon the 24th, and such an important event in the Kaiser's family is of particular interest to the people f this country. There was at one time an expectation that their Majesties would be accompanied by Princess Mary, who, although some few years younger, has many points of resemblance with her distant cousin Princess Victoria Louise. Both Princesses are only daughters in a family of boys, and are frank, companion- able girls, rather preferring the society of their brothers to that of friends of their own sex. Their home training and education have been on much the same lines, and both have unmistakable gif's of mind. Princess Victo.ia is of middle height with a slender girlish figure, whilst Princess Mary, who is now in her seventeenth year, is of stronger build, bu,t, both have fair hair and they have similar tastes in a love of ou'door life and are pat ticularly expert in horsemanship. In Germany the universal bridal flower is the beautiful little myrtle blossom, which the most ancient of nations regarded as the emblem of Jove and marriage. It first became a rival of the orange blossom in this country, when Queen Victoria's eldest daughter married the Crown Prince of P, ussia, and the German Royal wedding is not unlikely to restore it to favour in the fl nal adornment of this season's brides. WOMEN TRAVELLERS.

Women, it must be allowed, are daring travellers, and their records of feats in this line compare favour- ably with the records of not a few explorers of the sterner sex. One woman, Miss E. L. C. Watson, recently rode a motor-bicycle for thousands of miles aer, as the lovely African Veldt, with nothing to pro- tect her but a revolver. Another quite unconcernedly pitched her tent and made herself quite comfortable on an uninhabited island of the South Pacific Ocean. Yet another rode through Persia, whilst one still more intrepid Voyagettse scaled frozen reaks of the Himalayas that never before had been trodden by the human foot. Atrek from the Cape to Cairo was successfully carried out by one woman traveller,whilst another member of the timid sex croised Africa alone with twenty native servants and was often hundreds of miles from the nearest white man or woman. Some of these brave women, notably Miss G. and L. Bell, have done valuable scientific work during their explorations and have beens exposed to every kind of danger and experienced the most hair-breadth escapes from storm, flood and savages.

DOING WITHOUT SERVANTS. " First aid to the Servantless " is the title of a little book which Mrs. J. G. Fraser has written to show how easy it is for women to solve the servant problem by doing their own housework. For this purpose chief reliance is placed upon labour-saving devices, and it is claimed for an American invention, that it will soon be possible to do much of the housework by electricity obtained from the air. Magnetic appliances are attached to the roof of the house and sufficient energy is obtained for cooking, laundrying, and workii g generally. Such an invention, if it has any real practical merit, ought to go some way towards solving the servant problem. Doubtless many married house- keepers wish it were already an accomplishcd fact. DRESS FOR OUTDOOR SPORTS.

With the opening of the tennis and bcating season thoughts naturally turn to the various suits and their tccessories required for outdoor sperts. Former'y, the girl of fashion had only one garment to consider in this connection—her riding habit—but nowadays she has to dress for many pastimes, and tennis, g if, c 5 cling and boating, all demand special costumes if they are to be serviceable and comfortable as well as smart. The knitted skirt has not had the vogue with us that it has had abrcad, and it is generally rejected in favour of light, soft woollen tweeds or linens. For tennis the skirt is cut rather wide at the hem, to allow free play in running backwards, and with these are worn a comfortable loo,e jaoket of fr;eze. There is, however, no restriction of choice of sports coats in silk or fancy wool, which may be had in all the loveliest shades and colourings. With tweed skirts, stockings to match in colour must be worn, but it is possible to affect many variations in a sports c3sturne by changes in minor details concerning the belts, collars, cuffs and ties. THE LOW CUT NECK. There is no manner of doubt that the low cut neck will carry all before it this summer and already it is seen in the streets. It is certainly more comfortable than the high-boned collar, also more hygienic, and the girl with a short neck will hail its popularity with ky for she has suffered riot a little from the discom- fort of the other extreme. It is to be hoped,however, that the low neck will be kept within certain limits. It should not exceed two or three inches in depth below the throat for outdoor wear. If kept within the bounds of moderation it is highly probable that the fashion may remain permanent, but if carried to the length of vulgarity, it will surely be banned. There are, of course, many people who ought not to wear low collets, because their necks are neither young, plump, nor white. But for these fashion has provided styles that at least do not emphasise defects. Such are the various forms of the Medici collar in wired lace. The

height must depend on the neck of the wearer; the prettiest of these are finished with a satin tie which falls on the corsage. A thin neck should always be softened by a collar high at the back, with deep points on each side, leaving the neck bare only in front. The skin can be improved by a very narrow black iibbon or a piece of ribbon velvet fastened as high as possible with a buckle or other piece of jewellery.

div.head: RECORD IMMIGRATION.
div.p: RECORD IMMIGRATION.

The official immigation returrs of the Canadian Government for the fiscal year ending Marah 31st last have now been issued. The total of 402,432 immigrants from all sources constitutes a record one, being more than 48,C00 in excess of last year. Of the t0ta1,150,512 were British, 1311,009 were from the United States and 112,881 from other countries. Despite these huge totals, however, applicltions from Manitoba farmers for farm help are received at Winnipeg at the rate of 75 a day, while the entries for homesteads at the Dominions Lands Office in the Edmonton district alone number 35 per day.
