happy you eould be in 'Fairy .11 aii it only you chose! Married to a nice wife—one who would be a daughter to me—" "But I have no desire to marry!" broke in Desmond. rather irritably. "Why. I havo oeen too well occupied to give a single thought to that subject. And now I'm afraid I'd find ii difficult to make myself agreeable to girls if I were condemned to associate with them." • "Well, my dear, I hope you will neverthe- less make. yourself agreeable to your cousin when she comes here on a visit to-morrow," said Mrs. Nugent. "So we are not to he to ourselves, after all " returned Desmond, annoyed. "Do you remember Nora?" asked his mother. "She grew to be a very pretty girl." "Did she?" said Desmond, in an in- different tone. "I don't imagine I've thought of her half a dozen times since I left here. Then she was seventeen—and a rather plain girl, as well as I recollect. But even then I had grown out of companionship with her, and she was only a lanky child when I used to play with her. No, I can't imagine Nara Duffy 'being even passably good-looking!" "She is more than that, and, what is better, she is one of the nicest girls I have ever known," returned his mother, warmly. "Indeed, Desmond, you could not understand what a comfort Nora was to me when Harry died—l really think I would not have sur- vived that trouble had she not come to me then. And your poor father took to her greatly in his last days. He had not liked her father, and had never really forgiven his favourite sister Mary for marrying wild Jack Duffy. But when your father came to know his niece well he soon appreciated her worth. He intended to leave her a little annuity, but deferred that until too late. However, I hope she will not be the loser by that, for he had a desire to secure a more complete benefit for her."

" Indeed? " said Desmond, to please hie mother rather than to satisfy any curiosity of his own. "In what way?" "By arranging a marriage between her and you, Desmond," replied Mrs. Nugent. "That was your father's most earnest wish before he died.'

"You amaze me, mother—though I really do not know mhether to be more astonished or amused ! " exclaimed Desmond, looking greatly annoyed. And it is hard to say in what words he would have further expressed his indignant feelings had not Patsy at that moment entered with the dinner.
That evening, Patsy, who had been making close observations, said, with a ehake of the head and a disconsolate face:

"Sure, Mr. Desmond is changed entirely— destroyed with the travelling in foreign parts. He's picked up a way of speech that's not like a Christian's. And then he's sometimes a way with him like an ould drill-sergeant turned young—l never heard the like in the family, that was all GO easy-going. Whethen, he's not a Nugent at all at all ! "

Desmond Nugent saddled a horse next morning and rode to the nearest large town, ten miles distant. With characteristic energy he had decided to make prompt in- quiries about the procuring of workmen for the renovating of Fairy Hall. The journey and this business together used up a good deal of time, and the afternoon was well ad- vanced when he found himself once more in sight of his mother's home. _ _

The day had been a glorious one. An in- tensely blue sky, just flecked with an odd white cloud that occasionally tempered the sun's heat and threw light shadows that chased one another over hill and moorland, seemed to smile at the recollection of the pre- vious day's deluge and gloom, and almost to persuade one that they were but an uncom- fortable dream. The low hills wore their holiday dress of purple heather and golden furze- the meadows, that yesterday looked so prostrated with the rain, now waved proudly their wealth of long grasses plentifully sprinkled with meadowsweet and wild flowers of innumerable hues. Even the bogs, that yesterday were sodden morasses, had now taken on a wild beauty as the sun shone on the rich brown of the turf cuttings, and the sky was reflected on the rippling surface of the water-filled bog-holes, while on the sur- rounding rugged moorland floated the ban- ners of a multitude of yellow irises and white bog-cotton. Desmond, who walked his horse back in order to look about him. leisurely, found him, self fully under the spell of his surroundings, and at the moment felt almost as lighthearted as the larks that trilled above him or the countless other birds that made the hedge- rows joyous. When he got to the house, instead of going at once indoors he turned towards the back grounds, which he had not yet .visited. His vsay led by the right side of the house, through a small enclosed garden. This little space presented a striking contrast to its sur- roundings, for it was beautifully kept "and planted with a wealth of carefully tended flowers, and in its centre was a rustic seat. Desmond smiled to himself as he passed through it. Beyond lay the large garden. Once a place to delight the eye, it was now a wilderness. The paths had become almost obliterated; what had formerly been flower-beds now grew only a luxuriant crop of weeds, among which some degenerated flower, like the shabby ghost of its ancestors, occasionally shamefacedly showed itself; and shrubs had become unkempt trees. Even Desmond, un- sentimental as he thought himself, could not suppress a sigh as he compared the place with his recollection of it.

At the end of the garden was a wicket leading on to a wooded slope. This old playground of his boyhood was just as he re- membered it. His steps took him towards a tree with a low-spreading bough that had been a favourite perch of his in the old days. He came on it suddenly, and then stopped short in surprise. For a girl was seated on the bough, swinging herself gently while she read.

She was a very pretty girl, black-haired and fair complexioned. Desmond, who had approached noiselessly on the grass, had stood staring at her in his surprise for quite a minute before she looked up from her book and saw him. Then he recognised those big grey eye.

"Cousin Nora ! " he exclaimed. She started, and then, jumping lightly from the bough, made him a mock curtsey. I have the honour of being addressed by Cousin Desmond, I presume ? " she said. 'How you have changed, Nora ! " "By ' changed ' you mean 'improved '—and I am to infer that the improvement was needed ! " she retorted, with light mockery. And you, too, have changed, Cousin Des- mond—almost out of recognition." "Not altogether for the worse, I hope ? " he said, slightly piqued. "I don't know, but suppose I shall find that out before long," she returned, almost seriously. And then she added comprehen- sively, with a touch of that old imperiousness that recalled the days when she was a little girl, and he, a big growing boy, was her abject slave, "Tell me all your adventures since we last met."

He laughed, then he gave her some kind of account of the years of his absence. It was not a very detailed account, nor a highly inte- resting one, as it was a mere record of prac- tical work for the most part, and almost de- void of exciting incidents. But Nora Duffy listened to it with bright eyes and a pink colour in her cheeks.

"You haye done- well, Cousin Desmond," she said, when he at length paused. "You found the wisest way of getting over one of those crises that, if mismanaged, so often wreck lives. And now, you have come home a sensible and practical' man—but not too sen- sible or practical, I hope." "I couldn't well be that," he said, seriously. "You could— Oh, a mushroom!" she ex- claimed, darting forward to pick it. "Another—and yet another!" said Del- mond, securing his trophies. "ee4 I am better than you to start "Old times!" laughed the girl. "Do you remember, Desmond, how you could not en- dure my getting more mushrooms than you? And I wonder have YOU forgotten that 411-:

and wnen 1 got nearly twice as many, flung yours at me in a temper? "I could get twice as many as you now, I'l sure—and I challenge you to disprove th!ttt , he said, gaily. "Come, it's worth trying',„ir, "Yes," she returned, sharing his hulti,-.1 "And July mushrooms are the best. should appeal to your practical spirit, esPvii. ally if you miss your dinner through this IZA sorbing occupation, and have to be satisu'' with the mushrooms instead." it vail ne contest proved exciting. But, ea - ros spiced with reminiscences, the mushron were not the sole source of interest. /VIZI. the reminiscences somehow changed to no denees, it happened in a most unacootlaw way that one of the finest mushroom barli, ever obtained on that spot was shamefo.l. wasted, the fungi being dropped one by in the absorption of conversation. "Where, oh, where are my mushrooms, at length cried Nora' in comical disints 'And I'm sure I had three times as many

you!" led "And mine!" laughed Desmond. ;Nell mine are gone, or they would bille shamed you into admitting my victory!, "You want everything your own way 10" Desmond," she said, half-seriously. "Everything," replied Desmond, quite serious' V. "And so, when you come to do up -- place, you will follow your own inclinationgi and change it out of all recognition. Deg' mond, spare the old home!, "I shall make it a real fairy palace for BIY mother and yourself, Nora." / "Not for me," she returned, quickly. can pay only a short visit to Aunt Kate lin No, I cannot do as she wishes, and make tie; home mine—in spite of my love for the old place." "And so you insist on going away Yagriintf 13.1 a governess?" said Desmond, quite int, nantly: " Now, listen to reason. our aunt ' home is yours by every right." "It is not,, she returned, decisivelY. "And then I wish to be independent—as you yourself did." "Nonsense "

, Cousin Desmond," 51! "Nonsense yourself, retorted. "But I shall visit Fairy. Hall age'"' some time, I expect. And when I do I hope -- oh! I hope you will not have changed it toomuch. Make it like it was, but do not laY * desecrating hand on some places." d "'rho little garden, 'for instance?" 're Desmond, with a smile. "So my mother hae been telling you her romance?" "Yes," answered Nora, softly. "And th*,, memory should make the old home the desirable and wonderful place in the Ivor' for you as well as for her. What a pretti story. She did not wish to leave her girl' hood's home—she was very yoleg, and ref' Imps uncertain of her own heart—and tnen your father came on his horse one day, and": well, it is lovely to think of! No wonder Mut Kate will always cling to the old place, whie" she made her home again soon after her mar' riage. It is the dearest place in the world"" the very dearest." "Nora," said Desmond, suddenly athPPing short, "you must not leave this place you love, so well. Stay here and .teach me to think 91 it quite as you do. Marry me, and then--- " No, no! A thousand times no!" en° flashed, her cheeks aflame. "No? Why not? Do you so utterly dislike me now?" he asked, offended at het vehemence. "I shall hate you if you ever say that , again yes, hate you! she stammered. "You have said this just beeause—" She broke • off, and Desmond, almost 09 much agitated as herself, said nothing fer some moments. So in silence they weili through the desolate garden, and then enter° the little garden of memories. As they were crossing it, Nora, her head erect and her cheeks very red, walking in, front, Desmond suddenly put his arms roun° her and drew her to him.

"I have loved you from childhood, nil dearest, though I never realised that until to- day," he whispered. "Now do you hate ran for telling you that? No, you don't-1 see bY your dear eyes that you don't. So if you won't promise to be my wife—promise 'here and now—l'll carry you off, too, as my father would have carried off my mother if she had not pledged her troth. Yes, you'll have to come with me, by horse, or motor, or flying machine, with marriage by special licence a! the end of the trip. And remember that t mean what I say, for I am really a terriblY practical man Nora, my love." She returned the gaze of his dark eyes, un- certain for a moment, and then buried her face on his shoulder.
"I dare not say no," she whispered, with re happy lauo.

Mrs. Nugent, going out to look for Desrnonc! and Nora, saw them enter the garden 01 memories, and stood a moment watching them fondly. Patsy, coming after her to urgo haste for the dinner's sake, stopped too. Ana then, when the little drama was enacted, 111 cried joyously, " Hurroosh—his father's sou. He's Nugent after all; Heaven be praised. Do you mind that day, ma'am, long ago, wile° the poor master—" Mrs. Nugent smiled at the old man through tears of joy; then she stepped forward W clasp the lovers to her heart.

div.head: GARDEN OF MEMORIES.
div.p: THE GARDEN OF MEMORIES.
BY MARTIN J. McFIUGH
Author of. "Peacock Farm," "The Chance Guests," "The Choice of a Heart," "A Little Brown Her," "Straws in the Wind," &o.

I. The old home! Desmond Nugent loaed once more on the place of his birth as the side-car traversed the muddy avenue, and Mingled feelings surged through his mind as his eyes took in the scene of his earliest re- collections. How familiar it all Ns as after his absence of ten years' yet how changed also. For that short period seemed to have done its worst to Fairy Hall. The house itself had a shabby and weather-beaten aspect, and the grounds, which had once been so neat and pretty, now looked woefully neglected. Before the car had come to a standstill the hall-door had opened, disclosing a white- haired and ruddy-checked old man. Des- mond waved his hand and smiled. Patsy Connell, of course, just as he had expected to see him. "Welcome home, Mr. Desmond; welcome home, sir," cried Patsy, in a voice for all to hear. " Sure, sir, but this is a great day for us all—though, more's the pity, 'tis a mortal soft day to be arriving on. Bedad, but I'm hoping you'll take no harm out of the rain— and the cold wind that's with it—after being in them hot foreign parts all this time— though that same seems to have agreed with you finely. But come in, sir, for 'tis herself •',is waiting this blessed minute to welcome you." "Thanks, Patsy," said Desmond, walking briskly into the hall and taking off his drip- • ping overcoat. "It's a pleasure to see you so well and young-looking—why, you don't seem a day older than when I left. I can't .say that of the old place, though. It seems to have greatly changed." " Ah, Mr.. Desmond, and that's true for you—but if that 'was all the chi. nge there's been we'd have little cause for grieving. Wirra! but there's them you left well and hearty that you'll never see again in this world, and—" But the rustle, of a skirt had caught the young man's ear,. and he turned abruptly into a sitting-room. There, standing by the door, was Mrs. Nugent, a curiously nervous expression in her expectant face, and her hand laid tremblingly over her heart, as if to check its throbbings. "Mother," said Desmond, with suppressed emotion, "here I am back again to you." "My boy—my only loved one now," cried Mrs. Nurnt, the fent% that had clouded her face fleeing and giving way to a look of almost ecstasy as she drew him to her heart and wept tears of joy over him fondling him as if he were once more a child. "How young you look, mother! and how beautiful still ! " exclaimed Desmond, as he held her at arm's length. And indeed he spoke only the truth, for although Mrs. Nugent was well over fifty she looked years younger. Her tall, black-clad figure was straight and slender, and her proud face, to which trouble had given a new touch of patience, was smooth and white. • "As for you, Desmond, what a fine fellow you have become ! " she returned, with a look of happy pride. "If you have changed, it has been a marvellous change for the better. ,All those years I have borne your image in ''my heart, and it has been that of the timid boy I last saw you. Ah, Desmond, how I have missed you sometimes; yet I cannot now regret your absence, as it has done so much for you—so much in every way. And then you have missed a great deal of sorrow." She sighed deeply, and Desmond echoed her -sigh. Ten years before, when he had gone to the Cape, he had left his home wounded and angry with the knoIN ledge that his elder brother was the object of all his parents' • affections and hopes, and that ho himself counted as little. That grievance, indeed, had previously made him, while still a boy, go to -England and study mining en- „gineering there. As a fortune-hunter, he had been one of the few •to find what he sought, 'and in the abstraction of that exciting quest he had seldom thought of the home he had left, and when he had it was without regret. He had been nine years away when he learnt that his brother had been killed by a fall from a trap. The rapidly failing health of his father after that had brought urgent letters from his mother beseeching him to re- turn, but before he could do so his father had

passed away. "You must be wet—and cold," said Mrs. Nugent, after a pause, with a mother's solici- tude. "You should change your clothes at once." "It would take more than a 'soft day' in old Ireland to harm me now, mother," he answered, laughing. "We shall just have a good chat here before I think of anything else." She smiled, somehow pleased at his do- ; cisiveness.

"You must have your way, I suppose," she said. " But draw a chair to the fire while we ttilk. Patsy "—for the old man had come into the room and was walking about fussily, pretending to use a duster—" get dinner served as soon as possible, for Mr. Desmond must be hungry after his journey." Patsy went out, and then mother and son

sat chatting before the peat fire, the dull glow of which was grateful enough even on ' that July day, for the wind that had brought the rain was from the east. "Now that you have come back to me, Desmond, and are the last of my dear ones," said Mrs. Nugent, wistfully, when they had . been talking for some time, "will you not settle down contentedly in the old home ? " Desmond got up and went to the window. "How could I live here from clay to day?" he said, gazing at the rain-soaked outlook. And, indeed, the neglected lawn and what- ever view there was of the flat country, edged by the low hills that lost themselves in mist, was not exhilarating. "Why, mother, to live in such a place, with no object in life, would soon drive me out of my mind. After the • energetic times I've passed, I'm not the sort of man to settle down to loafing about here with a fishing-rod or a gun, merely try- ing to kill time. My poor father had to sell out the land to save this place at all and leave you something. If we still had the tenants, there might have been something to do looking after them. But now! Mother, how can you think I could keep myself alive here! " "After having lost you for a third of your life you won't stay with me now? " said Mrs. Nugent, dismayed. "I thought you would do up. the .old_ home and-"

" Certainly, mother," he interrupted; "I intend to renovate Fairy Hall until it will be the nicest place in the county, and then you and I shall spend a few weeks here every summer—unless we let it permanently. And that would be better, for then you could come with me to London—"

"I shall never let this old home go into the hands of strangers," replied his mother, with quiet firmness. "I had hoped your plan would be the very reverse of what you sug- gest—that you would be satisfied to spend an occasional week or two away." "You disappoint me, mother—you really do ! " said Desmond. " I had promised my- self the happiness, of showing you a little of the great world. I had planned to give you a good time in some pleasant place—" This place will always be the pleasantest one in all the world for me, dear," she re- joined. "Even the cruel sorrows that have come to me have been tempered by the memory of more happiness here than has fallen to the lot of most women."

"Well, if you must stay here, you must," said her son, rather disconsolately. "At any rate, the place will be made as nice as pos- sible—l'll see to that. And anything else I can do for you, mother, I shall do." • "I desire little for myself, Desmond," she said, in a soft voice, after a pause, "13ut have hoped and prayed that I could pass oh to you Ow of my sense of happiness here, as the best qf a motbeen blessings. And how

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 10, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 10, 1913.

(Bull's Head) lost to A. E. Lindley by a solitary point. The issue was not decided until 32 ends had been played. Andrews secured the block and ran the score to 10-3 at the 11th end, but at this juncture Lindley found his land and secured two doubles and a single in the next three ends. Andrews got away again, and at the 21st end the game was 17-11 in his favour. Lindley showed good judgment of land and length, and at the 29th end he peeled with 18. The game now became intensely exciting, and the odds were in favour of the Warrington maa. Singles only were the order and the scores were again equal when. each player wanted one. Playing his woods well, Lindley landed one wood amidst tumultuous applause.

H. Eyes (Bull's Head) had no sweet thing on with J. Howarth, although he finally won by eight chalks. Eyes led 18-5 at the 20th end, but Howarth got the block and teduce6 the lead to one of 19-13 at the 27th end. Eyes won with two singles on the 28th and 29th ends.
A. Gleave (Bull's Head) had hard lines in his game with Entwistle, for he kept within three points of his opponent all the way, only to lose by 17-21 on the 27th end.

div.head: RYLANDS MAGNIFICENT VICTORY__
div.p: RYLANDS MAGNIFICENT VICTORY__

It was only on three individual games that the ironworkers had to knuckle under to their opponent, the players to lose being S. Massey, W. Roughley (Capt.) and W. Langley. One was really surprised to see Langley go down, for under normal conditions he is one of the finest players in these parts.
II and J. Langley had only to send the woods on the green to beat their opponents, as the retults show.

A tight game was played between G. Shaw (jun.), and G. Berry (Peel Green), for it took 33 ends to com- plete. They peeled at 10, 11, 14, 17, and at the 30th end the score was 18 each. Berry landed a single on the next end, but Shaw meant business, and with a double and a single won the game by two points.
A. Poirette (Peel Green) waa in a sorry plight when he failed to record a chalk against T. Humphreys, who, leading 11-0 at the 17th end, was given the game.
In the majority of the other games the local men had sweet things on and they have every confidence for the second round. They are a well-organised set of players and are deserving of success.

div.head: WARRINGTON _CEMETERY WIN EASILY_
div.p: WARRINGTON _CEMETERY WIN EASILY_

The Lower Broughton men from the Griffin Hotel would have an uninspiring tale to tell when they arrived home from the ITimston Green. They met an altogether superior class .of players, and it was only on five games that victories were recorded in their favour.
W. J. Woods (Cemetery) played well against J. S. Kay, but, after leading 17-10 at the 20th end, he slackened down in his play and lost by two points.
P. F. Ainsworth (Griffin) had to play hard to defeat A. Forster, who had no luck at all, but had to exercise the utmost skill to secure the chalks he did.
W. Butterworth (Cemetery) gave R. Walmsley a good run. He led 18-14 at the 24th end, but after Walmsley peeled with 19 on the 29th end, the player landed a double by which he won.
-- The interest in the other games was keenly mani- fested and all were agreed that the best team won.

Much practice has been put in lately by local bowie's end the greens adjoining the various hotels in the town have been well patronised.

We think the suggestion made at the Council meeti ing on Tuesday that at least one of the municipa greens in the town should be allocated exclusively to ladies one afternoon each week, a very good one. Alderman Bolton's attempted joke about the Liberal Club was no doubt inspired by the fact that under the club's auspices several successful ladies' mains have been conducted. At the ladies' competitions we have attended an atmosphere of genuine sportsmanship has been evident and the ladies have shown themselves skilful exponents of the game.
We would also suggest that mixed mains be organised and thus the women would have the benefit of receiv- ing several hints from the male trundlers. " THUMB BIAS."

COUNTY CRICKET. Lancashire open the season on Whit Monday with the great match against Yorkshire. A good and attractive side will do duty for the County Palatine, especially when Spooner, Macleod, and Brooke are able to play, as they hope to do in several matches. Unfor- tunately Brooke is the only one of the three likely to appear in the opening match. The appearance in the trial match last week of J. King, a Horwich player, in A. H. Hornby's side, was looked to with some interest. King is a left-hand bowler with e natural swing in towards the batsman, and last year one or two good judges considered him as fast as Brearley. This season, however, his pace appears to have declined a little, and his twelve overs yielded 40 runs and no wicket. His first appearance, Therefore, wai not a success, but an extended trial may show him in a better light. A young player named Hallows, of Little Lever, a nephew of the late James Hallows, whose career for the county proved unfortunately brief, made a very promising debut. It was a notable achievement to score 19 and to come out as much the most successful bowler in the match, with five wickets for 36 runs. W. Tyldesley was the highest scorer of the day Iwith 56 not out. He has all the qualities of a big- innings batsman. Ernest Tyldesley, a really stylish run-getter, also made a good start with a score of 29, and L. Oliver, who opened the batting, made 55. Oliver, who plays regularly for Derbyshire, and is also a member of the Manchester Club, is a really attractive left-hand batsman, particularly strong on the on drive,

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
The Northern Union.
HUDDERSFIELD WIN THE LEAGUE CHAMPIONSHIP.

Huddersfield on Saturday at Wakefield became the League champions for the second year in succession by defeating Wigan by 29 points to 2. The previous weeks at Leeds Huddersfield won the Northern Union Cup, so they now share with Broughton Rangers, Hunslet, and Halifax the honour of winning the double event in the same season. They had a much easier task against Wigan than they experienced against Warrington in the cup final, and during the second half they made the Lancashire team look very weak.

. -- It was not until they had gets lead of about a dozen pointz. that Huddersfield began to develop their proper game and then the spectators witnessed some delightful football. The ball was scarcely ever still, and the whole team took part in passing movements which completely bewildered the Wigan players. So feeble did the Wigan tackling become that in the last five minutes Rosenfeld was allowed to score a couple of tries. There was not the slightest doubt after the first ten minutes as to which side would win, but Wigan's play in the first half gave promise of a much better finish. The Wigan passing, however, was not up to its usual standard. The Huddersfield forwards, splendidly led by Clark and Gronow, were in great form and their fine rushes completely threw Gleave and Thomas off their game. Clark played his finest game this season, and besides scoring three tries, took part in almost every other successful movement. HUDDERSFIELD'S RETURN HOME.

The Huddersfield team had a great reception when they returned home with the League Cup on Saturday night, and similar scenes were repeated as occurred the previous week when they took home from Leeds the Northern Union Cup. The team were entertained to dinner at the George tiotel,and when Wagstaff appeared at one of the hotel windows with both cups the crowd chaered themselves hoarse.

div.head: WORKS COMPETITION FINAL
div.p: WORKS COMPETITION FINAL

St. Halens Cable Co. Team Score a Smart but Narrow Victory. Finalists for the third time, the Pearson and Knowles rugby team have again failed to land the cup given by the Warrington Football Club in their works competi- tions. The forgemen lost to the Cable Co.'s team by a goal to nil on a wretched ground on Saturday. The teams were :

P. & K.—Full back, John Spencer; three-quarter back, P. Smith, Joe Grounds, W. Ashtou, J. Lee • half backs, Thos. Savage, Algy Stokes; forwards, J. Hayes, J. Harrop, E. Holbrook, G. Curless, J. Jones, and E Smart.

Cable.—Full back, Tweedle (capt.) ; three-quarter backs, Bradshaw, Grace, Moffat, Barnes ; half-oacks, Siddall, Summertield ; forwards, Graham, Gleave, Bowden, Barton, Woods and Mercer. The referee was Mr. G. Moore, of Runcorn. Heavy rain felt as the teams entered the field, before only a moderate gate. Early ou the Cable men pressed bard, but were all nerves " when near the danger zone. The forgemen got impatient and tried to force matters. After a splendid movement amongst the backs. Grounds and Ashton raced away past the Cable forwards. Tweedle, who made a brilliant effort to save the situa- tion, which was looking serious, slipped near the line, but the worthy wingman of the;forge team was grounded just in time. Another second, and first blood would nave been drawn by the P. and K. men. After about twenty-five minutes mud larking, the ground was a guagmire, and decent football was impossible. Several chances were missed by both sides, and the interval came with a blank score.

On resuming the Cable team became aggressive and Mercer made a splendid run, only to be tackled just in time by Tweedle. Play was now chiefly near the Cable line, the ironworkers showing grim determina- tion, but the pressure was relieved somewhat by the Cable backs who broke away. The forgeman renewed the attack, but again the Cable men cleared their lines in a capital manner. Their weakest spot was in the half- backs, who were very slow. Tweedle was playing a great game at back, and was responsible for several remarkable clearances. Although they pressed during practically the whole of the second half, the forgemen could not get over. In the latter stages the Cable men had their chances and, to say the least. of it, made more of the few opportunities they got than did their opponents. Just before the call of time, they were awarded a penalty near the line for offside. Grace gained the plaudits of the crowd when he kicked a beautiful goal. Final : Cable, 1 goal (two points) ; P. and K., nil. PRESENTATION OF TUE CUP.

From the grand stand, Mr. Thos. Locker (president of the Warrington Football Club), who was supported by a member of the club officials, presented the cup to the captain of the winuing team. He said the contest had bren a good Poe, and it was only a pity that there were not two trophies, as both teams had played equally bard. While coneratulating the Cable team; they must sympathise with tho P. and K. men, for that was the third time they had been unsuccessful in the final. It was pleasing to see a new team come up—(hear, hear)— it would be encouraging to the other works to come and do likewise. (Applause). Mrs. Locker than banded the watches to the members of the teams and had words of congratulation for the winners and encouragement for the losers.

div.head: STANDARD OF LIFE
div.p: STANDARD OF LIFE
MR. J. B. MARTINDALE ADVOCATES A MINIMUM.
Wheat Prices to fix Wages.

Mr. J. B. Martindale, prospective Liberal candidate for the Widnes division, is a courageous young man with a large store of optimism. Consequently the stiff fight which he has undertaken in that Tory strong- hold does not, in the least, dismay him—in fact his vigorous and convincing advocacy,of thetew Liberalism is maki6g such an impression on the constituency that it is now generally admitted that Colonel Hall Walker stands more than a sporting chance of being unseated when the next election comes. Mr. Martin- dale is a favourite with Warrington audiences, for he has a blunt and straightforward way of putting things, and his speeches are lightened with happy humorous touches and stories which point a moral. On Monday evening Mr. Martindale gave the War- rington Progressive Labour League a splendid send- off on its summer campaign by addressing a large and enthusiastic meeting at the Old Mill, Bridge Foot.

div.head: MINIMUM STANDARD OF LIFE.
div.p: A MINIMUM STANDARD OF LIFE.

The most striking part of his address was that in which he declared himself in favour of the enactment of a minimum standard of existence. He felt confident that we would never have a really satisfactory country until we laid it down that there was a certain line of existence, below which no deserving citizen should be allowed to fall. Such a standard might work hardly with some people, but he contended that industries which could not afford to pay the wage necessary to provide the workman with a minimum standard of exist- ence would be better done away with. They were of no use to this country, because they were existing on lines which should be relegated to the dark ages—on the sweat of people who ha ato go to an early grave. He did not think it was possible, at the moment, to intro- duce a Minimum Wage Bill which should have a schedule, but he had a cut and dried scheme which he thought would work perfectly u ell and smoothly. He suggested the appointment of a Royal Com- mission to inquire into the working conditions in all parts of England, and decide what was the lowest wage that could be paid in relation to the price of wheat. As the price of wheat advanced wages should rise automatically, and they would no longer have the absurdity of wages standing still while food prices went up, or of wages rising slowly while prices advanced quickly. If they supported the new Liberalism, it would not be very long before we had in operation in this country a minimum wage standard which would prevent Many strikes. HOUSES OR RACEHORSES?

Emphasising the necessity of housiug reform, Mr. Martindale said a scheme was in preparation and they might depend upon it that the Government would not waste moneyfon proposals which would involve doles to landlords. Under the recent Tory measure, the money asked for would have gone as a subsidy to purchase land at unreasonable prices. Did the workers want national funds to go in bricks and mortar or in race horses? When the Government had completed the laud valuation, they would be able to get land at a reasonable price, and then they would have a housing scheme. They must build the dwellings of the workers in such places and under such conditions as would ensure plenty of fresh air. "A place like Widnes, " declared Mr. Martindale, " is not suit- able for workingmen to live in. I would not like to live in the centre of that town ; the smells are some- thing awful. I don't know whether the odour of sanctity is there ; but certainly there are a great many odours which I don't like." (Laughter.) Mr-Martin- dale expressed astonishment that so many people could imagine that tenement dwellings were a suitable solu- tion of the housing difilcuity. He wondered how they would like to live in those barrack-like buildings.

div.head: REAL PATRIOTS.
div.p: THE REAL PATRIOTS.

Mr. Martindale claimed that the Liberal party, in their great social schemes, had had the noblest con- ception of Empire before them. They had been build- ing up a healthy nation and enabling people to live under better conditions. No nation could progress and no Empire retain its glory unless it paid attention to the people who constituted that Empire. Thb Liberal party had, therefore,been the greatest patriots. Lord Roberts was going about pleading for conscrip- tion. Lord Roberts was in his dotage. He (the speaker) said most emphatically that if, in a War- rington business concern, they had a partner who, at the age of eighty, wanted to reorganise that business, they would not give his opinions very much consideration. Tney would recommend him a tour round the world. (Laughter.) Mr. Martindale went on to urge the workers not to countenance anything that would bring conscription into England. He would fight it, not merely because he thought compulsion was bad, but because he believed we had ample defences at the present time. Our Territorials were quite sufficient and they would be very much more satisfactory if the people who were talking about National Service would devote their energies to assisting them. (Applause.)

div.head: ALTRINCHAM CONTEST.
div.p: THE ALTRINCHAM CONTEST.

Referring to the present plight of the Tory party, Mr. Martindale asked where they stood on the question of Tariff Reform. The Tory candidate for the Altrincham division said : "I would tell my Free Trade friends that I am not a Protectionist, although I am a Tariff Reformer." That meant: "Put the loathsome word at the hack. lam not going to have anything to do with it." Where did Mr. Hamilton stand on the old Tory policy of "two jobs for every man" and "keep the foreigner out ? " Moreover, he did not stand alone, for there were actually Tory members of Parliament now who were avowed Free Traders. There was not one glimmer of hope for the Tory party, notwithstand- ing their protestations of unity. There had been no Tory gains in the by-elections this year. There had been one Liberal gain and two Free Trade gains.

div.head: MARCONI COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE MARCONI COMMITTEE.

They had a Marconi Committee and the Tories seemed to have been delighted with all the nonsense that had been talked there. It reminded him (Mr. Martindale) of one of the low class music halls of years gone by, where they were impudent at the expense of everybody who happened to be in a little better position than them- selves. Touching upon the insurance Ant, Mr. Martin- dale said Liberals were content to rely upon the verdict of the people concerning that measure. He felt confident that in Warrington, as in other industrial centres, they already realized that the benefits were not fictionary, but were in actual being and could be obtained when the necessity arose.

NO DETAILS FOR. RADICALS. Alluding to the fiscal question, Mr. Martindale asked. Is Mr. Harold Smith a Free Trader yet? (Laughter.) Well, they must give him time. They were all drifting that way nowadays. (Laughter.) The Tory party had hidden Tariff Reform for the time being, in the hope that they would obtain more votes at a future general election. Their only policy at present was "Turn the Government out ! " When people asked: "But what afterwards ? " Lord Derby immediately replied that "he hoped no member of Parliament would give those Radicals any details." (Laughter.) Of course, when Radicals got hold of details they had a nasty habit of analybing them. Laughter.) The Tariff Reformers had been running down our country as much as possible. If the Tariff Reform League had been anything at all, it had been the moat disloyal institution that we had bad for many a year. They had been running down our trade, our workers, our methods of employment, and finally they had begun to run down the House of Commons. Yet a fortnight hence they would be addressing Empire Day meetings and saying what a glorious thing the British Empire was. They seemed to forget that the British Empire was founded or. something very solid, for if their arguments were true that foundation must have been dissipated long ago. Free Trade had justified itself over and over again, and not least in the Budget for 1913. Our present system had financed the country and had enabled us not only to find many millions for the Navy but to apply over twenty millions to social reform. (Applause.) There was not a Protective system in the world under which raw materials came in free.

div.head: ULSTER'S MOCK HEROICS.
div.p: ULSTER'S MOCK HEROICS.

Referring to Home Rule, Mr. Martindale said the mock heroics of Ulster had come to nothing. The Home Rulers had actually won a seat in Ulster and there were more Home Rule than Unionist members in that province at the present time. He saw it was proposed to take a detachment of men from Liverpool to help the Ulsterites to fight. He imagined Mr. Harold Smith would be in at that. (Laughter.) He was a very great man at dressing up. (Laughter.) Last year he was one of those marvellous knights who went jousting at a tournament. (Laughter.) No doubt he would make a very fine admiral when the fleet set sail for Ulster. (Laughter.) The Home Rule Bill appealed more and more to all reasonable classes of the community and was making converts month by month. Alluding to Welsh Disestablishment, Mr. Martindale contended that the measure would be in the best interests of Church life and that the Welsh people were fully entitled to home rule in religious matters. Mr. Martindale also dealt with electoral anomalies, and said the Government were determined that all men should have equal rights of citizenship. (Applause.) Mr. M. LLEWELLYN presided over the meeting and said the time had come when the workers should assert their manhood, and on that ground alone claim their fair share in the government of the country. (Applause.)

div.head: WHERE IS THE MEMBER?
div.p: WHERE IS THE MEMBER?

Mr. E. WYNNE JONRS referred to the determination of the League to oust the present member for War- rington who, he contended, misrepresented, the electors of Warrington. Speaking of licensing reform, he said that if there was to be any monopoly in licences it should belong to the State and not to the individual. Conservative majority ll9 Candidates: Mr. L. Kay-Shuttleworth (L).: Mr. G. C. Hamilton (C). Nominations, Tuesday, May 20. Polling, Wednesday, May 28. THE LIBERAL CHAMPION. Mr. Lawrence Kay-Shuttleworth, who is 25 years of age, and is described as a gracile young giant of sis feet five or thereabouts, was enthusiastically adopted by the Liberals. He announced himself as a warm supporter of His Majesty's Government.
MR. KAY-SHUTTLEWORTH AT LYMM.
PROUD OF THE GOVERNMENT RECORD

In his fight for the true principles of Liberalism in the Altrincham by-election Mr. Kay-Shuttleworth has undoubtedly the strong and holid support of the numerous Liberals in the Lymm district, as evidenced by the fact that on Wednesday evening the Drill Hall, where a meeting in support of his candidature was held, was crowded to overflowing, and the keenest enthusiasm prevailed. Mr. Kay-Shuttleworth was sup- ported by his brother, the Hon. E. Kay-Shuttleworth, and many stalwart Liberals. Mr. J. D. B. Smith presided, and ,others on the platform were: Mr. P. M. Oliver (prospective Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division), Messrs. W. E. Thompson, W. T. Moss, H. Cliff, J. H. Mather, C. J. Barnes and D. Daniels; Miss Welford (president of the Lymm Women's Liberal Association), and Miss White. READY TO FIGHT THE FIGHT OF THE __ MASSES.

Mn. Kav-Snurruwoa7ru—c—re—a—ted a favourable impres- sion, for one saw in the frank open features a sincerity of purpose and a determination to win the seat, which could not fail to inspire the confidence of any true-hearted Liberal. In an unostentatious manner, without any of the irritating tub-thumping tactics usually adopted by Tory speakers, Mr. Kay-Shuttle- worth clearly put to the audience his electioneering programme. He was proud of the Government's numerous victories in the cause of progress and in bettering the conditions of the working-classes, and if returned to the House of Commons he would co all he could to help to win the battle for the masses. A TRUE DEMOCRAT. The CHA ERMAN said Mr. Kay-Shuttleworth's thorough democratic views stamped him as a Liberal whom they would be proud to support. (Loud cheers.) A resolution supporting Mr. Kay-Shuttleworth was unanimously carried.

div.head: OUOTATIONS : AND THEM USE AND ABUSE.
div.p: OUOTATIONS : AND THEM USE AND ABUSE.
{C OP YRIGHT.I

"By necessity, by proclivity, and by delight we all quote," said Emerson. "Classical quotation is the ,parole of literary men all over the ,world," said Dr. Johnson_ in his slightly more ponderous way. Both statements are obviously- exaggerated, both contain an equally obvious quantum •of truth. To exploit the obvious is tiresome, but one may be permitted at least to rejoice that classical quotation is no longer strictly.. "the parole" 611 literary m:.>ll. Modern journalism is Insufferable enough as it is, but if one perpetu- ally had to drag in more or less appropriate quotations from the classics it ,would really be too sickening. Classical quotation as "the parole" of the literary .went out with the three bottle

men. Emerson i;o-n-s-oni'ider line, for by neces- sity we do all grote. Who can say ;with con - Vence that 1i defithless words have not already been utt-red by another? In proclivity and in ,!elight lie dangers—the easy mis-quotation, the gloriously inappropriate pne.

div.head: STANDING TEMPTATION.
div.p: STANDING TEMPTATION.

It cannot be denied, however, that the quota- tion is a standing temptation to which all of ua F necumb now and then. Occasionally it is really ,ISeful. Witness the English traveller at a. French railway station, who, wishing to explain to a porter that he drsired his bag to remain upon the platform until he returned to fetch it, and being handicapped by a lack of French, had resource to Latin: •• Requiescat in pace: liesur- gam !" he said pointing- to the bag. The intelli- gent perter expanded the palms of his hands and "Oui. oui, monsieur, parfaitement! ca reste là, ft moiNieur reviendra."

That is an episode of sheer joy that happens to few of us. It illustrates, exquisitely, the use of a quotation. Let me now tell the sorrowful story of a friend of mine, an otiose, opulent, bell- pushing person. An editor in short. Tie has an inv,qerate habit of quoting from Kennedy's Latin Grammar. If one remarks on the pre- vaienee of airships or hard felt hats • he coughs a little pompously and rolls forth: " Tempora mutantur nos et mutainur in illis." If one says one's had a good time 11- ,-:ighs reminiscently and says, "Et ego in Arcadia vixi." After Mr. Kruger's death he was heard to say. "De mortuis nil nisi bonum " no less than seventeen times in four clavo.

div.head: AIIUSE OF QUOTATION.
div.p: THE AIIUSE OF QUOTATION.

That is sad, but not uncommon. It illustrates the abuse of quotation in one of its simplest. but not least painful forms. If once the habit iO cultivated there is no knowing into what morasses one may not wander. There was once a certain Presbyterian minister (according to Mr. G. W. E. But=sell) who was called upon ua- expectedly to prefieh before Queen Victoria. Fed upon a too exuberant diet of quotation and mixed metaphor, and transported by the grat occaPion, he burst forth into the follow- ing peroration Grant that as she grows to be an old wontan she may be made a new man: and that in all righteous causes she may go forth beforf., her people like a he-goat upon the mountain."

..... This should teach the novice to eschew floridity in quotation. But, alas, there are pit- falls for the simpler-minded too. It is to Mr. Russell again (himself a real master in the art of apt quotation) that I am indebted for an inscription placed by a worthy man upon some benches on the sea front:— .

div.head: These Seats
div.p: These Seats
Were presented to the Town of Shingleton by Joseph Buggin J.P. for the Borough. "The Sea is His and He made it."

For crispness in textnal quotation, by the !way, think "Lean Hard," ,which once greeted rile in a Welsh bedroom, is difficult to beat! Moreover, "Watch and Pray," in a bathroom, Eeems excellently inappropriate. TIED -SNARE OF MISQUOTATION.

Apart from the danger of a mis+applied quota- tion there exists the even more frequent snare of the misquotation. It was Byron, I think. who referrea to the gentleman "with just enough of learning to misquote." and if I give one or two instances of familiar misquotations I trust it will induce a dcsire for humility and verification of reference. •

Who among9t 116 for example, has not re- ferred complacently enough, to "the .sere and yellow leaf F" And yet what Shakespeare .wrote was "My 'May of life i fall'n into the ee.ar, the yellow leaf." Shakespeare, again, wrote of "The undiscovered country from whaselourne

No Traveller returns." And yet we insist upon saying "the bourne from which. no traveller returns." And. "Water, water everywhere And not a drop to drink" is wrong., for the last line should be: "Nor any drop to drink."
So, too, it will stagger most of us to know that it is not the lion that is to lie down with the lamb, but the wolf that i to dwell with the lamb.
Moreover, though it may be true that "Music bath charms to soothe a savage beat," we have no literal authority for it, for Congreve (and not Shakespeare) referred to "breasts" and not " beasts."

STOCKTON. HEATH. SUDDEN DEATH.—Mr. T. Ridgway held an inquest at the Stockton Heath Police Station on Saturday after- noon, on the body of Elizabeth Ann Jones (21), wife of William Thomas Jones, 16, Eastford-road, Stockton Heath. The evidence showed that deceased had been suffering from rheumatism in her knee for a fortnight, and had been under the care of Dr. Binns. She appeared to be progressing favourably until Friday morning. About 11 o'clock she called her husband upstairs to turn her over in bed. After he had done so she seemed to gasp for breath and then died.—Dr. Binns said he bad conducted a post-mortem examination and found a clot of blood, the size of a walnut, in the heart.—A verdict of " Death from natural causes" was returned. PETER WALKER AND SON, WARRINGTON AND BURTON LTD., AhD THEIR WARRINGTON WORKMEN. Liverpool Workers and the Warrington Strike. Sympathy Refused. Liverpool (says the "Daily Dispatch ") did not until Saturday take any keen interest in the dispute among the labourers at Warrington in Messrs. Peter Walker's brewery, but the desire of the latter to enlist the sympathy of 'Liverpool workingmen by means of a demonstration in the city, and the scattering broad- cast of a circular explaining the alleged grievances of the men and attacking the firm, has had just the opposite effect to that intended. The name of Walker is honoure3 in Liverpool. It is associated with the splendid art gallery, the gift of the late Sir A. B. Walker; it has given impetus to many movements for the public good, and it is inscribed on funds for the support of wives and children dependent when the breadwinner has been called to do service in war time for his country, and for the provision of aocessities when sickness or unemployment as brought a crisis in a workingman's home. Keen resentment is therefore shown in regard to strong statements contained in the circular, which are declared to be absolute falsehocds. It is pointed out that Messrs. Walker have alwys led the way in the standard for labourers' wages. The lowest wage among labourers is 225. a week, and the highest is 28s. In addition, the men get 2s. worth of beer each week, nine days' holiday each year with pay, and an excursion each year for which they are given a railway ticket and 10s. in money. The dispute is apparently in regard to the recogni- tion of one union, and the directors, while willingly engaging men whom they consider suitable for the business whether they are trade unionists or not, cannot pledge themselves to engage only those men who belong to one union. At the Liverpool Court of Bankruptcy on Monday, Mr. Registrar Cooper had before him the public examination of Daniel Horrocks, licensee of the Queen's Head public-house, Sutton Ork, St. Helens, whose debts were returned at £177 17s. id., and free assets £2B ss. 7d. In reply to the Official Receiver, he stated that the closing of the Sutton Glassworks had caused his failure, and he had continued the business in the hope that they would be re-opened, and 'so things had gone on from had to worse. tie was a blacksmith's striker, and had £2OO of his savings in the Post Office Savings Bank in 1904, when he took the Horseshoe Inn,Whiston. He lost money there, and about six years ago he took the Queen's Head. and then had about £137 of his savings left. While his wife had been managing the public-house business he had workei at his trade. The examination was closed.
